descs.en: The clingiest psychology student alive dates the coldest criminal profiler in the city. Then she finds the notebook where he records her.

synopsis.title: Synopsis
synopsis.content:
Yen Si-Jie sits in the second row of a criminal-psychology seminar and asks the guest lecturer forty questions. Arthur Chen profiles the city’s worst people for a living, and he answers thirty-nine. The fortieth, in the car park at dusk, is whether she can kiss him.

She sends forty messages a day. He answers every one at nine at night, in order. She leaves a hair clip in his white flat, then a cardigan, then herself, and he clears a drawer.

Then she finds his notebook, full of her moods in neat columns. Is she his girlfriend or his experiment? And why is his newest case circling closer to her?

Sunshine and the cold one · Clingy heroine · A profiler in love · Ongoing

authorNote.title: Author Note
authorNote.content:
Arthur’s notebook isn’t creepy. It’s his clumsy way of learning how to love someone, because nobody ever taught him. ‘I’m not studying you. I’m learning you.’

It’s playful and intense, with a thriller running under a sweet romance. The man who reads everyone can’t read her in bed, and she makes him say what he wants.

chapters.title: Forty Questions
chapters.desc: Arthur Chen gives the seminar on what violent men do next. Yen Si-Jie asks forty questions and he answers thirty-nine. The fortieth, in the car park at dusk, is whether she can kiss him.
chapters.content:
Arthur Chen had given the same seminar eleven times, and nobody had ever counted the questions until Yen Si-Jie.

She told him the number later. She told him a great many things later, most of them at volume. But on that Wednesday in October, in the new law building with its glass walls and its foyer that made every conversation sound important, he only knew that a girl in the second row had a notebook, three pens, a coffee and the expression of someone who’d already decided the day was going to be about her.

He began at ten, without notes. He always did. The programme said THE CRIMINAL MIND: PATTERNS, MOTIVES AND THE MOMENT BEFORE THE ACT, and under it his name, and he’d agreed to it because the dean had asked twice and the task force liked its profilers to be seen being reasonable in public.

“People ask me what makes an offender dangerous. They expect intelligence, or violence, or a bad childhood. Those matter. The more useful question is what he believes he’s allowed to do,” he said.

The room wrote it down. The girl in the second row wrote it down and then put her hand up.

“Can I ask questions during, or only at the end?”

“At the end.”

“What if it’s relevant to the slide?”

A few people laughed. He looked at her properly then: dark hair falling out of a clip, a cream cardigan, a face that hid nothing at all. Beside her sat a quiet girl in black with her notebook turned towards herself, writing in small exact letters, and behind them two more faces so like the first that for half a second he thought the light was doing something strange. One of them was wearing sunglasses indoors and a cap pulled low and was watching him, he realised, the way he watched people.

“Then it had better be relevant,” he said.

It was relevant. It was relevant eleven times before the break. She asked whether a man who followed a woman for months without threatening her was less dangerous than one who threatened her outright, and he said not necessarily, and she asked why, and he said that the absence of a threat didn’t establish the absence of intent. She asked how you told a dangerous man from an obsessive one. He said evidence. She said that was a short answer for such a long question, and he said it was the important part, and the room laughed again, and she smiled at him like a person who’d been handed a present.

Halfway through the morning she offered an answer instead of a question. It was confident and possibly a little too confident, and he let her finish before he said anything.

“That’s one interpretation. What evidence would support it?”

She narrowed her eyes at him. “You’re asking me to justify my answer.”

“I’m asking you to tell what you know from what you’ve assumed.”

The sister in the cap looked down at her own notebook fast, and he had the distinct impression she was hiding a laugh.

✦ ✦ ✦

At the break he stood by the window with a paper cup of the faculty’s terrible coffee and didn’t look at the second row. He’d learned long ago that people told you most when they thought you’d stopped watching, and he’d also learned that it was rude.

He noticed anyway. The girl, whose name on the attendance sheet was YEN SI-JIE, PSYCHOLOGY, FINAL YEAR, had adopted the quiet one in black in the space of a quarter of an hour, and was steering her and the two sisters towards the canteen by the elbow. The quiet one didn’t look like a person who was easily steered. She went.

In the afternoon he put them in groups with invented case files. He stopped beside the quiet girl’s table because she’d written, that morning, a line about possession as control that he’d read upside down from the lectern and not forgotten. She disagreed with the case file’s conclusion before he’d finished reading it to her. He said she wasn’t in psychology. She said computer science, and that people left traces. He said they did, and moved on, and heard Si-Jie kick her under the table.

Si-Jie had a question at the next table. Of course she did.

“If an offender’s behaviour is escalating, how do you know if it’s because he’s losing control or because he thinks he’s gaining it?”

It was a better question than any he’d been asked that year. He told her so, which he hadn’t meant to. The same behaviour could mean either, he said; you had to know what came before it. What he’d tried, and what had happened when he tried it.

“So the meaning is in the history.”

“Most of it.”

She wrote it down. Under it she drew a small arrow and wrote something else, and when he asked, because he couldn’t not, she turned the notebook round.

He falls in love with his own version of her.

“That isn’t a clinical term.”

“No.”

“It’s a simplification.”

“I know. But I’ll remember it,” said Si-Jie.

He looked at the sentence a beat longer than he should have. Then he went back to the front of the room and finished the session, and found that he remembered it too.

✦ ✦ ✦

When it broke up she came straight to the lectern, towing the sister in the cap by the sleeve.

“She’s been studying how you stand,” Si-Jie told him.

The sister turned on her. “Si-Jie.”

“You have.”

He looked at the sister. “And what have you learned?”

She considered him from under the brim. “That you don’t move unless you have a reason.”

It surprised a smile out of him, there and gone. Then he turned to Si-Jie, who was watching him with her chin up and her pens in her fist. “That’s a fair observation. Are you coming to the next one?”

“Is that an invitation?”

“It’s open to registered participants.”

“That’s a very academic way of saying yes.”

“Then register,” said Arthur Chen.

She laughed, out loud, delighted, and he packed his laptop and didn’t look up again until she’d gone.

“Thirty-nine,” she called from the door.

He did look up then. She was halfway out, one hand on the frame.

“Questions. You answered thirty-nine. I’m saving the last one.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He stayed late with the dean, and it was nearly dark when he came out of the side door into the staff car park at the bottom of the hill. The camphor trees along the path had gone black against the sky. Down the slope, three girls were walking towards the gate arm in arm, arguing about something with great energy, and as he unlocked his car one of them stopped dead, handed her bag to the sister beside her, and came across the tarmac towards him.

The other two stood under a lamp and watched with undisguised interest.

Si-Jie stopped a careful distance away. She’d taken the clip out of her hair. In the yellow light of the car park she looked younger than she had in the lecture theatre, and much more nervous, and she’d plainly decided to do this anyway.

“I said I was saving one.”

“You did.”

She held her notebook against her chest with both arms. “Number forty. Can I kiss you?”

He didn’t move. He’d been asked a great many things by a great many people in rooms with locked doors and recording equipment. He’d been lied to by professionals. Nobody had ever stood in front of him and said exactly what she wanted, without decoration, and then waited, looking up at him, for his answer and nothing else.

“You’ve known me for seven hours.”

“Seven hours and twenty minutes.”

“That isn’t long.”

“I don’t need two years to know if I want to kiss someone. And I’ve already told my sisters, so if you say no I’ll have to walk back over there,” said Si-Jie.

He looked past her at the two sisters under the lamp. The one in the cap lifted a hand. The other folded her arms.

He didn’t answer. It was the only one of her forty he didn’t answer, and she told him afterwards that she’d decided, standing there, that a man who didn’t say no was a man who meant something else. She came the rest of the way. She took a fistful of his jacket, rose up on her toes and kissed him: quick, warm, a little clumsy, tasting of the canteen’s terrible coffee.

He stayed absolutely still.

She let go. Her face had gone pink to the ears. “Well. That was nice. You’re not very responsive,” she said.

“Is that a complaint?”

“An observation.”

He recognised his own word. He looked at her mouth, and at her eyes, which were bright and determined and a little afraid, and he put one hand on her waist and bent his head and kissed her back. Slowly. Thoroughly. Giving her every second she needed to step away, and she didn’t take any of them; her hand curled tighter in his jacket and she made a small surprised sound against his mouth, and across the car park one of her sisters said something that sounded a lot like finally.

When he lifted his head she was still holding on.

“That was better,” she whispered.

He took his hand from her waist, not quickly. “You’re very direct.”

“Would you prefer I pretended I needed help with my books?”

“No.”

He opened the passenger door. She stared at it.

“You’re standing in a car park in the dark. Your sisters have your bag. Where do you live?” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

He drove her home. She talked the whole way: about her final-year project, about a professor who failed anyone a minute late, about her sisters, who were triplets, which he’d worked out, and about the eldest, who was an actress, which he hadn’t. He listened. He asked, once, why she wanted to study forensic work, and she said because she liked understanding people, and he said that understanding people wasn’t always pleasant, and she said she hadn’t said it would be.

Outside her building she got out, and then bent back down into the open door.

“Thank you for the lift, Mr. Chen.”

“Arthur.”

She went still, and then she smiled, slowly, the way people smile at something they mean to keep.

“Goodnight, Arthur,” said Si-Jie, and shut the door, and walked into her building without asking for his number.

He sat outside with the engine running for longer than a sensible man would have. He had a report to read before morning and an interview at nine and no intention whatsoever of seeing a twenty-year-old psychology student again. Someone knocked on the passenger window.

She was back, out of breath, her keys in one hand. He let the window down.

“Forty-one. I know I said forty. Can I have your number?” said Si-Jie.

He gave it to her. He didn’t decide to; it was out before the sensible part of him had finished objecting. She typed it in with her tongue between her teeth, said thank you very much, and ran back inside, and the door swung shut behind her.

His phone went before he’d reached the end of her road. He pulled over, and saved the number, and after a moment’s thought gave it a name.

Si-Jie (Question Forty): This is me. In case you were wondering who was going to text you at night.

Arthur: I know who this is.

Si-Jie (Question Forty): You remember me?

Arthur: You asked forty-one questions.

Si-Jie (Question Forty): You answered thirty-nine.

Arthur: I remember the others too.

A long pause. Three dots that came and went twice.

Si-Jie (Question Forty): Coffee? Saturday?

He looked at his calendar. He had a meeting at three on Saturday. He moved it.

Arthur: Three o’clock.

Si-Jie (Question Forty): It’s a date.

He read that, and didn’t correct her, and put the phone face up on the passenger seat where she’d been sitting, and drove home. He was good at recognising the start of a pattern. He knew what attachment looked like, and fixation, and the stories people told themselves about why they couldn’t stop.

He didn’t yet know he’d already started looking forward to Saturday.

chapters.title: Logical Reasons
chapters.desc: He writes down eleven reasons not to see her, and she answers every one in his office. He already knows her bus and her coffee order. Reason twelve ends against his office door, and she bites his lip.
chapters.content:
By half past nine on Thursday morning Arthur Chen had eleven reasons not to see Yen Si-Jie again, and he’d written them down, because a thing written down could be examined, and a thing in his head only went round.

1. She is a student.
2. She is four years younger than I am.
3. She has known me for one day.
4. My hours are unpredictable.
5. My work involves violent cases, and it comes home.
6. I can’t guarantee my own safety.
7. I can’t guarantee hers.
8. I am not good company during an investigation.
9. She is impulsive.
10. She wants a great deal of attention, and I am not in the habit of giving it.
11. I am not interested in a relationship.

It was on his desk on the sixth floor of the task force building, under a case file and beside a cup of black coffee that had gone cold. He read it through twice. Every line was true. He was satisfied with it as a document. His phone lit up beside it.

Si-Jie (Question Forty): Good morning, Arthur.

Si-Jie (Question Forty): You’re probably already at work.

Si-Jie (Question Forty): Did you sleep? I didn’t. I kept thinking about question forty.

He looked at the list. He looked at the phone. He’d seen the first message arrive at a quarter past eight and noticed, without meaning to, that it had come exactly seventeen minutes after the time she’d told him in the car she usually woke up.

Arthur: Good morning.

Si-Jie (Question Forty): HE LIVES.

Si-Jie (Question Forty): What did you have for breakfast?

Arthur: Breakfast.

Si-Jie (Question Forty): You’re so difficult. Are you busy today?

Arthur: Yes.

Si-Jie (Question Forty): How busy?

He typed Si-Jie, we need to talk about something, and read it back, and heard how it would sound, and sent it anyway, because it was accurate. The dots appeared and vanished and appeared.

Si-Jie (Question Forty): Are you breaking up with me?

He put the phone down on the list and leaned back in his chair. They’d known each other for a day. He hadn’t asked her out. She’d asked him, and he’d agreed to coffee, which wasn’t the same thing, and she was already asking whether he intended to end it.

Arthur: We aren’t together.

Si-Jie (Question Forty): Oh. So you’re not breaking up with me. Good.

He began, for the first time in his professional life, to understand why people in interview rooms asked for a lawyer.

✦ ✦ ✦

At a quarter to eleven reception rang up to say there was a young woman downstairs with a paper bag who said she was his friend.

Eugene Chak looked up from the next desk. Eugene had been on the task force for six years and in the next desk for three, and he had a long face and a short haircut and the deceptive calm of a man who’d decided long ago that the best way to find out anything was to wait.

“Friend,” said Eugene.

“A student.”

“From yesterday? The one who asked forty questions?”

Arthur stared at him. “How do you know about that?”

Eugene went back to his screen with an expression of perfect innocence. “The dean’s office rang to say thank you. The coordinator mentioned you’d been very patient with a girl in the second row. She said it was like watching someone try to stop the tide with a clipboard.”

Arthur picked up his jacket and went down.

She was standing by the fish tank in reception, peering at a sulky orange carp, in a different cardigan and the same clip, with a paper bag held in front of her in both hands. When she heard the lift she turned round and her whole face lit up, which was a thing he’d never once seen happen at the sight of him and didn’t know what to do with.

“Arthur!”

“You’re not supposed to be here.”

“I know. I brought you breakfast.”

“I’ve had breakfast.”

She held out the bag. “I know. You said. I brought it anyway.”

Inside was a sandwich, a small box of cut fruit and a bottle of unsweetened soy milk. He looked at the bottle.

“How did you know I drink this?”

“You don’t take sugar. You said so when I asked about your coffee. I extrapolated.”

“That isn’t how extrapolation works.”

“It’s how breakfast works,” said Si-Jie, and smiled at him.

The receptionist was watching them over her glasses with the quiet joy of someone who’d be telling this story at lunch. He took the bag.

“Upstairs,” he said.

“Are you going to interview me?”

“No.”

“Interrogate me?”

“I’m going to explain something.”

“That sounds serious.”

“It is.”

She followed him to the lift with every appearance of delight.

✦ ✦ ✦

His office was clean to the point of strangeness. She noticed it the way other people noticed a smell, and walked round it touching nothing, looking at everything: the empty desk, the filing cabinet, the board on the wall with its photographs turned face in, the window over the road. Then she sat down in the chair opposite his and folded her hands in her lap.

He didn’t sit. He’d meant to, and found he couldn’t, so he stood beside the desk with the list underneath the case file where she couldn’t see it.

“About yesterday,” he said.

“Yes.”

“I’m not suitable for a relationship.”

She waited. He went on, and found as he went that he was going through it in order, one to eleven, which he hadn’t intended either. His hours. The cases, which were violent and which followed him home. The fact that he might have to leave in the middle of a meal, or not ring for two days, or come home at three in the morning and not want to talk. That he wasn’t expressive, and didn’t send messages, and wouldn’t reassure anyone every few hours.

“All right,” said Si-Jie.

He’d expected an argument. He had a rebuttal ready for the argument.

“You’re a student. You’re in your final year. You have your own work and your own plans. I don’t want you arranging your life around someone you can’t predict.”

“That’s fair.”

“You don’t know me.”

“Then I’d like to.”

“I don’t know you.”

“Same answer.”

“You’re answering before I’ve finished.”

“Because I can see where you’re going. Sorry. Go on,” she said, and then pressed her lips together.

He went on. He told her that being attracted to someone and being suited to them were different things. She nodded. He told her she was impulsive, and that she’d kissed him after seven hours.

“Seven hours and twenty minutes.”

“That doesn’t improve it.”

“It makes it accurate.”

He told her that his work could become dangerous. That there’d been cases where an investigator was threatened, where a suspect became fixed on someone in a team, where families were drawn in. He said it more sharply than he meant to, and she stopped smiling and listened to all of it with her eyes on his face.

“I don’t want someone I care about anywhere near that,” he said.

She was quiet. “Is that a reason you don’t want to date me, or a reason you’re afraid to?” she said at last.

The question went in clean, the way the good ones did in an interview, and he heard himself answer it before he’d decided to.

“Both.”

“Thank you for telling me.”

He looked down at the desk. “There are more.”

“How many?”

“Eleven.”

She tilted her head. “Did you write them down?”

His hand stopped on the case file. It was a fraction of a second. She saw it; he watched her see it.

“You did. You made a list,” said Si-Jie, in a voice of wonder.

“It was a mental exercise.”

“On paper?”

“Si-Jie.”

“Can I see it?”

“No.”

She came round the desk. He moved the file an inch further over the list, which was the most incriminating thing he could have done, and she stopped and looked at the file and then at him with her whole face shining.

“You’re hiding it.”

“I’m working.”

“You’re adorable.”

“Don’t use that word.”

“Handsome, then.”

He turned his head away towards the window. It was a small movement. She caught it, as she seemed to catch everything, and her smile became frankly unbearable.

“Fine. Read me the last one. Number eleven,” she said.

He didn’t need the paper. “I’m not interested in a relationship.”

That one landed. He watched it land, and watched her take it, and look down at her hands for a second, and then look back up at him with a steadiness he hadn’t expected from someone who’d spent a morning texting him about breakfast.

“All right. That’s your decision,” she said.

She went and picked up her bag from the chair. Something in his chest went tight and dissatisfied in a way it had no business doing.

“That’s all?”

“What else?”

“You came here because you wanted to see me.”

“I did. And now I’ve seen you, and I know what you think.” She hitched the bag onto her shoulder and went to the door.

He watched her hand go out to the handle. There were several sensible things he could have said, and he didn’t say any of them.

“How are you getting back?”

She turned round. “Bus.”

He heard it come out of him in his reporting voice, the one he used in court. “The eighteen. You’ll want the one at twenty past, if your lecture’s at two. You take the eighteen because the stop’s nearer your faculty. You told me in the car. And your coffee’s an iced oat latte, less ice, no syrup. You told the woman at the canteen yesterday. Twice.”

Si-Jie stood still with her hand on the door.

“That’s a lot of information for someone who isn’t interested,” she said slowly.

“Knowing things about someone isn’t the same as pursuing them.”

She nodded gravely. “Of course. Very logical.”

She let go of the handle. She came back across the office, not quickly, until she was standing in front of him with her bag still on her shoulder and her chin up, and he realised he’d backed up a step and that the door to the corridor was shut behind him and he was standing against it.

“Have you got a reason twelve?” she said.

“No.”

She looked up at him. “Liar. You’re a profiler. You’ve got a reason for everything. What is it?”

He looked down at her. He’d spent the morning writing eleven true sentences. The twelfth was also true, and it was the only one that had never needed writing.

“That I want to kiss you,” said Arthur.

Her face changed. It went from triumph to something softer and much more frightened, and then she was the one who reached, and took hold of his tie, and pulled.

He’d meant it to be brief. A sensible decision: one kiss, and then his meeting, and then a long hard look at his own judgement. But she came up into it like someone who’d been waiting all morning, and when he began to draw back she followed him, and caught his lower lip between her teeth, and bit.

He stopped. He opened his eyes. She was looking up at him with a small satisfied gleam.

“Did you just bite me?”

“A little.”

“Why?”

“Because you were going to stop.”

“I was going to breathe.”

“You were going to leave. Those aren’t the same.”

He looked at her for a long, blank second against his own office door. Then he put his hand flat on the small of her back and kissed her again, without waiting to be asked, and this time it was nothing like sensible. Her bag slid off her shoulder and hit the floor. Her fingers went up into the short hair at the back of his neck. When he finally lifted his head they were both out of breath.

“You’re going to make me late,” he said.

“Good.”

“I have a meeting in four minutes.”

“Three. Saturday. Three o’clock. Don’t cancel,” said Si-Jie, looking at his watch upside down, and bent and picked up her bag, and straightened her cardigan, and opened the door behind him by reaching round him for the handle.

“I’ll tell you if something comes up.”

“That’s not a promise.”

“It’s an honest answer.”

She sighed enormously, and went, and turned at the end of the corridor and called “Have a good meeting!” loud enough for the whole sixth floor, and he stood in his own doorway and touched his lower lip, and it stung.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was two minutes late to the meeting, which had never happened. Eugene was already in his seat with a coffee and the case file open, and looked up as he came in, and kept looking.

“You’re late.”

“Two minutes.”

Eugene’s eyes travelled down an inch. “You’re never late. What happened to your lip?”

Arthur opened his folder. “Dry weather.”

Eugene said nothing at all, at length, and Arthur began the meeting. For forty minutes he talked about the case on the table: a man who rang a woman from a different number every night and said nothing, and whether that silence was a threat. He was exact. He was methodical. He was the same as he always was, except that halfway through his phone lit up under the table.

Si-Jie (Question Forty): I’m in class. Just wanted to say I liked seeing you.

Si-Jie (Question Forty): Also sorry about your lip.

Arthur: You don’t sound sorry.

Si-Jie (Question Forty): I’m a bit sorry. I might do it again.

Eugene, across the table, watched his face for three full seconds and then wrote something on his pad and underlined it.

“Chen?”

“Go on,” said Arthur.

✦ ✦ ✦

At nine that night he was at home with the case file and the list. He’d read the file. He’d read the list again. Every reason on it was still true. He was still four years older and his hours were still impossible and his work still came home with him. She still deserved someone more available. His phone lit up.

Si-Jie (Question Forty): Goodnight, Arthur. Don’t work too late. I like you.

He looked at that for a while. Then he picked up his pen and, at the bottom of the list, under the eleventh reason, he wrote a twelfth.

12. I want to kiss her more than I should.

He considered it, and wrote one more.

13. She knows.

He typed I know, and deleted it, and sat with the phone in his hand like a fool.

Arthur: I like you too.

The reply came so fast she must have been holding the phone.

Si-Jie (Question Forty): I KNEW IT.

He put the phone down and the list in his drawer. He had eleven logical reasons not to see her, and by the end of Thursday he’d written two more, and neither of them had persuaded him to stop.

chapters.title: Clingy
chapters.desc: Forty messages a day, every one answered at nine, in order. His flat is white and empty until she makes a mess of it. Explicit: he describes her pulse aloud until she covers his mouth. Breakfast, weighed.
chapters.epigraph: “Thank you for letting me be clingy.”
chapters.content:
Arthur had a system. He read every message. He answered every message. And he answered them in order, at nine o’clock at night, when the day’s work was done and he could give them his attention, because a man who answered in the middle of a briefing was a man who wasn’t listening to either.

It had never been a demanding system. Before October he’d received perhaps four personal messages a day, three of them from his mother asking whether he’d eaten.

By the end of the month Si-Jie was averaging forty.

She sent pictures of her breakfast. She sent complaints about her supervisor, a man who returned drafts covered in green ink and the single word why. She sent the weather. She sent a ginger cat asleep on a bench outside the psychology building with the caption this is you, and then, four minutes later, no it isn’t, it’s friendlier. If he hadn’t answered in ten minutes she sent a row of question marks, and if he hadn’t answered in an hour she sent, without fail, are you alive.

He answered all of them. At nine. On the last Monday in October he sat down at his desk at home at one minute to the hour with his sleeves rolled up and a case file closed beside him, opened her name, and scrolled back to the morning.

Si-Jie (Question Forty): Good morning. Did you sleep? I dreamt about you but I can’t remember what happened. You were there though. Good enough.

Si-Jie (Question Forty): My eggs are ugly. Don’t laugh. I know you can’t see me but I can feel you laughing.

Si-Jie (Question Forty): How do you have your eggs? Never mind. I’ll ask in person.

Si-Jie (Question Forty): My supervisor wrote WHY next to my hypothesis. Just why. In green.

Si-Jie (Question Forty): If you’re late to a meeting do people wait for you? You look like someone people would be scared to start without.

Si-Jie (Question Forty): I’ve got a headache. Going home. Is coffee a good idea? No. Going to sleep.

Si-Jie (Question Forty): Actually. Arthur. I miss you.

Si-Jie (Question Forty): Don’t forget dinner. That’s all. I like you.

Si-Jie (Question Forty): Are you alive?

He answered them in order. Yes, he’d slept, adequately. He’d have liked to know what happened in the dream. Scrambled. People started without him; he preferred it. Her supervisor was asking whether her hypothesis followed from her literature review, and she should answer the question rather than the ink. Water, not coffee. Then he came to the last two and stopped.

Arthur: I’m alive. I had a late briefing. I’ve eaten. Have you?

The reply came three seconds after he sent it, which meant she’d been sitting with the phone in her hand.

Si-Jie (Question Forty): YOU’RE HERE. I missed you.

Arthur: I know.

Si-Jie (Question Forty): You’re supposed to say it back.

He leaned back in his chair and looked at the ceiling of his silent flat.

Arthur: I missed you too.

There was a long pause.

Si-Jie (Question Forty): Oh. Okay. I’m going to go and lie on the floor for a bit.

He smiled at his phone, properly, in the empty room, and if anyone at the task force had seen it they’d have rung for an ambulance.

✦ ✦ ✦

She came to his flat for the first time that Saturday, after their second coffee and a walk round the harbour in a wind that made her hold his arm with both hands and complain loudly about her hair.

She’d imagined it, she told him later. Dark wooden floors. A leather sofa. A bookshelf of grim volumes about the criminal mind, perhaps a photograph or two, something to prove that a person lived there and not just a profession.

It was white. White walls, a pale stone floor, white kitchen cupboards with no handles. One grey sofa. A glass table. A dining table with four chairs, three of which had plainly never been sat in. A long window over the lights of the city, and a bookshelf with every book sorted by subject and then by height. Even the cushions sat in a symmetrical line.

Si-Jie stood in the doorway in her coat and looked at it.

“Do you live here?”

“Yes.”

“Are you sure?”

He took her coat. “What does that mean?”

She walked in on tiptoe. “It looks like a showroom. It looks like a place a murderer would rent to make a good impression on the police. Where’s the evidence that a human being lives here?”

He watched her prowl. She looked at the sofa, the table, the shelf, and found a photograph at last: Arthur at about twelve in a school blazer between a tall grey-haired man in a dark suit and a slender woman with one hand on her son’s shoulder.

“Your parents?”

“Yes.”

“Your mother’s beautiful. You’ve got her eyes and your father’s everything else.” She put the frame back precisely where she’d found it, square to the edge of the shelf, and he noticed that, and noticed her noticing him notice.

“I’m trying not to disturb the museum,” she said.

In the kitchen she opened his fridge without asking and stood in front of it in silence. Eggs in one compartment. Milk in another. Vegetables cut into batons and stored in clear boxes with dates on the lids. Rows of water. No fruit. No chocolate. Nothing anyone had bought because they’d walked past it and wanted it.

“Do you ever eat anything bad for you?”

“When there’s no alternative.”

“That’s the saddest thing anyone’s ever said to me. You have biscuits,” said Si-Jie, and began opening cupboards, and in the third one found a box of almond biscuits with the seal unbroken.

“They’re for guests.”

She turned slowly towards the empty white living room and then back to him.

“Arthur. I’m a guest,” she said.

Within half an hour his flat had acquired a biscuit wrapper on the glass table, two used glasses, her cardigan flung over the arm of the sofa, and a hair tie on the floor. He noticed every one. He didn’t move any of them.

She put a documentary on and sat cross-legged on the sofa while he read a file beside her, and every few minutes she said “Look,” and he looked, and it was a dog, or an otter, or a man in a hat explaining badgers. Each time she moved closer, until her head was on his shoulder and her arm was through his and one of her legs was over his knee and he was reading the same paragraph for the fourth time.

“You’re making it hard to read,” he said.

“Should I move?”

He turned the page he hadn’t read. “No.”

She held up a small pink hair clip in front of his face. “Can I leave this here? So I don’t have to bring everything every time?”

He shut the file. “If you’re going to leave things here, you should have somewhere to put them. I’ll clear a drawer.”

She stared at him. Then she put both arms round his waist and squeezed until he grunted, and kissed his jaw, and his cheek, and the corner of his mouth, and he caught her chin in his fingers.

“That’s enough.”

“Why?”

“Because I can’t concentrate.”

“That’s the point,” said Si-Jie, and he gave up on the file entirely and kissed her.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was she who started it. It usually was, he’d learn: she reached for whatever she wanted with the perfect unselfconsciousness of someone who’d never once considered that he might refuse.

She was sitting in his lap by then, on the grey sofa, and she’d been playing with the top button of his shirt for some time, and she stopped and looked at him.

“Can I?”

He understood the question. He looked at her face for any sign she was less sure than she sounded, and found none. “Are you certain?”

“Yes.”

He brushed his thumb along her cheekbone. “Then yes.”

She undid the buttons one at a time and kissed each new inch of him as it appeared, collarbone and breastbone and the flat of his stomach, slowly, intently, as if it were coursework. He watched her. He couldn’t stop watching her. And because he’d spent ten years saying what he saw out loud to rooms full of people who needed to hear it, he began, without quite meaning to, to do it now.

“You’re breathing faster.”

She lifted her head. “Arthur.”

He touched the side of her throat where her pulse showed. “Your hands are warm. They weren’t, an hour ago. This is faster too. You’re—”

“Are you narrating?”

“I’m observing.”

“That’s worse,” said Si-Jie, and pushed his shirt off his shoulders.

He took her jumper over her head and unhooked what was underneath with steadier hands than he felt, and told her she was beautiful, which wasn’t an observation, or not only. He laid her back on the sofa and kissed his way down her neck and over her breasts, and felt her arch, and heard the small surprised noise she made, and of course he said so, low, against her skin: that her breath had caught, that her fingers had tightened in his hair, that her heart was going so hard he could feel it under his mouth.

She put her hand flat over his lips. He stopped. Above her palm his eyes creased.

“Stop describing me and use your mouth for something else,” she said, pink to the collarbones.

He kissed her palm. Then the inside of her wrist, where the pulse he’d been reporting was beating against his lips, and she took her hand away, and he didn’t say another word.

He undressed her the rest of the way, and she pulled at his belt until he helped, and on the wide grey sofa in the white flat he put his mouth on her where she wanted it and learned her the way he’d learned everything worth knowing, by paying attention: what made her gasp, what made her laugh, what made her stop laughing and grab his shoulder and say his name in a voice he’d never heard her use. When she came apart under him it was loud and sudden and she pressed the back of her wrist to her mouth afterwards, shocked at herself, and he kissed her knee and waited until she could breathe.

Then she reached for him, and he went.

He went into her slowly, watching her face, and stopped when her eyes went wide, and she wrapped both legs round him and said don’t you dare stop now, and so he didn’t. She held on to his back. She moved with him, and against him, and said Arthur into his neck over and over, and somewhere in it he lost every careful habit he owned and stopped watching anything at all. When it took him, it took him with her name in his mouth and her hands in his hair.

Afterwards they lay tangled on the sofa under the throw she’d dragged off the back of it, with her cheek on his chest and the city glittering outside the long window and her cardigan, at some point, on the floor.

“Arthur?”

“Hm.”

“Are you happy?”

He looked down at her bent head. “Yes.”

A pause. “Good. You’re not going to analyse that, are you?”

“No.”

“Promise?”

“Promise.”

She settled closer. Just as he thought she’d fallen asleep, she said, into his chest, “Because I really liked it,” and he put his arm over her and held on and didn’t say anything, because there was nothing he could add that was more accurate.

✦ ✦ ✦

She woke to the smell of eggs. She lay for a while without moving, in his bed, which she didn’t remember getting into, in one of his white shirts, which she did. Then she found her phone under the pillow.

Si-Wei (Business Hours): Are you alive

Si-Yuan (Eldest, Allegedly): Did you go home?

Si-Wei (Business Hours): Don’t tell me you’re still at the profiler’s.

Si-Jie: Good morning 😊

Si-Wei (Business Hours): OH MY GOD

Si-Yuan (Eldest, Allegedly): Let her have breakfast first.

She padded out barefoot and found him in the kitchen in a dark T-shirt with his sleeves pushed up, in front of a frying pan, weighing strawberries on a small digital scale.

She stopped in the doorway. “What are you doing?”

“Breakfast.”

“You’re weighing the strawberries.”

“For consistent portions.”

“You’re measuring breakfast.”

“If I estimated, you’d take more than you needed.”

“Excuse me?”

He tipped the strawberries into a bowl. “You ate most of the ones I bought on Wednesday.”

She opened her mouth and shut it. “You bought strawberries on Wednesday?”

“You said you liked them.”

She didn’t answer that. She came across the kitchen and put her arms round his waist from behind and her cheek between his shoulder blades and held on, and he stood with the spatula in one hand and let her.

At the table her plate had eggs and toast and strawberries and a glass of milk. His had eggs and toast and black coffee.

“Why’s mine bigger?”

“Yesterday you had half a sandwich, a glass of milk and three biscuits.”

“You counted my biscuits?”

“I pay attention.”

She stole a piece of toast off his plate. He looked at it in her hand and pushed the plate an inch towards her.

“Can I come back next weekend?”

“Yes.”

“Can I leave more things here?”

“One drawer, Si-Jie.”

“Can I have a toothbrush?”

He went on eating. “There’s one in the bathroom cabinet. I bought it on Friday.”

She put the toast down. “Already?”

“You said you might stay.”

She got up, came round the table and sat sideways on his lap with her arms round his neck, and he put his coffee down out of range.

“Your breakfast,” he said.

“Thank you for letting me be clingy.”

He looked at her for a second, and brushed his thumb across her cheek. “You don’t need to thank me for that. You do need to eat.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He walked her to the lift at nine. At the doors she turned round.

“Will you miss me?”

“Your flat is twenty minutes away.”

“Twenty-three, with traffic.”

He tucked a strand of hair behind her ear. “Yes, Si-Jie. I’ll miss you.”

When he went back in, the flat was different. There was a cardigan over the sofa. A hair tie on the glass table. A pink clip on the bedside table, her phone charger plugged in beside the bed, a second toothbrush in the bathroom glass, and in the fridge a box of strawberries with a great many fewer strawberries in it than he’d bought.

He stood in the middle of the white room and looked at all of it.

Arthur: You’ve forgotten your cardigan.

Si-Jie (Question Forty): I’ll get it next time. Is my clip there? And my charger?

Arthur: Yes.

Si-Jie (Question Forty): Oh no. I think I’m moving in by accident.

Arthur: You’re leaving things behind.

Si-Jie (Question Forty): Same thing.

He considered correcting her.

Arthur: There’s still room in the drawer.

At nine that evening there were forty more messages, and he answered every one, in order, and then sent one of his own.

Arthur: I bought more strawberries.

Si-Jie (Question Forty): FOR ME??? I LOVE YOU

He held his thumb over the screen and didn’t type anything. He wasn’t ready to say it. He wasn’t sure she’d meant to.

Arthur: You haven’t had dinner.

Si-Jie (Question Forty): ARTHUR

He put the phone down, smiling, in his flat that wasn’t white any more, and found he was already waiting for the next forty.

chapters.title: Her Sisters
chapters.desc: Dinner at Si-Yuan’s flat with all three sisters. He tells Si-Wei she’s in love with a criminal; she says she knows. Si-Jie is furious, and kisses him against a lamp post anyway.
chapters.epigraph: “Please don’t ever make her feel foolish for loving you.”
chapters.content:
Arthur Chen had interviewed men who’d killed people. He’d sat four hours across a table from a man who refused to admit that his own fingerprints were his. None of it had prepared him for dinner with three Yen sisters, one of whom was holding his hand under the table, one of whom was studying him like a part she might have to play, and one of whom had decided, before he’d taken his coat off, that he was a problem.

It was the Saturday before the end of November, at the eldest sister’s flat, which was on the twelfth floor of a building near the studios and full of scripts. Si-Jie had told him on the way up to behave.

“I always behave.”

“You behave like a man in an interview room. Behave like a boyfriend.”

“I’ve had very little practice.”

“I know,” said Si-Jie, and squeezed his hand and rang the bell.

✦ ✦ ✦

Si-Yuan opened the door. He’d seen her once before, under a cap, studying how he stood; tonight her hair was loose and she was barefoot and she had a ring on her left hand, a single stone, which she touched with her thumb when she wasn’t thinking about it.

“Arthur. Come in.”

“Thank you for having me.”

She looked at him, and at Si-Jie, and at their joined hands, and back up at him with a perfectly bland face. “Oh,” she said, and nothing else, and stood aside.

“What?” said Si-Jie.

“Your hands are very busy.”

Si-Wei was at the counter, opening wine. She was in a plain shirt with her hair tied back and she put the corkscrew down and came and shook his hand. Her grip was firm and her eyes were the most attentive in the room.

“So you’re the profiler.”

“Yes.”

“The one who answered thirty-nine questions.”

He looked at Si-Jie. Si-Jie looked at the ceiling.

“I see you’ve heard about that.”

“Repeatedly,” said Si-Wei, and went back to the wine.

As he passed the counter he heard Si-Yuan murmur, behind him, “He’s handsome.”

Si-Wei answered without any change of tone. “Unfortunately.”

He decided not to have heard either.

✦ ✦ ✦

They ate at Si-Yuan’s small table with the scripts pushed to one end. Si-Yuan had made soup and a dish of greens and bought everything else from the place downstairs, and she apologised for it and Si-Jie told her not to, and Si-Wei passed him the rice without looking at him and then watched him serve himself.

They asked him questions. They took turns, which he noticed, and which he suspected had been agreed in advance. Si-Yuan asked about his work and listened to the answers with her chin on her hand. Si-Jie answered half of them for him. Si-Wei said almost nothing, and watched what he did with his hands when Si-Yuan asked about his parents, and he let her.

“Your father was a judge?”

“He’s retired.”

“And your mother does post-mortems?”

“She still consults.”

“That must have been an interesting house to grow up in,” said Si-Yuan.

He considered it. “It was informative.”

Si-Jie laughed. “That’s his way of saying it was normal.”

“Was it?” said Si-Wei.

“No,” said Arthur, and Si-Yuan laughed into her glass.

Si-Yuan’s phone went on the counter. She looked at the screen, and her face did something he’d only seen a few times in his life and never on anyone who knew they were being watched: it went soft from the inside out. She took the call by the window with her back to them.

Her voice was lower and warmer than it had been all evening, and careful at the end. “Yes, I’m with the girls. No, I haven’t forgotten. All right, I’ll be there. Tell your mother thank you.”

She came back and sat down and put the phone face down beside her plate.

“Pengcheng?” said Si-Jie.

“His mother’s asked me to lunch tomorrow.”

“Again?”

“It’s Sunday,” said Si-Yuan, which seemed to settle it for her, and smiled at her soup.

Arthur knew the name. Their families had sat at the same dinners since before either of them was old enough to understand why they disliked each other: two old legal houses with their roots in Hong Kong, a great deal of port, and a long tradition of being polite across a table. He’d known Yang Pengcheng since they were both eight years old and Pengcheng had corrected his grammar at a wedding. He’d disliked him ever since, comfortably and without effort, the way one dislikes a draught.

“I know him,” he said.

Si-Yuan’s eyes lit. “You do?”

“Our families have met. For years.”

“How long?” said Si-Jie, suspicious.

“Since we were eight.”

“And?”

“He was very good at grammar,” said Arthur.

Si-Wei put her glass down and looked at him properly for the first time all evening, and he thought he saw her decide something.

“How long have you been together?” he asked Si-Yuan.

“Nearly three years.”

“Two years and nine months. Since February. The one with the noodles,” said Si-Jie.

“You’re counting?”

“Somebody in this family has to.”

Si-Yuan turned the ring on her finger. When she spoke about his mother her shoulders came up a little, and her back straightened, and she chose her words, and Arthur watched all of it and understood it the way he understood most things, from the outside, a little too clearly.

“You’re close to his mother?” he said.

Si-Yuan smiled. “She’s very particular. I’m learning.”

Then, quite unexpectedly, she looked up at him. “Do you think it’s hard to marry into an old family?”

The table went quiet. Si-Jie’s hand went still in his. He understood that it wasn’t a polite question, and that she wasn’t asking it to make conversation, and that whatever he said she’d keep.

“It depends on the family. Tradition can hold people up. It can also be an excuse for asking someone to be less than she is,” he said slowly.

“Should people compromise?”

“Yes. Compromise isn’t the same as disappearing.”

Si-Yuan was quiet. Then she smiled, and it reached her eyes. “I like that answer.”

“That’s a good answer,” said Si-Wei, grudging.

Si-Jie leaned her head on his shoulder for a second, in front of everyone, and said “See? He’s clever,” with the pride of an inventor.

✦ ✦ ✦

It went wrong over the fruit.

Si-Yuan had cut a pear and Si-Wei was talking about a group project at the business school when her phone lit up beside her bowl. Arthur had been reading screens upside down for a decade and could no more not read one than not hear a raised voice: Geum Sung Jae (Ignore). Si-Wei’s face changed. It was tiny. A tightening at the corner of the mouth, a breath held a fraction too long. She turned the phone over and went on with her sentence without missing a word.

Si-Jie was laughing at something Si-Yuan had said. Si-Yuan was laughing back. Neither of them saw. He saw. Si-Wei saw him see.

“May I ask you something, Mr. Chen?” she said pleasantly.

“Of course.”

“Do people who study criminals become more suspicious than the rest of us?”

“Sometimes. Knowing more about risk isn’t the same as judging it better.”

“And people who know someone is dangerous and get involved anyway? Are they being stupid?”

“Not necessarily. I’d want to know what they believe they’re getting.”

“You seem very interested in that question,” said Si-Wei.

“So do you.”

She picked up a slice of pear. “Maybe.”

He should have left it there. He knew he should have left it there. But the question was sitting on the table between them like a file left open, and he’d spent his whole adult life finishing the sentences other people wouldn’t.

“You’re in love with a criminal,” he said.

Si-Jie turned so fast her chair scraped. “Arthur!”

Si-Yuan put her fork down.

Si-Wei only looked at him. Then she nodded, as calmly as if he’d said it might rain. “I know.”

“Wait. What?” said Si-Jie.

Si-Wei put the pear down. “He isn’t wrong. He’s in things I don’t approve of. He’s dangerous. I know that too. I’m not asking anyone to approve.”

There was no defence in it. It was the voice of someone who’d already done the arithmetic and made her decision and wasn’t going to redo the sum for a man she’d met two hours ago. Arthur recognised it, because it was his own.

“Knowing something’s dangerous doesn’t make it less dangerous,” he said.

“I know.”

“Then I hope you’re careful.”

“Thank you,” said Si-Wei, and meant it, which was the strangest part.

Si-Jie looked from her sister to him and back. “Can somebody please explain what’s happening?”

Si-Yuan reached for the wine and topped up everyone’s glass. “Welcome to the family,” she said, to no one in particular.

✦ ✦ ✦

Si-Jie took him out onto the balcony before he could reach the dishes, and shut the glass door behind them, and stood with her back to it and her arms folded in the cold.

“How did you know?”

“Her phone lit up. I read it.”

“You read her screen?”

“I read everyone’s screen. I can’t help it. It’s upside down and lit and it’s in front of me.”

She stared at him. Below them the road went on hissing in the dark, and twelve floors down somebody was laughing outside the noodle place.

“Have you read mine?”

He considered lying, and didn’t. “Every time.”

“Every time?”

“You hold it at an angle when you’re typing to me. You think it hides it. It doesn’t.”

Her mouth opened. “What does it say? What have I saved you as?”

“Arthur. Then a bracket. Then Thirty-Nine.”

She went red to the hairline, all at once, in the light from the kitchen. “That’s private.”

“You asked.”

“You’re supposed to pretend you haven’t seen!”

“Then I’d be lying to you, and I don’t want to start,” said Arthur.

She looked at him for a second with her arms still folded, furious and pink, and then she unfolded them and put them round his waist instead and her face in his shirt, and said something into it that sounded like you’re the worst man I’ve ever met, and didn’t let go until Si-Yuan knocked on the glass and held up a tea towel.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was rinsing bowls at the sink, because it was the only useful thing he could see to do, when Si-Yuan came and stood beside him with a tea towel.

“Do you like my sister?”

“Yes.”

She blinked. She’d expected, he thought, something more complicated.

“She’s been smiling at her phone for five weeks. She talks about you when you’re not there. A lot,” said Si-Yuan.

“I’ve gathered.”

“She’s clingy.”

“I’ve noticed.”

“She’s stubborn, and when she likes someone she gets carried away.”

“I worked that out in the car park.”

Si-Yuan dried a bowl and put it away. When she turned back there was no teasing in her face at all.

“Please don’t ever make her feel foolish for loving you. Some families do that. They don’t say anything. They just let you feel it,” she said.

He looked at her. He thought of a boy at a wedding correcting his grammar, and a woman who was particular, and a ring turned round and round on a finger. He didn’t say any of it.

“I won’t,” he said.

She smiled again. “All right. Then you can stay.”

Si-Wei’s verdict came at the door, while Si-Jie was hunting for her other shoe.

“You notice everything,” said Si-Wei.

“Occupational habit.”

Si-Wei nodded at her sister, on her knees under the sofa. “She’s happy. She doesn’t get attached this fast. Don’t mistake that for bad judgement.”

“I wouldn’t.”

She folded her arms. “Then I approve. For the record, your profiling’s annoying.”

“Why?”

“Because you’re right too often,” said Si-Wei, and went back to the kitchen.

✦ ✦ ✦

Si-Jie didn’t speak in the car. She didn’t speak for four streets, which he’d never known her manage, and then she did.

“You called her boyfriend a criminal. At dinner. In front of everyone.”

“Yes.”

“That was incredibly rude.”

“Yes. I should have said it to her alone.”

She folded her arms and looked out of the window. “You should have. She’s my sister. She doesn’t need you judging her.”

“I wasn’t wrong.”

“That isn’t the point, Arthur.”

“I know.”

He parked outside her building. She got out without saying goodnight, and he sat for two seconds and then got out after her, and caught her up on the pavement under a street lamp.

“Si-Jie.”

She turned round. “What?”

“I’m sorry. I’ll apologise to her.”

She’d plainly expected another argument. The apology took the ground out from under her and she stood there with her arms folded and her eyes too bright.

“You’re so difficult.”

“So I’ve been told.”

She turned to go. He took her hand. Not hard; just enough. She looked down at it, and then up at him, and saw where he was looking, which was her mouth.

“Don’t.”

“Don’t what?”

“Look at me like you want to kiss me. I’m angry with you.”

“I do want to kiss you,” said Arthur.

She made a sound of pure exasperation, took two fistfuls of his coat and kissed him so hard his shoulder hit the lamp post. He put his hand on her waist and kissed her back, and felt her mouth curve against his, and she pulled away at once.

“Don’t laugh.”

“I’m not.”

She glared up at him. “You are. You’re smiling. I can feel it. I’m still angry.”

“Understood.”

She kissed him again, and then once more, slower, and then put her forehead against his chest and stood there under the street lamp with the city going past.

“You owe me three more,” she said into his coat.

“That seems excessive.”

She looked up. He paid all three.

✦ ✦ ✦

At home he found the number Si-Jie had put in his phone at dinner with the name she’d chosen, Si-Wei (Verdict Pending), and wrote to her.

Arthur: Si-Wei. I’m sorry I said that in front of everyone. It wasn’t mine to say.

Si-Wei (Verdict Pending): Apology accepted.

Si-Wei (Verdict Pending): You weren’t wrong. Don’t tell Si-Jie I said that.

He put the phone down. He’d profiled three sisters in one evening and come away with three verdicts, and he wasn’t sure which of them mattered most. He knew only that he wanted to be asked back, and that next time he’d keep his mouth shut at least until the fruit.

chapters.title: His Father’s House
chapters.desc: The day after her twenty-first birthday, his parents’ flat in Hong Kong: a family of judges, and nobody touches him. She holds him in the lift for nine floors. The hotel, explicit: he asks her to stay.
chapters.content:
The first thing Si-Jie noticed about Hong Kong was that Arthur went quiet.

He was always quiet. But there was his ordinary quiet, the kind that could sit beside her for an hour reading a report and reach over now and then to move her coffee back from the edge of the table, and there was this one, which he’d put on at the airport with his coat. He checked his watch more than he needed to. He read messages and didn’t answer them. When she slid her hand into his on the walkway he held on hard enough to stop one of them being swept off.

“Are you nervous?”

“No.”

“You’re holding my hand like I’m going to fall into the sea.”

He looked down and loosened his grip. She tightened hers at once.

“I didn’t say let go.”

She’d turned twenty-one the day before. She’d spent most of it on the floor of Si-Yuan’s flat with her sisters and a cake with too much cream, and the rest of it at dinner with him in a restaurant so quiet she’d whispered, where he’d put a long flat box beside her plate and watched her open it with an expression of total dread. A fine gold chain, with a single small pearl. She’d put it on at the table. She was wearing it now under her collar, and she’d caught him looking at the place where it was four times since breakfast.

He hadn’t told her where they were going until they were at the gate. She’d packed for rain, because Si-Wei had told her to.

“Did you sleep?” he asked.

“Yes.”

“How many hours?”

“Arthur.”

“How many?”

“Seven.”

“That’s acceptable.”

She laughed at him. It was the first time she’d laughed properly in a week, and she felt his thumb move once across the back of her hand, and knew he’d noticed that too.

✦ ✦ ✦

His parents lived at the top of an old building on the hill above Central, nine floors up, in a flat that looked exactly like what she’d imagined a family of judges would live in. Dark wood. Paintings hung at precisely the same height. Photographs arranged by some principle she couldn’t work out. No shoes left by the door, no cushion out of place, no sign that anyone had ever been in a hurry there.

His mother opened the door. Dr. Chen was slim and grey-haired and composed, in a dark silk blouse, and she looked at her son first and then at Si-Jie, and something in her face eased.

“You must be Si-Jie.”

“Hello, Auntie.”

His mother took both her hands and glanced at her son. “Arthur told us you were coming. Briefly.”

“Mother.”

“Very briefly,” said Dr. Chen, and Si-Jie decided on the spot that she liked her.

His father came down the hall behind her. He was tall and silver and carried himself with the kind of authority that had never once needed to raise its voice, and he and Arthur shook hands. That was all. No hand on the shoulder. A handshake, firm and formal and over in a second, between a father and the son he hadn’t seen since summer.

Si-Jie saw it. She filed it, the way Arthur filed things.

“Yen Si-Jie. Welcome,” said Judge Chen.

“Thank you, Uncle.”

“Your flight was on time?”

“Yes, Father.”

A pause. “Good. Lunch is ready.”

As she passed Arthur in the hall she touched his wrist, once, with two fingers. He looked down. She didn’t look back.

✦ ✦ ✦

Lunch was quiet, and kind enough, and controlled in a way she’d never seen a family meal be controlled: nobody interrupted, nobody spoke over anybody, and even the silences seemed to have been allocated places at the table. His father asked about her degree, her supervisor, whether she meant to do postgraduate work. His mother asked about her family. She answered everything, and under the table she found Arthur’s hand, and he let her hold it, and his mother’s eyes went to their arms for half a second and came back to her plate without a word.

Over the soup his father said, in the tone of a man mentioning the weather, “I understand Madam Yang’s sixtieth was well attended.”

Si-Jie went still.

“Three hundred. Your aunt went,” said his mother.

Judge Chen looked across at Arthur. “And the younger Yang? The son. I’m told he conducted himself correctly. You know him.”

Arthur put his spoon down. Si-Jie felt his hand close on hers under the table, hard, and then let go.

“He sat in his chair,” said Arthur.

His father regarded him. Something passed over his face that might, in a less controlled man, have been interest.

“That’s a judgement,” said Judge Chen.

“It’s an observation.”

Nobody said anything else about it. His mother asked Si-Jie whether she liked fish. Si-Jie said she did, and looked down at her bowl, and thought about Si-Yuan on the floor of her flat yesterday blowing out candles with her mouth smiling and her eyes somewhere else, and found that she couldn’t speak for a while. Arthur didn’t look at her. He moved the dish of greens a little nearer to her side of the table, which was what he did instead.

✦ ✦ ✦

Dinner was more formal. His father had put on a jacket. His mother came in late from a call and sat down and, between the second course and the third, began to talk about a case.

It was a death that had been brought to her department as an accident. The scene didn’t support it. She kept the details back, as a matter of course, but Arthur put his chopsticks down and asked what didn’t fit, and she said the sequence of injuries against the sequence of the account. He asked about timing. She said among other things. He asked whether she thought it had been staged, and she looked at him and said she wasn’t going to speculate before the evidence was in, and he accepted it without argument.

“The family’s already decided. They’ve decided what kind of person she was, and from that, how she died,” said his mother.

“That’s not motive.”

“No.”

“People mistake a convincing story for a proven one,” said his father.

Si-Jie watched them. She’d seen Arthur talk about cases before, late at night in his white flat with his sleeves rolled up. She’d never seen him talk about one like this: as somebody’s son, with two people who understood the work without needing it explained, who never once said anything to impress each other.

And still, something was missing. When his mother asked whether he’d like more, he said no. When his father asked whether he was staying, he said he’d booked a hotel. Neither of them asked why. Neither of them said stay here.

They cared for him, she thought. They cared for him through arrangements and questions and the right food on the table. They’d just never once touched him while she was in the room.

✦ ✦ ✦

At the door his mother hugged Si-Jie and told her to come again. His father shook Arthur’s hand and told him to let them know when he reached the hotel. Then the lift doors closed on the two of them and Arthur stood in the corner of it with his hands in his coat pockets, looking at the numbers. Nine. Eight.

“Arthur?”

“Hm.”

“Do your parents hug you?”

He looked at her. The question had plainly gone in somewhere he hadn’t been guarding.

“Not particularly.”

Seven.

“My mother did, I think, when I was small. I don’t remember much.”

“And your father?”

“No.”

Six. He went on before she could say anything. “It wasn’t an unhappy childhood. They gave me everything I needed. They’re good parents.”

“I believe you,” said Si-Jie.

He’d expected to have to argue for it; she watched him not know what to do with the space where the argument should have been. She held her arms out.

“We’re in a lift,” he said.

“I know.”

“Someone might get in.”

“Then they’ll see something extremely ordinary,” said Si-Jie, and when he didn’t move, she went to him instead and put her arms round his waist and her cheek against his chest and held on.

His hands stayed at his sides. Five. Four. She didn’t let go. Somewhere around three one hand came up and rested flat against her back, carefully, the way he’d put his hand on a piece of evidence. She tightened her arms.

“It’s all right,” she said into his coat.

She didn’t ask him to explain. She didn’t tell him he should have been held more. She just held him. And at two, his other arm came round her, and she felt his shoulders come down for the first time since the airport.

The lift stopped. The doors opened on the lobby. Neither of them moved.

“We’re here,” she said.

“I know.”

“Are you going to let go?”

“No,” said Arthur, and reached past her and pressed the button that held the doors, and when she laughed and asked what he was doing, he said he wanted another minute, in a voice she’d never heard from him, and she put her arms back round him and stayed.

✦ ✦ ✦

The hotel room was warm, and high up, and the whole harbour was lit up in the window like something spilt. She took her shoes off and stood at the glass looking down at the traffic. Behind her she heard him put his watch on the table and loosen his collar.

“Do you want the shower first?”

She turned round. “Are you being polite or do you want the bathroom?”

“Both.”

But he didn’t move. He was looking at her across the room with nothing in his face she recognised from interview rooms or lecture theatres, nothing measured, only a quiet, total attention that made her feel like the only lit thing in the city.

“What?”

He came over and touched the chain at her collarbone with one finger. “You wore it.”

“Of course I wore it.”

“It isn’t your usual style.”

“I like it because you gave it to me,” said Si-Jie, and reached up and undid the knot of his tie.

He bent his head so she could. She drew it out from under his collar and dropped it on the chair, and began on his buttons, and he let her, watching her hands. She kissed him then, gently, the way she kissed him every day now without thinking, and when she drew back he followed her, and kissed her again, slower, and stopped with his forehead against hers and his eyes shut.

“Stay,” he said.

She went still.

“Tonight?”

He shook his head a little, against hers. “With me.”

He didn’t give her a reason. He didn’t list the hotel’s two pillows, or the hour, or the rain. He’d asked for something out loud, plainly, for himself, and she understood that he might never have done it before in his life.

“I’m staying,” said Si-Jie.

His breath went out of him. She felt it on her mouth.

She took his shirt off his shoulders and kissed his chest, and he caught her hand and pressed his mouth to her knuckles, and then he undressed her, slowly, as if he had the whole night and intended to use all of it. He laid her down on the wide white bed with the harbour light across them both. He kissed her throat and her shoulder and the small pearl in the hollow of her collarbone, and the place beneath it where her heart was going fast, and he didn’t say so this time; he just kept his mouth there until she laughed and pulled his head up to hers.

“You’re thinking,” she whispered.

“Yes.”

“About what?”

“How to ask you to stay without it sounding like an instruction.”

“You already asked. I said yes. Stop thinking.”

“That’s difficult.”

“I know,” said Si-Jie, and wrapped her legs round him, and he stopped.

He went into her slowly, with his forehead on hers, and stayed still a moment, both of them breathing, and she put her hands on his face and felt him tremble under her palms. Then he moved, and she moved with him, and it was slow and deep and quiet in a way it had never been in the white flat. He said her name against her cheek. She held on. He watched her the whole time, not like a profiler, like a man memorising something, and when she came she came with his name in her mouth and her nails in his shoulders, and he followed her a moment later with a sound she’d never heard him make, low and unguarded, into her neck.

Later, with the lights off and the city a blur beyond the curtains, he lay with her held against him so close there was no space at all.

“Arthur?”

“Hm.”

“Are you comfortable?”

His hand moved over her back. “Yes. Are you?”

“Extremely.”

He was quiet for so long she thought he’d fallen asleep.

“Thank you,” he said.

“What for?”

“Staying.”

She lifted her head. “You don’t have to thank me for that.”

“I wanted you to know I wanted you to.”

She lay looking at him in the dark. “Then ask me again tomorrow.”

“Stay tomorrow,” said Arthur, at once, and she laughed and said yes and put her head back down on his chest.

✦ ✦ ✦

He woke first. There was a strange ceiling, and a strange window, and a warm weight across his chest that had taken most of the duvet in the night. He looked at what was left of the duvet, and at her, and decided not to retrieve it. His phone buzzed on the table.

Mother (Two Questions): Did you arrive safely?

Arthur: Yes.

Mother (Two Questions): Is Si-Jie comfortable?

He looked at the girl asleep across him with her hair in her face and the pearl caught on the edge of her collarbone.

Arthur: Yes. She’s still asleep.

His mother sent a single red heart. He kept looking at it. In twenty-four years his mother had never sent him a heart.

Si-Jie stirred. “Morning.”

“Good morning.”

“You’re still here.”

“Where else would I be?”

“I don’t know. You looked like you might get up in the night and rearrange the furniture.”

“It’s already arranged.”

She laughed and burrowed back in. “Was it nice? Staying with me,” she said into his shoulder.

He thought about the question properly, because she’d asked it.

“Yes,” he said.

He’d spent his whole life learning to stand straight and speak carefully and keep his hands still. He’d never thought much about what was missing. Then a girl from Taipei had stepped into a lift, held out her arms and held him for nine floors, and he’d found out that he wanted another minute.

chapters.title: The Task Force
chapters.desc: She sees him go to work for the first time: a woman dead in a stairwell, a man not yet caught. He comes home in the middle of the night and holds on without a word.
chapters.epigraph: “But you have to come home. To me.”
chapters.content:
The first thing Si-Jie learned about Arthur’s work was that he didn’t look like himself when he was doing it.

He was still quiet. He was still the man who corrected her when she mispronounced a word on purpose to annoy him, and answered forty messages at nine every night, in order, even after a day of meetings. But at work he was someone she’d never met, and by the end of that week in January she understood she’d only ever known the man who came home. She hadn’t known the one who went into other people’s worst nights and stayed there until he understood them. She hadn’t known how hard it was for him to leave.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the Thursday her morning seminar finished early, and she took the bus across the city with a paper bag on her knee and went up to the sixth floor, because the receptionist knew her now and had stopped pretending to ring first.

He was in the doorway of the team room with a folder under his arm and his tie already loose, and he stopped when he saw her.

“You’re not supposed to be here.”

“I brought lunch.”

“It’s twenty past eleven.”

She held up the bag. “Early lunch. Sandwiches. Fruit. Real coffee, because yours is a crime.”

“It’s black coffee.”

“Exactly.”

He looked at the bag, and then at her, and she saw him decide not to argue. Then she saw the folder, and his coat over his other arm.

“Are you going somewhere?”

He watched her face. “A scene. There’s been a death. I might be gone for hours.”

He was waiting for something, she realised. A complaint, or a question about when he’d be back. She’d known him three months and she’d learned that he braced for things before they happened, the way some people flinched before a hand had moved.

“When did you last eat something that wasn’t coffee?” she said.

“I don’t have time.”

She held out a sandwich. “Two minutes. One and a half.”

He took it. He ate it standing by Eugene’s desk while she told him about a lecturer who’d spent an hour on a paper without once mentioning its method, and he listened, and asked one question, and then his phone rang and his face changed.

He answered with his surname and listened. “Where? How long ago? I’m on my way.”

She was already folding the top of the bag shut. “Go.”

“Eugene will see you down.”

“I can find a lift, Arthur.”

He picked up the folder and stopped. “I know you can. Don’t wait for me.”

“All right.”

He bent and kissed her forehead, there in the team room with Eugene pretending to read, which he’d never done at work before. She reached up and straightened his collar.

“Be careful.”

He looked at her a second longer, and went.

✦ ✦ ✦

The building was old: sixteen floors, a lift that stuck at nine, and a narrow service stairwell with a window on every landing. The cleaner had found her a little after eleven, on the half-landing between seven and eight. A woman in her late twenties. The first officers had called it strangulation.

Arthur put on gloves and went in without speaking.

Detergent. Old concrete. Under both, the smell places kept after people had tried too hard to make them normal again. He looked at the landing, then the stairs, then the door, before he let himself look at her.

She was on her side. Her bag was beside her, closed, and her purse was still in it. Her shoes were flat and sensible and one heel was scuffed white along the edge where it had dragged on something. There was nothing on the landing above, or the one below, to say there’d been a fight anywhere but here.

“Who found her?”

“Cleaner. Came up from six. Called security,” said Eugene.

“Who came in before us?”

“Guard. Building manager. Two residents who heard the cleaner scream.”

“Take them separately. Where each of them stood. What they touched.”

He walked up one flight and stood looking down. He walked back. He looked at the door between seven and eight, at the handle and the frame and the gap underneath, and at the window, which didn’t open.

“Cameras?”

“Lobby and lifts. Nothing in the stairwell.”

“Key cards?”

“Being pulled.”

He went back down to her and crouched, and was quiet for so long that Eugene stopped writing. Eugene knew that silence. It meant Arthur was building a sequence: what had happened before she came into the stairwell; why she’d come; whether she knew who was waiting, or whether anyone had been waiting at all.

He didn’t know her. He’d never hear her voice or learn what she had for breakfast or who she rang when she couldn’t sleep. Her family would know all of that, and none of it would help him. What would help was the man: what he’d chosen to do around her, in what order, and what he’d done afterwards. Somewhere in that order was a person who’d gone home last night, and slept, and might already be thinking about the next time.

Eugene was back on the landing. “Arthur. A resident on nine says he’s seen a man on these stairs three nights this month. Same time, more or less. Looked like he was waiting for someone.”

“Description?”

“Average build. Dark clothes. Never saw the face.”

“Did he report it?”

“No.”

Arthur looked at the stairs above them. “Find out whether anyone else in this building’s complained about someone hanging about. Following people. Trying doors. And don’t assume the man on the stairs is our man. Get everyone with a reason to be in here: residents, cleaners, deliveries, contractors. Find out why she was in a stairwell when there’s a lift.”

He stayed on the landing another forty minutes after that.

✦ ✦ ✦

At headquarters he didn’t take his jacket off. He stood in front of the board with the building’s floor plan, three stills from the lobby camera, a list of names and a timeline that still had gaps in it like missing teeth.

“Her phone?”

“Still with the lab.”

“Last contact?”

“Her sister. Last night.”

“Anything to say she was meeting someone?”

“Nothing solid.”

“Then we don’t write that she was meeting someone,” said Arthur.

A second resident had heard the stairwell door close sometime around midnight. He asked whether that door closed on its own, and whether it made the same sound whoever went through it. He looked at the plan: three ways into the stairwell, from the lobby, the car park and the residents’ corridor. He looked at the lobby stills, where she came in at nine minutes to eleven with a carrier bag from the shop on the corner. Her usual way home, her sister said, was along the main road. This one cut down the side of the building where the street lights didn’t reach.

“Find out if that was a one-off. Or if she’d changed her route recently,” he said.

“You think someone was watching her,” said Eugene.

“I think we need to know if her habits were easy to learn. Don’t call it stalking yet. We haven’t got enough.”

He wrote three words under the timeline and underlined the last.

ROUTINE. ACCESS. OPPORTUNITY.

Then he stood back, and the room went away. He was on the landing again: the angle of her shoulder, the closed bag, the scuffed heel. Where had the man stood? How long? Had he gone down the stairs or up? Had he passed someone in the lobby and said good evening? He tried an argument and let it go when it didn’t fit. He tried an ambush, and a meeting arranged by text, and let each go. He didn’t need to imagine a monster. He needed a person, with habits and limits, who’d made a decision, and could make another.

“Arthur. You’ve been standing there twenty minutes.”

He looked at his watch. Eugene was right. He drank his coffee, which had gone cold, and didn’t notice.

✦ ✦ ✦

Si-Jie had a key now. He’d given it to her at New Year, on a ring with a small brass fish, without a speech, and she’d held it in her palm for a whole minute before she trusted herself to say thank you.

She let herself into his flat that evening and finished an essay at his glass table and ate the dinner she’d cooked at his stove, and covered the other plate, and had a shower, and sat on the grey sofa in his shirt with her laptop and her phone. She’d sent him thirty-seven messages since lunch. He hadn’t answered any of them. She wasn’t hurt; she knew where he was. But she was beginning to learn the difference between knowing someone was busy and knowing what busy did to him.

Si-Jie: Are you coming home tonight?

It was nearly nine before the phone buzzed.

Arthur (Thirty-Nine): Yes.

Si-Jie: When?

Arthur (Thirty-Nine): I don’t know yet.

Si-Jie: Did you eat the other half of the sandwich?

Arthur (Thirty-Nine): No.

Si-Jie: Arthur.

Arthur (Thirty-Nine): I’ll eat. You don’t have to wait up.

Si-Jie: I know. I want to.

In the team room he read that and didn’t move for several seconds. Eugene, across the desks, looked at his face.

“She’s waiting?”

“Yes.”

“Go home.”

“There isn’t enough.”

Eugene leaned back. “There’s enough for tonight. The landing’ll still be there in the morning. You won’t catch him by staring at the board till three.”

Arthur looked at the board. The photograph, the plan, the gaps. He picked up his coat and his papers and told Eugene he’d read the statements at home, and Eugene said that was better, in the voice of a man who didn’t believe a word of it.

✦ ✦ ✦

She’d fallen asleep on the sofa with the blanket over her legs and her phone on her chest. She heard the lock in her sleep and didn’t wake for it. It was the silence afterwards that woke her: the absence of the sounds he always made coming in, keys in the dish and shoes off and his coat on the hook.

He was standing in the middle of the room, looking at the covered plate on the table.

“Arthur?”

He turned. He looked at her, and she sat up and the blanket slid off, and she saw that he was looking at her without quite seeing her. His shirt was creased. There were shadows under his eyes she’d never seen. Part of him was still on a landing somewhere, and she didn’t know the way there.

She got up. “Come here.”

He didn’t move. So she went to him, and as she reached him he stepped forward all at once and pulled her into his arms.

It wasn’t rough. But it was hard, and sudden, and she felt the whole day in it: the weight of him came down on her as he put his face into the side of her neck and held on. She stood still for a heartbeat. Then she put both arms round him and pressed her cheek against his chest.

“Hi,” she said.
