Si-Jie’s comment: he is also persistent. Particularly when kissing.

Arthur watched the pen move. “What are you doing?”

“Writing.”

“I can see that.”

“Then why ask?”

He read the margin, and a faint smile appeared.

She closed the notebook halfway. “I’ve decided something. You can keep it.”

He went attentive. “The notebook?”

“With conditions.”

“Tell me.”

She opened it to a blank page and wrote across the top.

NEW RULES, 1 APRIL 2025

“Rule one. You can keep it if I can read it. All of it. No secret sections. No tearing out pages because you’re embarrassed.”

He considered that. “That depends on the page.”

“Arthur.”

“Agreed.”

She smiled. “Rule two. I can write in the margins, without asking. Rule three. If you write something about me I disagree with, I get to correct it.”

“That seems reasonable.”

“Rule four. You tell me when you’re making an observation.”

He paused. “Every time?”

“Not every time. I’m not asking you to announce it when I blink. But if you catch yourself studying me, say so. Don’t pretend you aren’t.”

“All right.”

She wrote it down, and looked up. “Rule five. You have to ask me things.”

He raised an eyebrow. “I do ask you things.”

“Not just questions with answers you can check. Ask me what I think. What I want. What I feel. And listen when I tell you.”

His face softened. “All right.”

She looked at the list. “That’s it. And one more condition.” She turned the notebook towards him. At the bottom of the page she’d written:

The notebook is not allowed to become more important than the person in it.

Arthur read it twice. Then he took the pen out of her hand and wrote one word underneath.

Agreed.

“Good,” said Si-Jie.

He closed the notebook and reached across the table for her hand. “Thank you.”

She squeezed his fingers. “Don’t thank me yet. I haven’t finished correcting your handwriting.”

“My handwriting is perfectly legible.”

“Your handwriting is emotionally unavailable.”

He looked at her. “That isn’t a recognised description.”

“It is now.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The notebook changed after that. Not its contents, exactly. Arthur still wrote in his small, precise hand. He still dated every entry and still recorded the things he thought worth remembering. But now there were two kinds of handwriting on the pages: his in black, hers usually in blue. Sometimes hers were corrections.

Arthur: She appeared irritated when I asked whether she had eaten.
Si-Jie: I was irritated because you asked me while I was eating.

Sometimes they were arguments.

Arthur: She says she does not like very sweet drinks.
Si-Jie: Correct. Unless it’s strawberry milk. Don’t be ridiculous.

Sometimes they were simply affectionate.

Arthur: She fell asleep while reading.
Si-Jie: Your shoulder is comfortable. Don’t look so pleased.

Sometimes they went on for days.

Arthur: She sings in the shower. Not well.
Si-Jie: Beautifully. Strike this.
Arthur: Disputed.
Si-Jie: You can’t write DISPUTED in your own notebook about your own girlfriend.

He didn’t strike it. Under her last line he wrote that he’d consulted the neighbours, and she laughed at the dining table until he had to take the notebook away from her before she drew on it. For a week afterwards she sang louder than necessary every morning, and every morning he stood outside the bathroom door with his coffee and listened to the whole thing, and never once wrote down that he liked it.

And sometimes she wrote things that made him stop reading.

Arthur: She appears more relaxed when she is physically close to me.
Si-Jie: I like being close to you. That isn’t a behavioural mystery.

He read that one twice and looked across the room. She was on the floor, sorting photographs on her phone. She felt him looking. “What?”

“I’m looking at you.”

“You’re allowed. But under rule four you have to tell me why.”

He glanced at the notebook, and back at her. “Because I like looking at you.”

Her smile went soft. “Better.”

He turned back to the page and added a sentence.

She likes being told directly.

Si-Jie leaned over his shoulder. “That’s not an observation. That’s a fact.” She took the pen and wrote underneath it.

And I like being kissed.

Arthur looked at her. She looked back. Neither of them said anything. Then he closed the notebook and put it aside.

“That is something I can accommodate,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

On a Saturday night in the middle of April the notebook lay open on the bedside table. Si-Jie was sitting up against the headboard in one of his shirts with her hair still damp from the shower, and Arthur was beside her, reading. She’d been quiet for several minutes. Then she reached for the notebook.

“Can I read you something?”

“Of course.”

She found a page from November, and Arthur closed his book, and she read it to him.

8 November. Fell asleep during a film, approximately twenty-three minutes after the opening credits. Woke when I moved. Asked whether I was leaving. Went back to sleep after I told her I was not.

She stopped. “That’s quite sweet.”

He didn’t say anything. She turned the page.

14 November. Cried at a documentary. Do not ask straight away. Wait until she is ready.

She looked at him. “You remembered that?”

“You told me you didn’t want to talk.”

She studied his face, and turned another page.

2 December 2024. She asked whether I would still want her if she became difficult to understand. I said yes. She asked whether I was certain. I said yes. She kissed me. She appeared reassured.

She smiled. “That was a good answer.”

“It was an honest one.”

She traced the words with a fingertip and read on.

7 January 2025. She fell asleep against my chest with her hand curled into my shirt. I did not move for approximately forty minutes after waking. There was no practical reason to stay still. I did not want to wake her.

She looked up. “Forty minutes? You had to go to work.”

“I wasn’t late.”

“You were late.”

“By four minutes.”

She laughed. “Why didn’t you just move me?”

“You looked comfortable.”

She lowered the notebook. “You’re very sweet sometimes.”

“Don’t tell anyone.”

She found one more.

18 January 2025. She kissed me while I was reading. I lost my place. She asked whether I was annoyed. I said no. She kissed me again. I did not recover the page.

“That happened. Did you ever find the page?” she said, delighted.

“No. I stopped reading.”

She put the notebook on the bedside table and moved closer, and rested her hand on his chest. “Can I test something? The entry about how you stop reading when I kiss you.”

She leaned in and kissed him. His hand settled at her waist. When she drew back he looked at her, and then he kissed her again, slower, with his other hand at the back of her neck and his thumb on her skin. She shifted closer, and the book on his lap slid to the floor.

She smiled against his mouth. “Lost your place?”

“Completely.”

“Good.”

The notebook lay open beside them.

She glanced at it. “There’s another one.”

“Later.”

“You’re avoiding the reading.”

“I’m prioritising,” said Arthur, and she laughed and kissed him again.

✦ ✦ ✦

He set the notebook aside when she reached for him. He kissed her without narrating anything, without turning her face into a list. Once he stopped to look at her.

“All right?”

“Yes. More than all right.”

He kissed her hair, her cheek, the corner of her mouth.

She caught his face between her hands. “You’re thinking again.”

“I’m not.”

“You are.”

The ghost of a smile. “Then tell me what you’d prefer.”

She leaned in until her lips touched his. “Less talking.”

He understood. He drew her T-shirt up and over her head, slowly enough that she could have stopped him, and she lifted her arms and let him. The lamp stayed on. He looked at her the way he looked at nothing else, without a single note in it, and then he bent his head to her collarbone, and lower, to the curve of her breast, and she forgot whatever she’d been about to say.

She tugged at the buttons of his shirt until he took it off himself, and laughed at him for folding it, and stopped laughing when his hand slid down over her stomach and under the waistband of her shorts. He learned her the way he learned everything, by paying attention. He watched her face. He changed what he was doing when her breath caught, and did it again when she said his name, and didn’t stop until she was arching off the pillow with her fingers in his hair, shaking, his name coming out of her in two pieces.

Then she pulled him over her, impatient. He was careful, and then, when she wrapped her legs round him and told him she wasn’t made of glass, less careful. He pushed into her slowly and held still with his forehead on hers, until she moved first. They found the rhythm together, slow and then not slow at all. She held on to his shoulders. He said her name against her neck, over and over, as if it were the only word he had left. When he came apart it was with his face in her hair and her arms locked round him, and she felt him shudder and go still, and kissed the side of his head until he could breathe again.

The notebook lay open beside them with its pages undisturbed.

Later she lay with her head on his shoulder while he reached for the glass of water on the bedside table. “Which entry were you remembering just now?”

He reached for the notebook.

She caught his wrist. “No. Don’t read it to me. Tell me.”

He thought about it. “The one about the film.”

“Why?”

“Because you asked whether I was leaving.”

She looked down. “I used to ask that a lot. Do you mind?”

“No.”

She kissed his shoulder. After a moment she found the entry herself and wrote in the margin in blue.

Si-Jie’s comment: I don’t ask because I think you’ll leave. Sometimes I just like hearing you say you’re staying.

He read it and took the pen.

I’m staying.

“That’s not an observation,” she said.

“No. It’s a promise.”

She closed the notebook, and this time she put it on the bedside table herself.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the last Saturday in April Si-Yuan was home from Paris for two weeks, and the three of them went up to the university because Si-Jie said she missed it. Si-Wei said she missed Arthur, who’d been impossible to book for dinner all week because of a case. They sat on the steps by the upper courtyard in the sun: Si-Wei with a coffee, Si-Yuan in a loose white shirt with her sunglasses on.

Si-Jie was halfway through a sentence when she saw them, and stopped with her mouth open. Eliana Lin was coming up the hill from the library with her hand in Wang Yu Chen’s, their fingers laced together, not caring who saw.

“Don’t,” said Eliana.

“I haven’t said anything.”

“You’re about to.”

“I am about to. Are you two finally—” Si-Jie put a hand over her heart.

“Yes,” said Yu Chen.

Eliana turned and stared at him.

“You were taking too long,” he said.

Si-Jie made a noise like a kettle. Si-Yuan took off her sunglasses to see better. Si-Wei looked at Eliana over her coffee with the face of someone who’d predicted this on a whiteboard, and said only, “So that’s why you smile at your phone.”

“I don’t smile at my phone.”

“You absolutely do,” said all three of them.

Si-Jie couldn’t help herself. She said she needed to know what she was allowed to tell people. Eliana opened her mouth, and Si-Jie watched her decide, with Yu Chen beside her saying nothing at all and waiting to see what she’d choose.

“You can tell people we’re together,” said Eliana.

Si-Jie stepped forward and hugged her. Eliana went stiff for half a second and then hugged her back. They went on up towards the gates, and the three of them sat down again.

“Did you see how he held her hand?” said Si-Jie.

“Yes,” said Si-Wei.

Si-Jie leaned back on her elbows. “And she didn’t let go. She looks happy. Arthur should hold my hand more.”

“Doesn’t he?” said Si-Yuan.

“He does. He should do it more.”

“Then tell him.”

“I shouldn’t have to tell him.”

“That’s a dangerous philosophy,” said Si-Yuan, and put her sunglasses back on.

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening she let herself into his flat and went straight to him in the living room, where he was reading a report. “Something happened today. Eliana and Yu Chen. They held hands all the way up the hill in front of everyone, and he told us they were together before she could, and she said we could tell people.”

Arthur put the report aside. “That sounds fairly conclusive.”

“Exactly. I made a noise. Si-Yuan took her sunglasses off.”

“That’s a strong reaction from Si-Yuan.”

“It was a strong afternoon.” She sat beside him, and then she looked at the coffee table, where the notebook lay open on a fresh page dated 26 April. He saw her looking and handed her the pen.

Saw Eliana and Yu Chen holding hands on the hill. Si-Wei and Si-Yuan were there. Si-Jie made an unusual noise.

She paused, and added a line.

Everyone looked happy.

“Accurate,” said Arthur.

She turned the pen round. “Your turn. Write something about me.”

He took it and wrote under her entry.

She came home and told me about it.

She looked at the sentence, and added one of her own in blue.

Because you’re the person I want to tell things to.

He read it. She leaned over and kissed him, and when she drew back she rested her forehead on his and took his hand and laced their fingers together and held it up between them.

“Rule five. Ask me. Don’t just observe.”

He looked at their hands. “Then I’ll ask. Are you happy?”

She thought about it, and nodded. “Yes.”

“Good,” he said, and kissed her again, and didn’t let go of her hand.

Before she fell asleep she told him to write something nice about her in the morning. He said he already did. She said to write something nicer, and not to consider it, to do it. When he opened the notebook the next morning he wrote one sentence.

She is not a problem to solve. She is the person I want to spend my life learning, and she is allowed to change every answer.

chapters.title: Graduation
chapters.desc: Two gowns in the Great Hall, Si-Jie and Si-Wei; Si-Yuan on a phone at three in the morning in Paris. Her father won’t shake Sung Jae’s hand, and Si-Wei kisses him anyway. Arthur writes one line.
chapters.content:
Just after seven on a Friday in July, Arthur’s phone showed him a photograph: two women in front of a full-length mirror in graduation gowns. One was beaming, holding her cap at an angle. The other stood beside her looking a great deal more composed, though the corners of her mouth gave her away.

Si-Jie (Question Forty): WE ARE GRADUATING TODAY.

Si-Jie (Question Forty): Two gowns. Two sisters. One very proud family.

Arthur: You look happy.

Si-Jie (Question Forty): I AM.

Arthur: I can see that. The gown suits you.

Si-Jie (Question Forty): Si-Wei says you’re being evaluated today.

Arthur: By whom?

Si-Jie (Question Forty): Me.

Arthur: Understood.

Si-Jie (Question Forty): Don’t be late. And don’t sit too far away.

Arthur: I’ll sit where your family tells me.

Si-Jie (Question Forty): No. Sit where you can see me.

He looked at the photograph again.

Arthur: I will.

He finished his coffee standing at the window. He’d laid out a suit the night before, the dark grey one, and a tie she’d once told him made him look less like he was about to arrest someone. He put it on. On the way out he stopped at the flower stall by the station and stood in front of the buckets for longer than he’d have admitted to anyone, and bought white tulips, because they were the ones he knew she liked, and because he’d learned in February what her face did when he remembered something.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was at the Great Hall before nine. It was already crowded. Families moved along the rows taking photographs and hunting for their seats, and graduates in dark gowns stood in knots adjusting their caps and checking their names in the programme. He found the Yen family by the entrance.

Mr. and Mrs. Yen had come up from Taipei the night before. Si-Wei was with them, already in her gown with her cap in her hand. Si-Yuan was present only as a face on her mother’s phone. It was three in the morning in Paris, and she’d set an alarm.

“Arthur,” she said from the screen.

“Si-Yuan. You’re up early.”

“I’m up late. It depends how you count. You’re early.”

“Si-Jie asked me not to be late.”

Si-Wei looked at him. “She told you to come early, didn’t she?”

“She said not to be late.”

“That’s the same thing, coming from her.”

Their mother laughed. Then Arthur saw someone coming from the other side of the entrance: Geum Sung Jae, in a dark suit that Arthur suspected was the only one he owned, with a small bouquet in his hand. He walked straight to Si-Wei.

“You’re here,” she said.

“I said I’d come.”

“You could have been doing something else.”

“I could have.”

She looked at the flowers. “Are those for me?”

“No. I brought them for the university.”

Si-Wei gave him a look, and he handed them over. Then he saw Arthur.

“Chen.”

“Geum.”

There was a short pause in which neither man looked especially pleased.

Si-Wei sighed. “It’s a graduation. Please behave like normal people.”

“I am behaving normally,” said Arthur.

Sung Jae glanced at him. “So am I.”

“That’s unfortunate,” muttered Si-Wei, and her mother laughed again.

Then Si-Jie came in through the side entrance with two other graduates, holding her cap. Her gown was slightly crooked. She was talking to the girl beside her, and a small pin held her hair back on one side. She looked round the entrance once, twice. Then she saw Arthur, and her face changed. Not dramatically. Just enough. Her smile widened and her steps quickened.

“Arthur!”

He turned.

She stopped in front of him, extremely pleased with herself. “You’re here.”

“I said I would be.”

“I know. But you’re here.”

He looked at her gown. “Congratulations. You look beautiful.”

Her smile went soft. “Thank you.”

She stepped in and hugged him, and he put his arms round her carefully, mindful of the gown and the cap.

She pressed her cheek to his chest. “You’re the first person I found.”

“I noticed.”

She pulled back and looked over her shoulder. “Si-Wei! Over here.”

The two sisters stood together in their gowns, and their mother lifted her phone at once. “Both of you. Closer.”

“We’re already close,” said Si-Wei.

“Closer.”

Si-Jie hooked her arm through her sister’s.

On the screen Si-Yuan was smiling. “Turn a little. Si-Jie, your cap’s crooked.”

“It isn’t.”

Si-Wei straightened it for her. “It is.”

“You’re supposed to be on my side.”

“I’m on the side of correctly worn caps.”

Arthur reached over and straightened it again. “There.”

She looked up at him and said thank you, and their mother took a photograph, and another, and another.

“One more,” she said.

Si-Wei sighed. “Mama.”

“Let her take them. You’ll want them later,” said Si-Yuan from Paris.

That quietened both of them. For a moment they stood together, shoulders touching, two matching gowns and two different expressions, and their mother lowered the phone with her eyes shining.

“Both my girls,” she said.

Si-Jie reached for her hand. Si-Wei leaned in. On the screen Si-Yuan asked whether finishing a film in Paris counted as graduating too, and Si-Wei said no, and Si-Yuan called that cruel, and everyone laughed. Arthur stood a little behind them and didn’t interrupt. He watched.

✦ ✦ ✦

The ceremony began a little after ten. Arthur sat several rows behind the graduates, beside Mr. and Mrs. Yen, while her mother held the phone upright for Si-Yuan and whispered at it every few minutes to ask whether she could see.

Mr. Yen leaned towards him. “Long ceremony.”

“Probably.”

“Have you been to many?”

“Not many graduations.”

Mr. Yen nodded and looked back at the stage. The hall settled. Names were read, speeches delivered, and lines of graduates moved in good order. Arthur listened politely, but his attention kept going back to the row where Si-Jie sat. She was trying to look composed, and not entirely succeeding. At one point she turned her head and her eyes went searching across the audience. He watched her look. Then she found him, and her face lit, and he gave her a small nod, and she turned back to the stage satisfied.

A few minutes later she did it again. This time he lifted his hand.

Near the back, by the doors, Sung Jae stood with his hands folded in front of him. There’d been no seat for him in the family’s row, and nobody had offered to find one. He didn’t seem to expect it. He watched the stage the whole time, and when Si-Wei turned round once, Arthur saw her find him there and turn back without any expression at all, which in Si-Wei meant a great deal.

He took the black notebook out of his inside pocket and opened it to a clean page. There were plenty of things he could have written: the way she sat on the edge of her seat, the way she fiddled with her gown whenever she was nervous, the way she kept checking the audience while pretending to watch the stage. He didn’t write any of them. He wrote one line.

11 July 2025. She looked for me first.

He closed the notebook. When her name was called she stood, straightened her gown and walked to the stage. She climbed the steps, took her certificate and shook the official’s hand while the photographer took her picture, and for a second she looked out at the audience again, not long, just enough to find him. He met her eyes. She smiled and went on across the stage.

When she sat down Si-Wei leaned over. “Stop smiling.”

“I can’t.”

“You look ridiculous.”

“You’re smiling too.”

Si-Wei looked straight ahead, and her mouth curved anyway.

A little later it was Si-Wei’s name, and when she came back from the stage Si-Jie clapped harder than anyone round her.

“You’re embarrassing,” said Si-Wei, sitting down.

Si-Jie put her head on her sister’s shoulder for a second. “I’m proud of you. Congratulations.”

Si-Wei’s face went soft. “Congratulations to you too.”

Their mother was crying. On the phone, Si-Yuan had gone quiet.

✦ ✦ ✦

Outside the hall the day was bright, and families were gathering on the steps and along the paths, taking photographs under the university banners. Their mother called her daughters over at once, and Si-Yuan’s face appeared on the screen again.

“Do we look like graduates?” said Si-Jie.

“You look like yourselves in gowns.”

“That’s not very poetic.”

“The gowns are doing the poetry,” said Si-Yuan, and Si-Wei laughed.

Their father hugged Si-Jie first, then Si-Wei, and told them both they’d worked hard.

Then he turned to Arthur and held out his hand. “Thank you for coming.”

Arthur took it. The handshake was firm and warm and deliberate.

“She talks about you quite a lot,” said Mr. Yen.

“More than quite a lot,” said Si-Wei.

Si-Jie turned on her. “Si-Wei!”

Her father smiled. “She seems happy.”

Arthur’s face softened. “She makes me happy too.”

Mr. Yen looked at him, and nodded. “I can see that.”

Sung Jae had been standing a little way off, letting the family have their photographs. Now he came over, said congratulations to Si-Wei, and turned to her father and held out his hand.

“Uncle.”

Mr. Yen looked at the hand. Then at Sung Jae. He didn’t take it. “Congratulations to my daughter,” he said.

Sung Jae lowered his hand. “Thank you, Uncle.”

Si-Wei shut her eyes briefly. “Papa. Please.”

“I congratulated you.”

“That isn’t what I meant.”

“I know,” said her father.

Sung Jae said nothing. He stood beside Si-Wei with his face perfectly steady. Arthur watched and didn’t intervene. Then Si-Wei turned, took Sung Jae’s face in both hands and kissed him, in front of her father and half the faculty, and let go and picked up her cap, and that was the end of it.

Mr. Yen turned to his wife. “Let’s take another photograph.”

Si-Jie leaned in towards her sister and whispered that that had gone well.

“Don’t.”

“I’m being supportive.”

“You’re being irritating.”

“Congratulations,” said Si-Jie, and Si-Wei laughed despite herself.

✦ ✦ ✦

The photographs took nearly half an hour. Their mother wanted one of both sisters. Their father wanted one of the whole family. Si-Yuan demanded a screenshot of the video call and then complained that she looked as though she was attending from inside a cupboard. Si-Jie had one taken with Si-Wei, one with her parents, one with Si-Yuan on the phone, and one with Arthur. In that one she stood close against his side with her arm round his waist while he held the white tulips he’d brought her. She looked at the camera. He looked at her.

“Arthur, look at the camera.”

“I am.”

“No, you’re looking at me.”

“I know.”

She laughed, and their mother took it anyway, and said it was a nice one. Si-Jie looked at it on the screen and decided she liked it.

While the sisters posed for the family one, their mother handed the phone to Arthur so that she could fix Si-Wei’s collar, and Si-Yuan’s face looked up at him out of the dark of a Paris night.

“Turn me round. I can’t see them.”

He turned the phone towards the steps.

“She looked for you. In the hall. Mama had me pointed at the stage the whole time, and I watched her look,” said Si-Yuan.

“I know.”

She was quiet, watching her sisters argue about where to stand. “Of course you do. It’s three in the morning and I’m crying at a graduation through a phone. So be kind to her.”

“I intend to.”

“I know you do. That’s why I’m only saying it once.”

Their mother took the phone back, and Si-Yuan’s voice went back to telling everyone to move to the left.

Then Sung Jae drew Si-Wei aside to answer a message, and her parents started towards the car, and for a moment Si-Jie and Arthur were alone on the steps. She looked at him.

“Did you write something?”

He didn’t answer at once.

Her eyes narrowed. “You did.”

“Yes. Something about you.”

“That’s not specific.”

He took out the notebook and opened it.

She read the line, and read it again, and looked up. “That’s all? Only one line?”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“Because it was the first thing I noticed.”

She stared at him, and then she smiled. “That’s very unfair.”

“Why?”

“Because now I want to kiss you.”

“That sounds manageable.”

She laughed and stepped closer. He closed the notebook and slipped it back into his jacket, and she put both hands on his chest. “Congratulations to me.”

“Congratulations.”

“And to Si-Wei. And to you.”

He looked at her. “Why me?”

“For surviving my final year.”

“I wasn’t aware it was difficult.”

“You’re unbelievable.”

“I’ve been told.”

She took hold of his lapels and pulled him down and kissed him. It was a simple kiss at first. Then she kissed him again, slower, smiling when he reached for her waist. When they parted she stayed close.

“Did you know I was looking for you?”

“Yes.”

“How?”

“I saw you.”

“That’s a very short answer.”

He brushed his thumb against her cheek. “It’s the whole of it. I was looking for you too.”

Her face softened, and for a moment the noise round them seemed to fall away. She kissed him once more, and this time he kissed her back without hesitating. From a little way off, Si-Wei called her name.

“What?”

“Mama wants another photograph!”

She called back that she was coming, and turned to Arthur. “Wait here.”

“I will.”

She went a few steps down, and turned round. “Arthur? Don’t leave.”

His face softened. “I won’t.”

She smiled and ran back to her family. Arthur stayed on the steps and watched her join her parents and her sister, her gown moving round her ankles and her laugh carrying across the courtyard. Then he took the notebook out once more and added a second line under the first.

She asked me not to leave. I told her I wouldn’t.

He closed it. Across the courtyard Si-Jie looked back, found him, and smiled. This time he didn’t need to write it down to know what it meant.

chapters.title: Her Parents
chapters.desc: She takes him to Taipei to meet her parents, and he profiles them at dinner by accident. He tells her father his own tell. Her mother likes him for it.
chapters.content:
Arthur had met her parents before: briefly, at her graduation, where he’d shaken her father’s hand and exchanged polite greetings with her mother and been photographed with the family while Si-Yuan watched from Paris through a phone. That had been a public occasion. This was different. In August they flew to Taipei, and this time he was going to their house.

“You’re quiet,” said Si-Jie from the passenger seat of the hire car.

“I’m thinking.”

“About my parents? Are you nervous?”

“No.”

“Not even a little?”

“I’ve met them.”

“You met them for about twenty minutes.”

“Twenty-three.”

She stared at him. “You counted?”

“I was aware of the time.”

“That’s worse.”

He kept his eyes on the road. She leaned back, thoroughly entertained. “Don’t worry. My parents like you.”

“I haven’t given them a reason not to.”

“That’s not the same as liking you.”

He considered it. “Your mother smiled when we met.”

“Mama smiles at everyone.”

“Your father shook my hand.”

“Papa shakes everyone’s hand.”

“He didn’t shake Geum Sung Jae’s.”

Si-Jie burst out laughing. “That’s true.”

“Then perhaps I have an advantage.”

She turned in her seat. “Don’t get too confident. Papa thinks you’re a bit strange. You look at people as if you’re trying to solve them. Arthur. Please don’t profile my parents.”

“I don’t intend to.”

“Promise?”

He paused. “I’ll try.”

“That’s not a promise.”

“It’s an honest answer.”

She sighed theatrically. “You’re going to be difficult.”

He reached across the console and took her hand for a moment. “Your parents raised you. I have every reason to be polite.”

She looked down at their hands, and smiled. “Good answer.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The house was in a quiet residential street on the edge of the city: large, modern and plainly expensive. The front door opened onto a wide living room with warm stone floors, carefully chosen furniture and a long window over the garden. There were fresh flowers on the dining table, family photographs all down the hall, and enough small things on every surface to make it feel lived in rather than staged. It was new money, but not careless money. They’d spent it on being comfortable.

Si-Jie was barely through the door before her mother appeared and hugged her, and then looked past her. “Arthur. Welcome.”

“Thank you for having me, Mrs. Yen.”

“Don’t be so formal. Call me Auntie, if you’re comfortable.”

“Of course, Auntie.”

She took the gift he’d brought and told him he shouldn’t have, and he said it was a pleasure, and she told them to come in, they’d been travelling. Si-Jie kicked off her shoes and took his hand. “Come on. I’ll show you round.”

“Don’t take him upstairs. Dinner’s nearly ready,” her mother called after them.

“We’re not going upstairs!”

“You always say that.”

Si-Jie looked at Arthur. “She’s suspicious of me.”

“Is she wrong?”

“Arthur!”

He smiled: a small expression, but her mother saw it, and looked between the two of them, and smiled to herself.

Her father was in the living room by the window, reading something on a tablet. He looked up. “You’re home.”

“Papa, this is Arthur.”

Mr. Yen stood and shook his hand. “I know. How was the journey?”

“Fine. The traffic from the airport was manageable.”

“Traffic in this city is rarely manageable.”

“That’s true.”

Mr. Yen waved him towards the sofa. “Sit. Your auntie’s making too much food again.”

From the dining room Mrs. Yen called that she’d heard that.

“Good,” said her husband.

Si-Jie laughed and sat down next to Arthur and leaned close. “See? Normal.”

He looked round the room. “Your definition of normal is unusually broad.”

She nudged his knee.

✦ ✦ ✦

Dinner was generous: steamed fish, braised beef, greens, soup, and several dishes Si-Jie announced were her favourites. Her mother kept putting food on Arthur’s plate.

“Eat more. You’re too thin.”

“She says that to everyone,” said Si-Jie.

“Not everyone,” said her father.

Mrs. Yen gave him a look. “Don’t interrupt.”

Arthur bent his head to hide a smile, and Si-Jie nudged him under the table and told him not to laugh, and he said he wasn’t, and she said he was. Across the table her father had moved on to his work.

“Si-Jie says you’re a profiler.”

“Yes.”

“Criminal behaviour?”

“Behavioural analysis for criminal investigations.”

“That must be difficult work. Do you work with suspects?”

“Sometimes. More often I look at the behavioural evidence, the victims and the patterns, and offer the investigators hypotheses.”

“So you tell the police who did it?”

The answer came at once. “No. I help investigators think about what the evidence might suggest. A profile doesn’t establish guilt, and it doesn’t replace evidence or investigation.”

Mr. Yen seemed pleased with the distinction. “Good. I’d worry if you claimed otherwise.”

Si-Jie smiled into her soup.

“Do you find it hard to separate work from the rest of your life?”

Arthur considered it. “Sometimes. Some habits are hard to switch off.”

“For example?”

He glanced at Si-Jie, who was concentrating on taking a small bone out of her fish. “Noticing things. Changes in routine. Contradictions. When someone says one thing and seems to be thinking about another.”

Her father smiled. “That sounds exhausting.”

“It can be.”

Mrs. Yen put another piece of fish on his plate. “Then you should eat properly. You can’t spend all your time thinking.”

“Yes, Auntie.”

Si-Jie looked at him. “You’re very obedient today.”

“I’m being fed.”

She laughed, and her father watched her. “Is she always like this?”

“Like what?” said Si-Jie.

“Talking while other people are eating.”

“Papa!”

Arthur answered before she could go on. “Yes.”

She turned on him. “You’re supposed to defend me.”

“I was asked a question.”

“You’re supposed to lie.”

“That would be inappropriate.”

Her mother laughed. “He’s honest. I like that.”

Si-Jie gave Arthur a look of deep betrayal, and he put a piece of fish on her plate, and she accepted it.

✦ ✦ ✦

It happened over tea. Dinner was over and they’d moved to the living room. Mrs. Yen was arranging fruit on a tray. Mr. Yen was pouring the tea. Si-Jie was beside Arthur, showing her mother photographs from the graduation.

“Look at Si-Wei’s face in this one.”

Her mother laughed. “She looks exactly like your father when he’s annoyed.”

Mr. Yen glanced over. “I don’t look like that.”

“You do,” said his wife.

Si-Jie turned to Arthur. “Does Papa look like Si-Wei when he’s annoyed?”

Arthur looked up. Mr. Yen was holding the teapot with his face perfectly composed, and his thumb pressed against the handle. Arthur answered before he’d thought better of it.

“Yes. Your father goes quieter when he’s displeased. He also pauses before he answers, particularly when he thinks a direct answer might be unnecessarily harsh.”

The room went quiet. Arthur realised what he’d done. Si-Jie turned slowly to look at him. Her mother stopped arranging the fruit. Mr. Yen put down the teapot.

“That’s interesting. Did you just profile me?”

Arthur set down his cup. “Not intentionally. I apologise.”

“Not intentionally,” Si-Jie repeated, looking delighted, and he gave her a warning glance, and she pressed her lips together.

Mr. Yen leaned back. “Then tell me something else.”

“Mr. Yen—”

“You’ve started. Finish.”

“Papa, don’t encourage him,” said Si-Jie.

Her father ignored her. Arthur could have offered something vague. He chose something specific instead.

“You tend to ask questions when you already have an answer you prefer. You leave the question open, but your attention sharpens when the other person gets close to the answer you expect.”

Mr. Yen’s eyebrows went up. A short silence followed. Mrs. Yen looked at her husband, and then at Arthur. “That’s true.”

“Is it?” said her husband.

“Very.”

Si-Jie started laughing. Her father looked faintly amused. “And what does that tell you?”

Arthur answered carefully. “That you like to understand someone’s reasoning before you tell them what you think. You don’t necessarily want agreement. You want to know whether they’ve considered the same things you have.”

Mr. Yen looked at him, and smiled. “That’s rather accurate. Does my daughter do it too?”

Arthur glanced at Si-Jie, who shook her head at once. “Don’t.”

He looked back at her father. “Yes. Differently. She asks because she wants to understand the answer. But if she thinks someone’s avoiding the question, she asks again. Usually with less patience.”

Mrs. Yen laughed. “That’s exactly right.”

Si-Jie covered her face. “Why did I bring you here?”

“You invited me.”

“Regrettably.”

He smiled, and Mr. Yen laughed out loud. It was the first time that evening he’d laughed quite so openly.

✦ ✦ ✦

Mrs. Yen brought the fruit over and sat down opposite him, and studied him. “Can I ask you something? Do you notice everything about Si-Jie?”

Si-Jie nearly choked on her tea. “Mama!”

“What? I’m curious.”

Arthur thought about it. “Not everything.”

“That sounds like a professional answer.”

“It’s the true one.”

“Then what do you notice?”

Si-Jie looked at him with a familiar warning in her face. Not because she wanted him to lie: because she knew how easily he could turn an ordinary question into an analysis.

Arthur put his cup down. “I notice when she’s happy. When she’s tired. When she’s pretending not to be upset. But I don’t always know why. So I ask.”

Si-Jie had gone quiet. Her mother looked at him a moment, and smiled. “That’s good. She’s always been expressive. Even when she was little I could tell what she wanted from her face. Your father isn’t so easy to read.”

Mr. Yen looked up. “Why am I involved again?”

“Because Arthur noticed something.”

Arthur glanced at him. “Your tell is your hands. When you’re weighing something important you go very still, but your fingers keep moving against whatever you’re holding. You were doing it when we talked about my work. You stopped when I said a profile doesn’t establish guilt. I assumed that distinction mattered to you.”

Mr. Yen looked down at the teacup in his hands. Then he smiled. “You’re right.”

“Papa, you really do that?”

“Apparently,” said her father.

Mrs. Yen laughed and turned to Arthur. “What about your own tell?”

Something changed in his face. It was slight, but Si-Jie saw it, and sat up. “Oh. You’ve got one.”

“I didn’t say I hadn’t.”

“Then tell us.”

He glanced at Mr. Yen, who was watching him with open curiosity. He could have declined. He answered instead.

“When I’m uncomfortable, I become more precise. I choose my words more carefully. I go quieter. I answer only what I’ve been asked. It’s useful at work. Less useful elsewhere.”

“Why?” said Mr. Yen.

He looked at Si-Jie. “Because people sometimes take it for distance. She used to think I was withdrawing when I did it.”

Her eyes came up. “Used to?”

“Sometimes I still do it. But I’m learning to tell her when I need time, instead of making her guess.”

The room went quiet. Not uncomfortable: thoughtful. Mrs. Yen looked at him, and smiled, and reached for the teapot. “That’s a good thing to know about yourself. Have more tea.”

Si-Jie leaned close to him and whispered that he’d just told her parents his weakness.

“You asked me to be honest.”

“I didn’t ask you to confess your entire personality.”

“I didn’t. Only part of it.”

She bit her lip to stop herself laughing.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later, while Mr. Yen was showing Arthur photographs of the garden renovation, her mother asked Si-Jie to help in the kitchen, and turned round the moment they were through the door.

“He’s lovely.”

Si-Jie smiled. “You’re not just saying that?”

“No. He listens. And he’s careful with his words.”

“Sometimes too careful.”

Her mother started arranging the leftover fruit. “That may be his work. Does it bother you, the way he keeps looking at you?”

“No. I like it.”

“Then that’s what matters.”

Si-Jie reached for a grape, and her mother tapped her hand and told her to wash it first, and Si-Jie laughed.

Her mother picked up the fruit knife again. “There’s something else I like. He told your father his own tell. People who spend their lives studying others sometimes forget to let themselves be seen. Your father likes people who can be honest without trying to impress him.”

“Arthur doesn’t really know how to impress people.”

“Good. Then he won’t try too hard.”

They went back through. Arthur was still talking to her father, more relaxed now, with his jacket off and his sleeves folded neatly at the wrists, looking at something on the tablet. He said something, and Mr. Yen laughed.

Si-Jie stopped beside her mother. “Look. He’s smiling.”

Her mother looked, and smiled too. Then, quietly: “Keep him.”

“Mama.”

“What?”

“That’s the plan.”

✦ ✦ ✦

It was nearly ten when they stepped out onto the balcony. The city lights stretched out beyond the garden, and inside her parents were still talking.

Si-Jie leaned on the railing. “You’re popular. Mama likes you. Papa likes you. He even showed you the garden.”

“He’s proud of it.”

“He’s been talking about that garden for three months. Do you know what I found most interesting? You told them your own tell.”

“Your mother asked.”

“You could have been vague.”

He was quiet a moment. “I didn’t want to be. I don’t want you to be the only person who has to explain me. You shouldn’t have to translate my silences for everyone. Or for yourself.”

Her face softened. “Arthur.”

He reached for her hand. “I know I still get difficult when I’m uncomfortable. I know I still go into my head. But I don’t want you carrying the work of guessing what I’m not saying.”

She stepped closer. “You’re getting better at this.”

He looked at her face. “I’m trying. Your mother asked whether I notice everything about you. I told her no. I’d rather ask you. Are you glad I came?”

“Very.”

“Even though I profiled your father?”

“Because of it. You looked so serious when you realised what you’d done.”

He gave her a look, and she laughed and kissed him, and his hand settled at her waist.

“Welcome home,” she whispered, close against him.

From inside, her father called that her mother had packed fruit for them.

She shut her eyes. “Papa!”

Arthur smiled. “Your family is attentive.”

“My family is nosy.”

“They’re kind.”

She looked at him, and smiled. “Yes. They are.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They left a little after ten with enough fruit, snacks and food for several days. Her father walked Arthur to the door and told him to come again. At the car Si-Jie caught his wrist before he could close her door.

“Thank you for coming.”

“Thank you for bringing me.”

She kissed him, and he cupped her cheek for a moment. “One more thing. Mama asked me whether you’re always this serious. I said you’re serious at first, but you’re actually quite soft. With me.”

He considered that. “That’s different.”

“I know.”

He shut the door gently and walked round the car. Her phone buzzed.

Mama (Packs Fruit): Arthur is a good man. Be good to each other.

Si-Jie: I will.

Mama (Packs Fruit): And tell him to come for dinner again.

She turned the phone towards him as he got in. “You’re invited back.”

He read it. “Good.”

“You’re not worried about being profiled by my mother?”

“I think she’s already decided what she thinks of me.”

Si-Jie leaned over and kissed his cheek. “She has. She likes you.”

Arthur started the car. For once he didn’t try to work out what that meant. He reached across the console, took her hand, and held it all the way back to the hotel.

chapters.title: Her Placement
chapters.desc: Her placement at a charity for women who are being stalked. Her first case is a nurse followed for a year. He searches records he has no right to, and she finds out. He reports himself.
chapters.content:
In September Si-Jie started a master’s, and with it a placement at a charity for victims of stalking and harassment. On the first day she came back to his flat with a tote bag, a new lanyard and an expression Arthur had learned to associate with excitement.

He looked up from his laptop. “How was it?”

She dropped her bag by the sofa. “Good. Very good.”

He closed the laptop halfway. “Tell me.”

She sat down beside him and tucked her legs under herself. “I met everyone. My supervisor’s lovely. There’s a counselling team, a legal support team, and people who help clients with safety planning and documentation. They work with the police too, when clients want that. I’m mostly helping with intake and organising information and preparing resources. I won’t be handling anything on my own, obviously.”

“Good.”

She smiled. “I knew you’d say that.”

“Would you prefer something else?”

“Maybe: Si-Jie, you’re going to be wonderful.”

He looked at her. “Si-Jie, you’re going to be wonderful.”

She grinned. “See? You can do it.”

He reached for her hand. “What kind of cases?”

“Mostly women being stalked or harassed. Some of them for months. Some for years.”

His expression changed, slightly.

She saw it. “Arthur. Don’t make that face.”

“What face?”

“Your work face. Your eyebrows are doing something.”

He was quiet a moment. “Stalking cases can be difficult. Some perpetrators escalate when they think they’re losing access to the victim.”

“That’s why the charity has safety protocols. Nobody handles these cases alone.”

“Good.”

She pointed at him. “One more good and I’m charging you.”

He took her hand and kissed her knuckles. “Then I’ll try something else. Tell me about your supervisor.”

She smiled and began, and for the next forty minutes Arthur listened to every detail. He asked about her responsibilities, her training, the confidentiality policy and the procedure for raising concerns. All reasonable questions. At the time she didn’t think much of it. She was too happy about her first day.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her first case came in the second week: a nurse in her early thirties. Si-Jie wasn’t allowed to share identifying details outside the charity, and she was careful. She didn’t tell Arthur the woman’s name, where she worked or where she lived. She told him only what she was allowed to, in general terms.

The woman had been followed for about a year. At first the incidents had seemed unconnected: a man near her workplace, someone waiting across the road when her shift ended, messages from accounts she didn’t recognise. Then they became persistent. She’d started changing her routines. She didn’t like leaving work alone. She’d stopped going to certain places in case he was there. In the intake session she’d apologised several times: for taking up their time, for being frightened, for not reporting everything sooner. That was the part Si-Jie remembered most. Her supervisor had told the woman gently that she didn’t have to justify being afraid.

Afterwards Si-Jie spent nearly an hour organising the information under her supervisor’s eye. She kept what the client had experienced separate from what she suspected. She noted dates where there were dates, marked the gaps, and was careful not to present guesses as facts.

When she got in, Arthur was in the kitchen. “You’re late.”

She put her bag down and washed her hands. “Sorry. A longer session. She’s a nurse. Someone’s been following her for about a year.”

His face went still. “Someone known to her?”

“I can’t discuss identifying details.”

“I understand.”

“She’s frightened. And she kept apologising for being frightened. I think that was the hardest part.”

He put down the knife he’d been using. “Is there an immediate safety concern?”

“Her supervisor assessed that with her. There’s a safety plan.”

“Good.”

Si-Jie looked at him. “You’re doing it again. Thinking.”

“That’s what people generally do when they listen.”

She laughed a little. He came over and put a hand on her shoulder and asked whether the session had been hard, and whether she wanted to talk about it. She thought about it, and nodded, and did: not about the woman’s identity or anything private, only about how hard it had been to hear someone describe a year of fear as though it were an inconvenience she was causing other people. He listened. He didn’t interrupt. When she’d finished he kissed her cheek and said she’d done well.

At the time she thought that was the end of it. It wasn’t.

✦ ✦ ✦

Arthur didn’t like the placement. He’d known that from the beginning. He didn’t like the subject matter, or the chance of escalation, or the fact that she now spent several days a week among people whose lives had been wrecked by somebody else’s fixation. He knew the work mattered. He knew she was trained and supervised. He also knew, with a professional certainty that made it worse, how much harm a determined stalker could do.

He told himself his concern was reasonable. Then he began to check.

The first time, he read the charity’s public information and its safeguarding procedures. The second time, he searched its name alongside recent reports of stalking cases. The third time, he used a professional database he had through work to look up a man whose name had appeared in a publicly reported case connected to the charity. He told himself it was background research. Then he checked another, and another.

He had no legitimate reason to access those records. He wasn’t assigned to the cases. He had no authority to look into the charity’s clients. He did it anyway. He checked names he came across through his ordinary work and looked for connections, previous reports, any sign of threatening behaviour. He began keeping a private list. Not of her clients: of the men he thought might be a risk.

He told himself it was a precaution. It wasn’t. It was control dressed up as protection, and he was good enough at his job to see the difference. He simply chose not to apply it to himself.

✦ ✦ ✦

By the third week Si-Jie had noticed. It started over breakfast.

“Did you see anyone yesterday?”

She looked up from her toast. “At work? Lots of people.”

“Any men?”

She blinked. “Some.”

“Any who made you uncomfortable?”

“No.”

He nodded, and she kept eating. A few days later he asked whether she was still working with the same supervisor. Then whether the charity had received any threats. Then whether any of the cases involved men who’d been investigated before. She answered what she could. The questions kept coming.

One evening she was sitting on his bed reading through her placement notes, and he was at the desk.

“How was work?”

“Fine.”

“Any difficult cases? Anyone you were concerned about?”

She stopped reading. “Arthur. Why do you keep asking about the men?”

He turned round. “Because your work involves men who’ve been accused of stalking or harassment. It’s relevant to your safety.”

“I’m supervised. We follow procedures. I’m not meeting these people alone.”

“I know.”

“Then what are you worried about?”

“That someone might become interested in you because of your work. You’re with people who are frightened. You’re helping them organise what’s happened to them. Some perpetrators react badly when a victim gets support.”

“Arthur, I’m not investigating anyone. I’m not confronting anyone. I’m on a supervised placement.”

“I know what your role is.”

“Then why are you asking me to account for every man I meet?”

He didn’t answer at once.

She watched him. “Have you been looking into the cases?”

His silence lasted a second too long.

She sat up. “Arthur.”

“I’ve looked at some publicly available information.”

“About what?”

“People connected to the cases. Men whose names appeared in the material.”

She stared at him. “How did you get those names?”

He didn’t answer, and that was enough.

Her face changed. “Did you access work records?”

He closed the file on his desk. “Si-Jie—”

“Did you?”

“Yes.”

The room went quiet. She looked at him blankly. “You looked up the men in my clients’ files?”

“Not every one. Some.”

“How many?”

He didn’t answer.

She stood up. “How many?”

“Enough.”

She took a step back, and for a moment she couldn’t find the words. Then, barely above a whisper: “Did you look at the women too? Their personal information? Their addresses?”

“I didn’t use anyone’s details to contact them.”

“That’s not what I asked.”

He held her eyes. “I saw information I had no legitimate reason to access.”

Her mouth tightened. “Do you hear yourself? Those are real people, Arthur. They’re not suspects in one of your investigations. They’re women who came to a charity because someone’s made them afraid to live normally.”

“I know.”

“Then why are you treating their cases like yours?”

He stood up. “Because you’re involved.”

It came too quickly. Si-Jie looked at him, and for the first time that evening she seemed genuinely frightened of what he might say next.

✦ ✦ ✦

She took a breath. “Arthur, listen to me. I understand my work makes you uncomfortable. I understand you know more than most people about how stalking escalates. I know you’re worried about me. But you cannot use your position to look into people I’m working with.”

“I know.”

“Then stop. Stop checking the men in my files. Stop searching their names. Stop looking for connections. Stop treating everyone who might be in a client’s life as someone you have to investigate.”

His jaw tightened. “I can’t ignore a potential threat.”

“You can recognise a threat without secretly investigating everyone round me. Let the people responsible for those cases handle them. You keep telling me a profile isn’t proof. That a pattern doesn’t establish guilt. That investigators have to follow evidence. Then why are you doing exactly what you tell other people not to do? You’re making assumptions about men you’ve never met, from information that isn’t yours to use. You’re taking my work and turning it into your investigation.”

“I’m trying to protect you.”

Her voice cracked. “I believe you. That’s what makes this so hard.”

He looked at her. She was trying hard not to cry.

“You’re not protecting me if you make decisions about my life without asking me. You’re not protecting those women by going through their information without permission. And you’re certainly not helping me do my job.”

His face had gone unreadable. She hated that expression. Not because she couldn’t read it: because she knew exactly what it meant. He was retreating into the part of himself that could make any uncomfortable feeling sound like a logical conclusion.

“Say something,” she whispered.

“I don’t think I have a defence.”

She gave a small laugh with no humour in it. “Good. I didn’t ask for one.”

“I’ll stop.”

“Not just because I caught you. I need you to understand that I’m allowed to do this work. I’m allowed to meet people and hear difficult things. I’m allowed a professional life that makes you uncomfortable. If something really happens, I’ll tell you. I’ll ask for help if I need it. But you cannot turn every person I meet into a threat you have to eliminate.”

His face changed at the last word. “I wouldn’t—”

She wiped her cheek. “You’re already doing it. I don’t want to be afraid to tell you about my day in case you start searching for someone.”

He looked at her. “I’m sorry.”

She nodded, and didn’t move towards him. “Your job gives you access to things other people don’t have. That doesn’t mean you can use it whenever you’re frightened. Will you disclose what you accessed and report it through the proper process?”

He paused, and nodded. “Yes.”

She picked up her phone.

“Are you leaving?” said Arthur.

“I haven’t decided.”

“All right.”

She sat down on the edge of the bed, and for a while neither of them spoke. Then she said she’d had a hard day. One of the women had cried because she thought she was wasting their time, and Si-Jie had spent half an hour telling her she didn’t need to apologise for asking for help. “And then I came here, and you made me feel my work was something dangerous I had to justify to you. I don’t want that.”

“I know.”

“Do you?”

He nodded. “I do.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t try to touch her that night. He sat beside her and left enough space for her to decide whether she wanted him closer. After several minutes she reached for his hand, and he took it.

“I’m not asking you to stop worrying. I’m asking you to stop acting on it without me,” she said.

He looked at their hands. “I’ve spent most of my life treating uncertainty as something to reduce.”

“And I’m not an uncertainty. Neither are my clients.”

“No,” he said.

She leaned her head against his shoulder, and he didn’t move until she’d settled, and then his arm came round her. He said he was sorry again. This time she didn’t answer at once. When she did, it was a whisper. “I believe you regret it. But I need to see what you do next.”

“I understand.”

She stayed beside him. Not because everything was fine, but because she still wanted to be there. There was a difference.

✦ ✦ ✦

The next morning Arthur was at the task force earlier than usual. He went to the appropriate supervisor, disclosed which records he’d searched without any connection to his assigned work, and asked for guidance on the formal reporting process. He didn’t call it a precaution. He didn’t mention her placement as an excuse. He accepted that his conduct needed review. At nine that evening he wrote to her.

Arthur: I disclosed the access this morning and I’ve followed the reporting process. I won’t search your clients or anyone connected to their cases again. You don’t need to reassure me about your placement.

A few minutes passed.

Si-Jie (Question Forty): Thank you for telling me. I had a hard day again.

He didn’t ask for names. He didn’t ask whether there were men involved.

Arthur: Do you want to tell me about it?

Si-Jie (Question Forty): Yes. But I don’t want you to investigate anyone. I just want you to listen.

Arthur: I’m listening.

So she told him: about a woman who’d finally agreed to accept help, and a supervisor who’d been patient, and the small relief on someone’s face when she understood she was being believed. Arthur read every message. He didn’t search a single name or open a single database. He didn’t turn what she told him into a list of risks. At the end he wrote that he was glad the woman had had someone there, and she wrote back that she was too, and thanked him for listening.

He’d once believed that protecting someone meant seeing every possible danger before it reached them. She was teaching him that sometimes it meant something much less dramatic: respecting what someone had chosen to do, and not taking control, and listening to a woman talk about her hard day without trying to turn the world into a list of people to investigate.

✦ ✦ ✦

That weekend she came over with her placement bag and a takeaway. Arthur was at the dining table with the notebook beside him.

“Are you writing?”

“Not about you.”

“Good.” She sat down and opened the containers, and for a while they ate in silence.

“I want to add something to our rules,” he said, and turned the notebook towards her. On a blank page he’d written two lines.

A concern is not permission.
If I am worried about something in her life, I ask her. I do not investigate it behind her back.

She read them and took his pen and wrote in the margin.

And if I say I don’t want you to do something, you don’t decide you know better.

“Agreed,” said Arthur.

She put the pen down and reached across the table for his hand. “I don’t need you to be less protective. I need you to trust me.”

He turned his hand over and held hers properly. “I’m learning.”

“I know. But don’t make me teach you the same thing twice.”

“I’ll try not to.”

“Arthur.”

“I won’t.”

She smiled and leaned across the table and kissed him: brief, gentle and deliberately ordinary. When she sat back he asked whether that meant they were all right.

She picked up her chopsticks. “It means I wanted to kiss you. And that I love you. It doesn’t mean you get to stop working on this. Now eat. You’re getting thin.”

“Your mother said the same thing.”

“Mama’s usually right,” said Si-Jie, and he began to eat, and for once he let her look after him without trying to work out what it meant.

chapters.title: He Stops
chapters.desc: Every time he wants to check, he tells her instead, and she counts them in the notebook with a star. Seven in October. She rewards him, on her terms.
chapters.epigraph: “Don’t thank me for trusting you. Keep giving me reasons to.”
chapters.content:
The first time Arthur wanted to check, it was a Wednesday night at the start of October. He was at his desk reading an investigation report. Si-Jie was in the shower, and her phone was charging beside his laptop, and a notification came up on its screen: a message from her placement supervisor.

He didn’t read it. He looked away. Then, almost on its own, his mind began to build questions. Was it about a new case? Had something happened? Was there a new client? Had someone made a threat? He knew the answers were none of his business. He also knew exactly where he could find them if he wanted to. His hand moved towards his laptop, and stopped.

He sat there for several seconds. Then he picked up his phone.

Arthur: I want to check something.

Si-Jie (Question Forty): What?

Arthur: Your supervisor sent you a message. I saw the notification. I want to know whether it’s about a case.

A minute passed.

Si-Jie (Question Forty): Are you going to check?

Arthur: No.

Si-Jie (Question Forty): Good. Wait for me. I’m nearly out of the shower.

He put the phone down. He didn’t open the database. When she came out she found him sitting on the end of the bed, and climbed onto the mattress beside him, and asked what had happened. He told her. She listened without interrupting, and then she took his hand.

“Thank you for telling me.”

“I still wanted to. Quite badly.”

She smiled a little. “But you didn’t.”

“No.”

She leaned in and kissed his cheek. “One.”

“One what?”

She reached for the notebook on the bedside table. “One time you wanted to check and didn’t. We should count. Not because you need a score. Because I want you to see you can stop yourself, and I want to know when it’s hard.”

She opened it to a blank page and wrote across the top.

OCTOBER: TIMES ARTHUR WANTS TO CHECK AND DOESN’T
1. Wednesday night. Notification from her supervisor. Did not access records. Told Si-Jie.

Arthur read it. “You’re making this sound like a clinical study.”

“Would you prefer a sticker chart?”

“No.”

“Gold stars?”

“Definitely not.”

She drew a small star beside the first entry. He stared at it.

“Si-Jie.”

She laughed. “Too late. It’s official.”

✦ ✦ ✦

By Friday there were two. The second had happened at work. A case report mentioned a man who’d once been accused of stalking a woman in another district, and the name was familiar. Arthur recognised it at once, and he recognised the urge to look further. He knew the systems. He knew how to search. He knew how quickly a few pieces of information could turn into a pattern. Instead he closed the report and told his supervisor the name wasn’t connected to his assigned investigation, and left it there.

Eugene Chak noticed, because Eugene noticed most things that happened at the next desk. He wheeled his chair over with a cup of tea that had gone cold an hour ago.

“You closed that very decisively.”

“It wasn’t relevant.”

“You read it three times before deciding that.”

Arthur didn’t look up. “Twice.”

Eugene considered him, then wheeled himself back to his own desk without another word, which from Eugene was a kind of respect. Arthur sat there afterwards with his hands flat on the desk until the wanting passed. It took longer than he’d have liked. It passed all the same, and he wrote the time it took on a sticky note, and then threw the note away, because that was the sort of thing he was trying to stop doing.

That evening he told Si-Jie. She was on his sofa eating strawberries. “Again? What happened?”

He explained.

She put the strawberry down. “Did you know him? Had you ever worked on his case?”

“No.”

“Then why did you want to check?”

“Because I recognised the name, and I wanted to know whether there was a connection. To your work.”

She nodded slowly. “Thank you for not looking.”

He sat down beside her. “It was difficult.”

She picked up the notebook. “I know. Two.”

“You’re counting every time? Even the small ones?”

“The small ones are where it starts.”

She turned the notebook so he could see.

2. Thursday. Recognised a name in unrelated material. Wanted to search for a connection. Did not.

She added a star, and looked at him. “Do you want to know something? I think you’re getting better.”

He looked at the page. “I don’t feel better.”

“That’s because you’re measuring it by how often you want to.”

“Isn’t that the relevant measure?”

She took his hand. “No. The important part is that you can want something and still decide not to do it. You’re never going to be someone who doesn’t worry about me. I don’t want that. But you have to learn that worrying doesn’t mean you get to take control.”

“I know.”

She kissed his cheek. “Two.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The third time was different. It was a Sunday, and she was at the charity for a supervised training session, and she’d told him she’d be late. He’d accepted that. At 5.47 she wrote to him.

Si-Jie (Question Forty): Running late. Don’t wait for dinner. I’ll eat there.

Arthur: All right.

Then nothing.

At half past seven Arthur was reading. At a quarter past eight he checked his phone. Nothing new. At twenty to nine he checked again. Still nothing. He knew she was probably in a meeting. He knew schedules changed. He knew there was no reason to assume anything had happened. The uncertainty grew anyway. He found himself thinking about the cases she’d mentioned: the nurse, the year of being followed, the men who might have been involved. His mind supplied possibilities with the efficiency of a machine.

He stood up, went to his desk and opened his laptop. Then he stopped, with his hand on the trackpad. He could search the charity’s public updates. He could look for reports. He could search the names he remembered from the records he’d had no business reading. He could reduce the uncertainty, and make himself feel useful.

He closed the laptop and picked up his phone.

Arthur: I want to check.

No reply. He wrote again.

Arthur: I’m worried because you haven’t messaged since 5.47. I know you said you’d be late. I won’t look into your cases or contact anyone. Please tell me when you’re on your way home.

He put the phone down, and waited. Just after nine it rang.

“Arthur? Sorry. We finished late.”

“Are you all right?”

“Yes. Just exhausted.”

He breathed out. “All right.”

There was a pause. “Did you want to check?”

“Yes.”

“How much?”

“Quite badly. I thought about searching.”

“But you didn’t.”

“No.”

She sounded tired, and warm. “Good. I’ll be home in about twenty minutes.”

“I’ll come down.”

“You don’t have to.”

“I’d like to.”

He could hear her smile. “All right.”

When she arrived he was waiting outside the building. She came up the street with her bag, and he took it from her.

“You’re cold,” he said.

“It’s October.”

“That doesn’t make you less cold.”

She laughed, and looked up at him. “How many?”

“Three. Since we started counting.”

She took his hand. “Then three.”

They went upstairs together.

✦ ✦ ✦

By the middle of the month the notebook had become a familiar presence on the bedside table. Sometimes Si-Jie wrote in it. Sometimes he did. The entries weren’t all the same.

1 October. Wanted to check a notification. Did not.
2 October. Recognised a name in unrelated material. Did not search.
5 October. Worried when she was late. Sent one direct message instead of investigating.
8 October. Saw a news report about a stalking case. Wanted to find out whether it was connected to her placement. Did not.
11 October. Asked whether she wanted to talk about work. Accepted her answer when she said no.

She read them one evening and looked at him. “Do you know what I like about this? You tell me before I have to ask. You’re not hiding the hard parts.”

“I don’t want to.”

She moved closer. “That’s important.”

He looked at her. “Are you proud of me?”

“Very. But don’t start expecting a reward every time you behave properly.”

The corner of his mouth moved. “I wasn’t.”

She kissed him, and when she drew back she looked pleased with herself. “That was a reward. Don’t get used to it.”

He considered her. “I’d like another.”

“Ask nicely.”

“May I have another kiss?”

She gave him one. “Better.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On the last Friday of October he came home later than usual and found her already there, in his shirt, sitting on the bed with the notebook. He stopped in the doorway.

“What are you reading?”

“The October entries. All of them. Do you know how many times you told me you wanted to check?”

He put his keys down. “How many?”

“Seven.”

He considered it. “Only seven?”

She stared at him. “Arthur. You sound disappointed.”

“I’m not minimising it.”

She closed the notebook. “Seven times you wanted to check. Seven times you told me. And you didn’t do it.”

He sat down beside her. “I still feel the urge. Sometimes I’m thinking about it before I realise I’m thinking.”

She took his hand. “Then tell me when you notice. And if I’m not there, write it down, or talk to your supervisor, or find some other way to manage it that doesn’t mean going through someone else’s life. Don’t make me responsible for stopping you.”

“I won’t.”

“I mean it.”

“I’ll hold myself to it.”

She looked at him, and smiled. “Seven.”

He looked at the notebook. “Seven.”

She put it on the bedside table and turned to him and touched his face. “Tonight I want to do something for you. Reward you. For trying. For telling me. For stopping yourself when it was hard.”

He watched her. “Are you sure?”

“Yes. But I have rules.”

A faint smile. “Of course you do.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She turned the bedside lamp down, and the room went soft, and she stood in front of him.

“First rule. You don’t touch me until I say you can.”

He looked up at her. “Understood.”

“Second. You don’t decide what happens next. Third. If you want something, you ask.”

“All right.”

She bent and kissed his forehead. He stayed still. She kissed his cheek, then the corner of his mouth. He didn’t reach for her.

She smiled. “You’re behaving.”

“You gave me instructions.”

“Very obedient.”

“I’m capable of following instructions.”

“At work, perhaps.”

He looked at her, and she laughed and kissed him properly. His hands stayed where they were. When she pulled away, he looked at her mouth.

“May I touch you?”

“Not yet.”

He nodded. She stepped back just far enough to take off her earrings and put them on the bedside table, and came back, and kissed his jaw, his cheek, his mouth, slowly, deliberately, with enough of a pause between each one to make him wait for the next.

“You’re very patient tonight,” she whispered.

“I’m trying.”

She put her hands on his shoulders. “May I take your jacket off?”

“Yes.”

She slipped it off his shoulders and set it aside, and loosened his tie. He watched her.

“Can I touch you now?”

“Not yet.”

He breathed out through his nose, and she laughed. “You’re allowed to be impatient. I want you to tell me.”

“I want to hold you.”

Her face went soft. She took his hands and put them at her waist. “Thank you for asking. Now.”

His fingers settled there, carefully. She kissed him again, and this time he drew her closer, and still he waited for her to set the pace.

She unbuttoned his shirt herself, one button at a time, and pushed it off his shoulders. Then she stepped back and took off his shirt, the one she was wearing, and let it drop. He didn’t move. He looked at her, and his hands stayed exactly where she’d put them, and she could see what that cost him.

“Rule four. You can touch me now. But I decide where,” said Si-Jie.

She took his hand and put it on her breast, and watched his face change. She guided him back against the pillows and climbed over him, and when he reached for her hips she let him, and when he tried to turn them over she pressed one hand flat to his chest and shook her head, and he lay back and let her. She undid his belt. She took her time about it. By the time she sank down onto him he’d stopped trying to be patient and was simply holding on to her, his fingers pressed into her thighs, his eyes on her face.

She moved slowly, because she could, and because every time she slowed down he made a sound she’d never heard from him. He asked, once, in a voice she didn’t recognise, whether he could, and she said yes, and his hand moved between them. She came first, bent over him with her hair falling round both their faces. He followed a moment after, with her name in his mouth and her hands holding his face, looking at her the whole time. There was no notebook between them. No list. No analysis. Only her choosing, and him listening.

Later, when the room was quiet again, she lay against his chest and his hand moved slowly over her back. “Was that a sufficient reward?”

He considered the question. “Yes. More than sufficient.”

“Good.”

He kissed her hair, and after a while he said thank you.

She lifted her head. “For what?”

“For trusting me enough to let me try.”

Her face softened. “Don’t thank me for trusting you. Keep giving me reasons to.”

“I will.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The next morning she woke first and opened the notebook to October, and found one last entry in his handwriting.

31 October. Seven occasions on which I wanted to access information connected to her placement. I told her each time. I did not access the information. The urge did not disappear. I have learned it does not need to disappear before I can choose not to act on it.

She read it twice, and took the blue pen, and wrote in the margin.

Eight.

Arthur stirred behind her. “What are you doing?”

“Adding one.”

He looked at the page. “Why eight?”

“Because you wanted to check whether I was awake, and you didn’t.”

He blinked. “I was going to ask.”

She leaned over and kissed him. “I know. Eight times you chose to tell me instead of looking for something you had no right to know.”

He looked at the number, and then at her. “That’s not quite accurate. Last night I wanted to check whether you were all right.”

She burst out laughing. “That’s different! You’re allowed to ask me that!”

“I did ask.”

“Exactly!”

He smiled.

She shut the notebook, put it back on the bedside table, climbed over him and kissed him again. “Good morning. Do you want breakfast? Or do you want to check the kitchen first, to make sure I haven’t been replaced by another woman?”

“That would be unnecessary.”

“Good answer.”

He pulled her down for another kiss. When she finally got out of bed he let her go without asking where she was going, or how long she’d be, or whether anyone else would be there. He trusted her to come back. It was a small thing. For Arthur it wasn’t small at all, and for Si-Jie it was worth noticing.

chapters.title: The Letter
chapters.desc: A letter comes to the charity, addressed to her: three pages in green ink about her hair. She doesn’t tell him all day. He knows anyway, and he doesn’t go looking.
chapters.epigraph: “Your hair is different when you are tired.”
chapters.content:
The letter came to the charity at 9.23 on a Thursday morning in the middle of November. It was addressed to Yen Si-Jie: not to her supervisor, not to the department, not to the general office. Her name was written in the middle of a white envelope in handwriting she didn’t recognise. The envelope was ordinary, the kind sold in packs of fifty. There was no return address and no stamp. Someone had brought it by hand and left it with the receptionist.

Si-Jie signed for it and turned it over. Nothing on the back.

“Someone sent you a letter?” said the colleague at the next desk.

“Apparently.”

“Secret admirer?”

Si-Jie smiled without thinking about it. “Maybe someone wants to complain about my handwriting.”

She opened it at her desk. There were three pages inside, all in green ink, and she read the first sentence.

Your hair is different when you are tired.

Her fingers stopped. She read it again, and turned the page.

The letter was about her hair. Not her work, not her placement, not the charity: her hair. The writer described how she wore it when she came in in the morning, how she tucked it behind her ear when she was concentrating, how she tied it up when she was busy, how loose strands fell round her face at the end of the day. There were observations about its length and its colour and the way it looked under different lights. On the second page the writer mentioned that she sometimes twisted a strand round her finger while she was thinking. On the third there was a sentence that made her stomach tighten.

I wonder if the man who touches it knows how often other people notice it.

She put the pages down, and for a few seconds she didn’t move. The office went on round her. A printer started. Someone laughed near the kitchen. A colleague asked whether anyone had seen the latest referral form. Ordinary sounds on an ordinary morning.

She folded the letter, then unfolded it and read the last paragraph.

You should wear it down more often. It is a shame to hide something so beautiful.

There was no signature, only a short green line at the bottom of the page. She put the pages back in the envelope. She didn’t tell Arthur.

✦ ✦ ✦

Just after noon her phone lit up.

Arthur (Thirty-Nine): Have you eaten?

Si-Jie: Not yet.

Arthur (Thirty-Nine): Why?

Si-Jie: Busy.

Arthur (Thirty-Nine): Eat.

Si-Jie: Yes, sir.

Arthur (Thirty-Nine): I’m not your supervisor.

Si-Jie: You’re worse.

He sent a single question mark, and she smiled at the screen and slid the phone into her drawer.

The letter was in her bag. She could feel it there, folded between her notebook and a packet of tissues. She told herself she’d report it first. That was sensible. The charity had procedures for unwanted communications: she could show her supervisor, keep the envelope, record when it arrived and avoid guessing who’d sent it. She didn’t need Arthur for any of that. And she didn’t want to watch his face when he read the sentence about the man who touched her hair.

Mid-afternoon she took it to her supervisor. They photographed the pages and the envelope, recorded when and how it had arrived, and arranged for the original to be kept. Her supervisor asked whether she recognised the handwriting.

“No.”

“Does the writer mention anything you haven’t made public?”

Si-Jie hesitated. “Some habits. Things I do without thinking.”

“Have you noticed anyone watching you?”

“Not specifically.”

“Any contact before this?”

“None.”

Her supervisor wrote it all down. They agreed that nobody would contact the sender or try to find out who it was on their own. The charity would follow its safeguarding procedure and take advice. Si-Jie felt something in her chest loosen. At least she’d done something.

She left work after six. She still didn’t tell Arthur.

✦ ✦ ✦

When she got to his flat he was in the kitchen with his sleeves rolled to the elbow, making dinner. “You’re early.”

“Am I?”

“By twenty minutes.”

She put her bag down. “Maybe I missed you.”

He glanced at her. “Maybe?”

“Definitely.”

He came over and kissed her, and she kissed him back, and for a moment the familiar warmth of him put the day a long way off. Then his fingers brushed her hair, and she went stiff.

It was small, barely a movement. Arthur’s hand stopped at once. “What happened?”

“Nothing.”

His eyes stayed on her face.

She smiled. “Just tired.”

He didn’t look convinced, but he let his hand fall. “All right.”

He went back to the stove. Si-Jie stood in the hallway and watched him. She’d spent all day trying not to think about the letter. Now she couldn’t stop thinking about how he’d caught one small movement, and she began to wonder whether not telling him had been a mistake.

✦ ✦ ✦

Arthur knew something was wrong before dinner. He didn’t know what, and the distinction mattered. She’d been affectionate when she came in, but her attention kept drifting. She’d looked at her bag three times. She’d flinched when he touched her hair. She’d checked the lock on the front door after coming in, and then checked it again.
