She was answering questions differently too: not dishonestly, exactly, but carefully. He noticed all of it and said nothing while they ate.

She told him about a colleague who’d spilt coffee over a pile of forms. He listened. She asked about his day, and he told her about a meeting and a case review coming up. She laughed at something he said, but the laugh came a fraction too late. Towards nine he put down his chopsticks.

“Si-Jie. Something happened today.”

She looked up. “No.”

He waited, and she lowered her eyes.

He kept his voice low. “I wasn’t asking.”

She looked at him again. “You’re doing it. Reading my face.”

He was silent. “Yes.”

The honesty irritated her more than a denial would have. “You don’t get to know everything just because you notice things.”

“I’m aware of that.”

“Are you?”

He took a breath. “I can’t decide what you feel or what you want to tell me from what I observe. But I can see you’re uncomfortable, and I can ask whether something happened.”

“And if I say nothing happened?”

“Then I accept that.”

“Even if you don’t believe me?”

“Even if I don’t.”

The room went quiet. She picked up her water glass and put it down again without drinking. Arthur didn’t move closer. He didn’t ask again. He waited, and that was what made her speak.

“Someone sent me a letter.”

His face didn’t change dramatically. It went still. “When?”

“This morning. At the charity.”

“Have you shown your supervisor?”

“Yes.”

“Was it threatening?”

“I don’t know if I’d call it a threat.”

“What did it say?”

She looked at him. “Arthur.”

He stopped.

She rubbed her thumb along the rim of the glass. “It’s about my hair. Three pages, in green ink. Someone’s described how I wear it, what I do with it when I’m thinking, when I’m tired. Things like that.”

His jaw tightened. “Did it have your name on it?”

“Yes.”

“An address?”

“No.”

“Any direct threat?”

She hesitated. “Not exactly. There was a sentence about the man who touches my hair.”

His eyes lifted to hers. “What sentence?”

She repeated it. For a moment he said nothing at all.

“Do you have the original?”

“The charity’s keeping it. We photographed everything.”

“Good.”

She watched him. “You’re angry.”

“Yes.”

“At me?”

“No. At the letter.”

She looked down. “I didn’t tell you. All day.”

“I’d gathered that.”

Her head came up.

He met her eyes. “Why?”

“Because I knew you’d worry. And I didn’t want you to start looking for whoever wrote it.”

He was quiet. “I’d want to.”

“I know you would.”

“But I won’t.”

She searched his face. “Promise?”

“I won’t access anything I have no legitimate reason to access. I won’t look into your colleagues or your clients. I won’t make enquiries through work. If you want help deciding what to do next, I’ll help. If you want me to sit beside you while you deal with it, I’ll do that.”

She looked at him. “Thank you.”

He nodded, and then, carefully, he asked whether he could see the photographs.

She thought about it, and shook her head. “Not tonight.”

“All right.” He didn’t ask why.

✦ ✦ ✦

They moved to the sofa. Si-Jie sat with her legs tucked under her, and Arthur sat beside her with a little space between them.

She looked at him. “You’re thinking. About the letter.”

“Yes.”

“What are you thinking?”

He took a moment. “The writer knows enough about your appearance and your habits to describe you in detail. That could mean repeated observation, or some earlier acquaintance, or information from somewhere else. We don’t know which. The letter’s personal. It addresses you directly and refers to physical contact with someone close to you, which makes it intrusive. Whether it’s meant as a threat isn’t established.”

“You’re profiling the writer.”

“I was answering your question.”

“You’re still doing it.”

He stopped. “You’re right.”

She leaned back against the cushions. “I don’t know who it is. I don’t know if it’s someone at work, or someone who knows me, or someone who’s seen me outside. I don’t know whether this is the first letter or whether there’ll be another.”

His fingers curled once against his knee. “That uncertainty is hard.”

“For you?”

He turned towards her. “For both of us. But I don’t want to make it worse by turning your life into an investigation.”

She was quiet. Then she moved closer. “Can I ask you something? Did you know because of how I looked?”

“Yes.”

“How?”

He considered it. “You were careful with your movements. You kept looking at your bag. When I touched your hair you reacted as though you were expecting something unpleasant. You checked the door twice.”

She frowned. “That’s a lot.”

“It is.”

“And you put it together.”

“I noticed that something had happened. I didn’t know what.”

“That distinction’s important,” said Si-Jie.

“It’s the only one I’ve got.”

She rested her head against his shoulder. After a while she said she’d wanted one day when she could just be normal.

He looked down at her. “You were normal.”

She gave a small laugh. “I was hiding a three-page letter about my hair in my bag.”

“You were trying to have dinner with me.”

She turned her face towards him. “That’s a very generous interpretation.”

“It’s an accurate one.”

She smiled faintly, and then her expression changed. “Arthur? Can you touch my hair?”

He looked at her. “Are you sure?”

“Yes.”

He lifted his hand slowly, giving her time to change her mind. His fingers brushed the side of her head and moved a strand away from her face, and nothing more. Si-Jie closed her eyes. For the first time that day the touch felt like hers: not something watched, not something described by a stranger, but something she’d chosen.

✦ ✦ ✦

At nine he answered her messages. There’d been only six that day, and he replied to each in order, as always, and put his phone down. Si-Jie was brushing her hair in front of the bathroom mirror. He stood in the doorway.

“Your supervisor has the original?”

“Yes. They’re following the procedure. They’ll tell me if they need anything else.”

“All right.”

She watched him in the mirror. “You’re not going to ask for the charity’s records?”

“No.”

“Or look into the handwriting? Or ask someone at work about the ink?”

He paused. “No. I want to.”

She turned round. He didn’t hide it.

“I want to know who wrote it. I want to know whether they’ve been watching you. I want to know whether they know where you live.”

Her expression softened. “But?”

“But wanting to know doesn’t give me permission.”

She put the brush down and held out her hand, and he came and took it.

“That’s the rule. A concern is not permission,” she said.

“I remember.”

She squeezed his fingers. “You’re doing it. Stopping.”

“Not perfectly.”

“Nobody asked you to be perfect.”

She reached up and kissed him, and he kissed her back, gently. When she drew away she rested her forehead against his.

“Tomorrow I’ll go back to work. I don’t want to give up my placement because of a letter.”

“Then don’t.”

“And I don’t want you treating everyone who looks at me as a suspect.”

“I won’t.”

She searched his face. “Even if you think you know?”

“Thinking I know is exactly when I shouldn’t.”

She smiled. “Good.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Later, Si-Jie was asleep beside him and Arthur lay awake thinking about three pages in a stranger’s green handwriting, and a sentence about his hand in her hair. His mind kept coming back to the same questions. Who had seen her? How often? Where?

He could have started looking. He knew the systems. He knew people who could run checks. He knew how to turn a name and a place and a handful of observations into a starting point. But he had no name, no assignment and no authority to turn her private experience into his case.

He looked at her. Her hair had fallen across her cheek. He moved his hand towards it, and stopped. She’d asked him to touch it earlier, and he could still see the way she’d closed her eyes. He didn’t want the letter to take that from her. Carefully, he moved the strand off her face.

She stirred. “Arthur?”

“I’m here.”

“Don’t think too much.”

“I’ll try.”

She found his hand under the blanket and held it, and smiled without opening her eyes, and was asleep again almost at once.

He stayed awake a little longer. He didn’t open his laptop. He didn’t call anyone. On the bedside table the notebook lay open at the page from September, his two lines at the top and her margin beneath.

A concern is not permission.
And if I say I don’t want you to do something, you don’t decide you know better.

He read them, and closed the notebook. The letter had been written in green ink. He wasn’t going to let it write the next part of her life. Not without her.

chapters.title: The Pattern
chapters.desc: He recognises the letter’s language: two women in 2022, both students, both long-haired, both gone. A name he never proved. He reports the link and the conflict, and stays off the case.
chapters.content:
Arthur read the letter for the fourth time on a Wednesday evening at the end of November. Not the original: the charity had kept that. Si-Jie had agreed he could read the photographs once they’d talked about what it would mean, and he hadn’t asked her supervisor for them. She’d brought the copies to his flat herself, laid them on the dining table and told him he could look.

He’d read all three pages once, and then again. Now he was looking at the third.

I wonder if the man who touches it knows how often other people notice it.

His eyes moved to the last paragraph.

You should wear it down more often. It is a shame to hide something so beautiful.

He’d seen this language before. Not these sentences: the construction. The way the writer described a woman’s appearance like a privilege he’d been granted. The insistence that his attention was a form of appreciation. The small suggestion that she didn’t know how much of herself she was giving away.

He put the photographs down and didn’t move. Then he stood and went to his study.

The old case wasn’t in his current files, or in his personal records. He had no reason to keep a copy. But he remembered it. He remembered two women, and two letters, and the feeling of reading them three years ago without knowing what they’d turn into.

Si-Jie was standing by the dining table with two mugs. “Arthur? You’re not drinking your tea.”

He looked at the photographs, and then at her. “I recognise the language.”

Her hands stopped. “From where?”

“A case.”

“What kind of case?”

He was quiet. “Two missing women. In 2022.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t tell her everything at once. He asked her to sit down.

She put the mugs on the table and took the chair opposite. “Please don’t make me wait while you decide how much to tell me.”

He looked at her, and nodded. “The first woman was twenty-two. A university student. She had long hair, usually wore it loose, and lived alone near her campus. The second was twenty-four. Also a student: a different university, a different district. Long hair. Both had ordinary routines. Neither had any known connection to the other.”

“Did they know each other?”

“Not that we established.”

“What happened?”

“They disappeared.”

The word sounded too small. Si-Jie lowered her eyes. “When?”

“The first in March 2022. The second in August.”

“Five months apart. Did they find them?”

“No.”

She looked up. “Neither of them?”

“Neither.”

The room seemed to grow quieter.

He kept his voice level. “Before they disappeared, both women received letters. Handwritten. Personal descriptions: their hair, their habits, the way they dressed. Ordinary things, written down by someone who’d plainly been watching for a long time.”

Her fingers tightened round the mug. “Like mine.”

“Yes.”

“Did the letters mention their hair?”

“Repeatedly. The first described how she wore it when she was studying. The second described how the other woman tied hers back at work.”

Si-Jie looked down at her own hair. Arthur noticed, and didn’t comment.

“Was the ink green?”

“No. The first was blue. The second was black.”

“Then how do you know it’s the same person?”

“We didn’t know. We suspected a connection because of the language and the structure and the kind of observations. There were similarities, but no conclusive forensic link.”

“Did you profile him?”

“Yes.”

“Did you find him?”

“No.”

She looked at him. “Three years ago. And now someone’s sent me a letter that sounds like theirs.”

He held her gaze. “Yes.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He went back into the study, and she followed him. He opened a drawer and took out a small notebook: not the black one he kept about her, but an older one with worn corners and pages full of work notes. He opened it at a dated page.

September 2022.
Kot Siu-ming.

Si-Jie read it. “Who is he?”

“A person of interest in the original investigation. He was never formally charged. We had reasons to examine a possible connection to the women, but not enough evidence that he’d written the letters or had anything to do with their disappearances.”

“Did you interview him?”

“Investigators did. I was involved in the behavioural assessment.”

“What did you think of him?”

Arthur looked at the name. “He presented himself as someone who appreciated women. He talked about attention like a gift he was giving. He was very comfortable describing people he barely knew.”

“Did he know the women?”

“One had been to a public event where he was present. The other had been seen in the area where he worked.”

“That’s not proof.”

He closed the notebook. “No. At the time I considered several possibilities. The letters could have come from one person, or one could have been imitating the other. The disappearances could have been connected, or not. I thought Kot was a possible link. I didn’t have the evidence to conclude more than that.”

She looked at the cover as though she could still see the name through it. “Why didn’t you tell me about the case before?”

“Because I didn’t know there was any reason to connect it to you.”

“And now?”

“Now there’s a reason to consider it.”

He saw her face change. “Si-Jie—”

She shook her head. “Don’t say my name in that voice.”

“What voice?”

“The one you use when you’re about to tell me something terrible very calmly.”

He looked at her. Then he pulled out the chair beside his own. “Sit with me.”

She sat. He didn’t touch her until she reached for his hand.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Tell me what you mean,” she said.

Arthur took a breath. “The two women had certain things in common. Both were students. Both had long hair. Both received letters describing their appearance and habits before they disappeared.”

“And I’m a student.”

“Yes.”

She gave a small laugh with nothing in it. “I’d noticed. I’ve also got long hair. And a letter.”

“You fit the same broad pattern. That isn’t the same as saying you’re the third.”

“But you think the letters are connected.”

“I think the similarities warrant a formal review.”

She stared at the notebook. “Did the other women know someone was watching them?”

“We don’t know how much they understood. Their letters were reported, but we don’t have a full account of what they made of them.”

“Did they tell anyone?”

“Both told someone.”

“Did anyone take them seriously?”

His jaw tightened. “The letters were documented. Nobody understood what they meant until after the disappearances.”

Si-Jie went still and looked down at her hands. “So I’ve had the same kind of letter. And the other two disappeared.”

“Yes.”

She drew a slow breath, and for several seconds neither of them spoke. Then, so low he barely heard it, she asked whether he thought someone was going to take her.

His hand tightened round hers. He didn’t answer at once. He wanted to say no. He wanted to tell her she was safe, that he wouldn’t let anything happen, that he could keep her in this flat and never let her out of his sight. He wanted to promise something he couldn’t guarantee.

“I don’t know,” he said.

Her eyes filled.

He moved closer. “But I know this letter has to be taken seriously. And we can take the right steps without pretending we already know what’s going to happen.”

She looked at him. “You’re frightened.”

“Yes.”

It was the first time he’d said it so plainly. She leaned forward and pressed her forehead to his. “Me too.”

He closed his eyes, and held her hand, and for a while it was the only thing in the room he understood.

✦ ✦ ✦

The next morning, before she was up, Arthur rang the senior officer he was supposed to ring.

He didn’t search for Kot Siu-ming himself. He disclosed the new letter, the apparent similarities to the 2022 case and his relationship with the woman who’d received it. He made it clear that Si-Jie was his girlfriend and that he couldn’t be the one assessing the new material. He asked for the 2022 files to be reviewed alongside the new letter by an assigned team, offered his original behavioural assessment and set out the similarities he thought needed examining. He didn’t present his conclusion as fact. He didn’t claim that Kot had written the letter, or that Si-Jie was definitely being targeted by the same person. He said only that there was a possible link that needed investigating.

The officer asked him one question. “How certain are you?”

Arthur looked at the photographs on his desk. “Certain enough that I wouldn’t treat this as an isolated unwanted letter. Not certain enough to identify the author.”

“Understood.”

“And I want the conflict recorded.”

“It will be.”

When the call ended he stayed at his desk. Three years. Two women. Two letters. No resolution. He’d once thought the case was hard because the evidence was incomplete. Now it was hard because the next letter had come to someone who slept in his bed.

✦ ✦ ✦

When he came out of the study, Si-Jie was in the kitchen. She’d made breakfast: two plates, two coffees, and a bowl of strawberries between them.

Arthur stopped. “You made breakfast.”

“Don’t sound so surprised.”

“I wasn’t.”

She pushed his plate towards him. “You were. Eat first.”

“Si-Jie.”

“Eat.”

He did as he was told. She waited until he’d had several mouthfuls. “Did you report it?”

“Yes. And my connection to you. I’ve given them the old assessment and asked for a review. Someone else will handle the new investigation.”

She nodded. “Good.”

He looked at her. “You’re not angry?”

“Why would I be?”

“Because I didn’t tell you straight away.”

She put her fork down. “You told me as soon as you saw the connection. Arthur, I don’t need you to know everything instantly. I need you to tell me when you know something important.”

He was quiet.

She picked up a strawberry and didn’t eat it. “Can I see the old assessment? All of it? I want to understand what happened to those women.”

“I’ll arrange access to what you’re allowed to see.”

“Not your private notes?”

He understood what she was asking. “The original assessment is part of the case material. My own working notes aren’t automatically yours to read. But I can tell you what’s in them, and give you what’s relevant through the proper process.”

She considered that. “All right.”

He reached for her hand.

She let him take it. “If someone’s doing this again, I don’t want to be another woman who disappears.”

His expression changed. “You won’t.”

She looked at him.

He corrected himself. “I won’t promise what I can’t control. But I’ll take every proper step to make sure this is investigated, and that you have the support and protection you need.”

“That’s better,” said Si-Jie.

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening she sat beside him while he went through the parts of the old chronology he was allowed to share. The first woman had received her letter in March 2022, the second in August. Both letters had been written in a voice that sounded intimate though there was no relationship between the writer and the woman. Both had described their subjects through small, ordinary details. Both women had disappeared. Nothing had confirmed that Kot Siu-ming had written either letter, or that the two disappearances were connected. The investigation had stayed open.

Si-Jie read the summaries in silence. She stopped at a photograph of the first envelope.

“Did she have long hair like mine?”

He looked at the photograph. “Yes.”

“And the second woman?”

“Yes.”

She looked down at the page. “Do you think he chose us because of our hair? Does he watch women until he finds one who fits?”

“That’s one possibility the investigators should consider.”

She closed the folder. “I hate that.”

“So do I.”

She leaned against him, and he put his arm round her. After a while she asked what she should do if another letter came.

“Keep it. Don’t reply. Tell the charity and the assigned investigators straight away.”

“And if I see someone?”

“Go somewhere safe. Call the police. Don’t approach him.”

She nodded, and looked up at him. “And if I’m frightened?”

“Call me.”

“Even in the middle of the night?”

“The middle of the night most of all.”

She smiled faintly. “All right.”

He pressed a kiss into her hair, and she closed her eyes. For a while they stayed like that. Arthur could feel the weight of the old case coming back: not as a file, not as a set of unanswered questions, but as a woman asleep against his chest.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later, with Si-Jie asleep, Arthur opened the notebook on his bedside table. He turned past the page with the rules on it, his lines and her margin, to a blank one.

26 November 2025.
The letter Si-Jie received resembles communications associated with an unresolved investigation from 2022 involving two missing women.
Both women were students. Both had long hair. Both received letters describing their appearance and habits before they disappeared.
The name previously considered as a possible connection was Kot Siu-ming.
The current letter warrants formal review. Authorship and connection have not been established.

He stopped, and then wrote one more line.

Si-Jie is not a case. She is not an extension of the 2022 investigation. She is a person who has been frightened by something she did not ask for.

He closed the notebook. For three years he’d thought of the case as something that had stopped somewhere and was waiting. It hadn’t stopped. It had gone looking for someone else, and this time he knew her name.

He turned off the light and moved closer to her. She stirred, found his hand and held it, and was still again. Arthur lay awake long after that. Two women had disappeared in 2022. A third had received a letter in November 2025. And somewhere between those dates a man named Kot Siu-ming had stayed out of everyone’s reach.

chapters.title: Protective Custody
chapters.desc: He finds her a safe flat and she refuses it. A fight about control, and then he moves into hers. The triplets turn twenty-two with three cakes, two knives and a police car across the street.
chapters.content:
Arthur had found a safe flat. Si-Jie discovered this on the first Thursday in December, when she came home and found him at her dining table with a folder open in front of him. There were photographs: a residential block, a lobby, a security desk, an underground car park. Across the street, below her window, the police car that had been there since the weekend was parked where it always was.

She put her bag down. “What’s this?”

“Accommodation.”

She looked at the photographs again. “Whose?”

“Yours.”

A pause. Then she pulled out the chair opposite. “Arthur.”

“It’s temporary. The building has controlled access, round-the-clock security and a separate entrance for residents. The assigned officers have reviewed it.”

She stared at him. “You found me a safe flat. Without asking me.”

“I wanted to establish whether it was suitable before we discussed it.”

“That’s a very convenient explanation.”

He closed the folder. “The investigation has found enough similarities between your letter and the 2022 case that the police are treating it as possibly connected. We don’t know who sent it. We don’t know whether he’s been near you. We don’t know whether there’ll be another.”

“I’m aware of all that.”

“The team has advised extra precautions.”

“I’m aware of that too.”

“Then you understand why I think you should stay somewhere else.”

She looked at him. “I understand why you think it. I don’t agree.”

His face went still. “The flat is available.”

“I’m not moving.”

“Si-Jie.”

“I have work tomorrow. I have clients who expect me. I have a placement I worked hard for. I have a home.”

“You have a possible stalker connected to two unresolved disappearances.”

“And I have a life.”

He looked at her. When he spoke again, his voice was low. “I don’t think you understand the risk.”

Her expression changed. “Don’t.”

“I’ve spent three years looking at this pattern.”

“And I’ve spent the last fortnight being told I fit it. I understand more than you think.”

“Then why are you refusing?”

“Because I don’t want to be put away somewhere while everybody else decides what happens to me.”

“I’m trying to keep you safe.”

She pushed the folder back across the table. “You’re trying to move me somewhere you’ll feel better. Those aren’t necessarily the same thing.”

✦ ✦ ✦

It was the first time in months that Arthur raised his voice. Not by much, but enough.

“You can’t treat this as an inconvenience.”

“I’m not.”

“Then stop behaving as though everything can carry on as normal.”

“Why? Because someone sent me a letter?”

“Because two women got letters like it and disappeared.”

“And you think a locked building guarantees I won’t?”

“No.”

“Then don’t talk to me like it does.”

He stood and went to the window, looked down at the police car, and turned back. “The flat has security staff. The entrances are monitored. There’s a controlled visitor system. It’s a reasonable precaution.”

“Then tell the police you think I should use it.”

“I already have.”

“Good. They can talk to me about it.”

“They have.”

“And?”

“They recommended you consider temporary relocation.”

“Consider. Not obey.”

He looked at her.

She stood too. “Arthur, I know you’re frightened. I’m frightened as well. But you don’t get to turn that into a decision about where I live. You’re showing me a flat you’ve already chosen, expecting me to move into it, and telling me why my own decision is unreasonable.”

He said nothing.

Her voice dropped. “You did this before. Not with a flat: with my work. You were worried, so you looked into people behind my back. You decided that being frightened gave you the right to know things I hadn’t given you.”

His face tightened. “This is different.”

“Then explain the difference without telling me what to do.”

For once he had no answer ready.

“I love you. I know you want to protect me. But I won’t become someone you manage because you’re afraid of losing me,” said Si-Jie.

He lowered his eyes. “I don’t know how to watch this and do nothing.”

“I’m not asking you to do nothing. I’m asking you to stand beside me. Not in front of me. Not behind me, making decisions I don’t know about. Beside me.”

“And if I say I want you to move?”

“Then I’ll listen. I’ll think about it. I’ll make my own decision.”

“And if you say no?”

“Then you respect it.”

The silence stretched. At last he said he didn’t want her to disappear.

Her face softened. “I don’t want to disappear either.”

He looked at her a long time, and sat down. The argument wasn’t over. But he’d stopped trying to win it.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came back the next evening with no folder. He had dinner in one bag and a paper bag of pastries in the other.

Si-Jie opened the door. “Peace offering?”

“Food. And pastries.”

“Now you’re trying.”

They ate at her table. Afterwards he showed her the latest message from the assigned officer. The team had reviewed the risk assessment and recommended several temporary measures: a review of her travel, extra security at the charity, the police car to stay, and a conversation about relocation.

She read all of it, and put the phone down. “I’ll cooperate with the security. I’ll talk to my supervisor about the building. I’ll give the police my usual routes and times. And I won’t go out alone late at night for now. But I’m staying here.”

He was quiet. “Then I’ll stay here too.”

She blinked. “What?”

“I’ll move in. Your building’s familiar to you. Your work’s easy to reach from here. The police are already outside. I can be with you without you having to give up your home.”

She stared at him. “You’d move into my flat? You hate moving.”

“I dislike unnecessary movement.”

She almost smiled. “Your flat’s practically a laboratory. Arthur, you own six identical white shirts.”

“Seven. One is for formal occasions.”

She burst out laughing, and the tension broke at last. Then she reached across the table and took his hand. “Are you sure? You’re not doing this because you think I’ll be safer if you control everything?”

He looked at their hands. “No. I want to be here. You’re frightened, and I’m frightened, and I don’t think either of us should have to sleep alone if we don’t want to.”

She squeezed his fingers. “That’s a much better answer. Welcome to my very untidy flat.”

“I’d noticed.”

“Don’t start.”

“I haven’t said anything.”

“Your face has.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He moved in on Saturday with two suitcases, a box of books, his coffee things and a small set of neatly labelled folders. Si-Jie watched him for a full minute before she asked whether he was measuring her wardrobe.

“Yes. Your clothes take up about seventy per cent of the available space.”

“That’s because I live here.”

“I’m aware of that.”

“Then adjust.”

He looked at the wardrobe, and then at her. “All right.”

He moved his shirts to one side. She moved them back. He moved them again, and she hung her cardigan in the gap beside his jacket. He stared at the result.

“You’re doing this deliberately.”

“Yes. To remind you this is my home.”

He looked at her, and then, unexpectedly, smiled. “Understood.”

She came closer and put her arms round his waist, and his arms settled round her, and for a while neither of them moved.

Then he murmured that she had too many hair ties.

She pulled back. “Get out.”

He kissed her before she could push him away, and she laughed and kissed him back.

That evening he made dinner in her kitchen. He put his coffee machine on the counter and his books on the lower shelf and his toothbrush beside hers. At bedtime he stood at the window, checking the lock and the car across the street.

“Arthur. Come to bed.”

He switched off the light and came to her. She held out her arms, and he lay down beside her.

“You’re home,” she whispered.

He turned towards her. “So are you.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The triplets turned twenty-two on Saturday the thirteenth. Si-Jie woke to Three Exclamation Marks going off on the bedside table.

Si-Wei (Business Hours): Happy birthday to my two favourite people.

Si-Jie: There are only three of us.

Si-Wei (Business Hours): Exactly.

Si-Yuan (Eldest, Allegedly): Landed. Happy birthday, my girls.

Si-Jie: YOU’RE HOME.

Si-Wei (Business Hours): She’s been on the ground for ten minutes. Stop shouting.

Si-Jie: YOU’RE HOME.

Si-Yuan (Eldest, Allegedly): I am, darling. See you at yours.

Si-Jie sat up so fast that Arthur opened his eyes. “What’s happened?”

“Si-Yuan’s landed.”

He blinked at the ceiling. “Then it’s a good morning.”

She turned and kissed him. “It’s our birthday.”

“I’d gathered.”

“You’re not very enthusiastic.”

“I’m waiting for you to finish.”

She laughed and climbed over him. He caught her hand before she’d gone.

“Happy birthday, Si-Jie. Twenty-two.”

She smiled down at him. “Twenty-two.”

He kissed her knuckles and let her go.

The birthday was at her flat, because she couldn’t go anywhere else. Their mother had flown in from Taipei the day before with a suitcase of things nobody had asked for, and had been in Si-Jie’s kitchen reorganising it since breakfast. Si-Yuan came straight from the airport with her cases and her sunglasses pushed up into her hair, and hugged Si-Wei, then Si-Jie, then both of them at once. Si-Wei came with Geum Sung Jae, who carried a gift bag and a box of pastries and let her steer him round the flat for most of the evening.

“Why are there only two cake knives?” said Si-Jie.

“Because you’ve got two,” said Si-Wei.

“There are three cakes.”

“Then use a spoon.”

Si-Yuan laughed into her tea. It was the first birthday in two years that the three of them had been in one room. Arthur sat beside Si-Jie with his hand near hers on the cushion. He watched her instead of asking every few minutes whether she was all right.

“You’re staring,” Si-Jie told him.

“I’m listening. You’re arguing about knives.”

“It’s serious. Will you find another one?”

He got up at once and went to her mother in the kitchen, and Si-Wei watched him go. “That’s a useful skill. He knows when to lose.”

“I heard that,” said Arthur from the doorway, with a knife.

There were three cakes on the table: strawberry cream for Si-Jie, dark chocolate for Si-Wei, vanilla with fresh fruit for Si-Yuan. Arthur had brought a present for each of them. Si-Wei’s was a leather planner.

She turned it over. “Practical.”

“You’re welcome,” said Arthur.

“I didn’t say thank you.”

“You were going to.”

Si-Yuan’s was a small silver bookmark with her initials on it, and she thanked him and told him he was getting good at birthdays. Si-Jie’s was a flat box, and when she opened it she went quiet. Inside was a pair of earrings, two small silver stars, to go with the one she’d worn round her neck since February.

“You remembered.”

“You stopped at that window twice in Hong Kong.”

“That was months ago.”

“Yes.”

She leaned over and kissed his cheek, and put them in there and then, and turned her head so her sisters could see.

Their mother made the three of them stand behind the cakes for a photograph, and then another, and one with Arthur and Sung Jae in it, before she’d let anyone light a candle. They blew them out together. Si-Jie reached for the knife at once and said hers first, because she was in protective custody. Their mother took the knife away and gave it to Si-Yuan, because she was the eldest.

“By four minutes,” said Si-Jie.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was dark when Si-Jie went to the window. The car was across the street under the streetlight, where it had been for a fortnight. The officers changed at eight and eight, and the new pair had just come on. One of them saw her and lifted a hand, and she lifted hers back. Her smile went.

Arthur was beside her before she’d lowered her hand.

“I hate that it’s there,” she said.

“So do I.”

“I hate that someone can send three pages about my hair and make my birthday look like this.”

His jaw tightened.

She looked at him. “Don’t. I’m only telling you.”

He let his hand open. “I’m not doing anything.”

Si-Yuan came to stand on her other side and took her hand. “Are you all right?”

Si-Jie nodded, and then shook her head. “I don’t know.”

“That’s allowed.”

Si-Wei came up behind the three of them with her phone. “Then we’re taking another photograph. All three of us. At the window.”

“With the police car?” said Si-Yuan.

“Why not? It’s part of the scenery.”

Si-Jie laughed in spite of herself. They stood together with the room behind them and the street below, Si-Wei’s arm round Si-Jie’s shoulders, Si-Yuan leaning in from the other side, and Sung Jae took it.

Si-Jie looked at it and laughed again. “That’s terrible.”

“It’s memorable,” said Si-Wei.

Not long after that Si-Yuan looked at her phone, and put it away, and said she was tired and her own flat was calling. She kissed her mother and both her sisters. At the door she kissed Si-Jie’s cheek a second time and said happy birthday into her hair.

✦ ✦ ✦

That night, when everyone had gone, Si-Jie stood in the bedroom doorway. “I don’t want to sleep in the dark tonight.”

“Then we won’t.”

She sat down on the bed, and he sat beside her. For a moment she looked at her hands. “I was happy today. Having all of us together. The cakes. My earrings. And then I looked out of the window, and I remembered there are two women who never got to come home.”

“I’ve been thinking about them too.”

“Do you think they were frightened?”

He took a moment. “We don’t know what they went through.”

“I keep picturing them reading their letters. Thinking it was strange, but not dangerous enough to tell anyone. I wish someone had been able to bring them home.”

He brought her hand to his mouth. “So do I.”

She leaned against him. “Are you frightened?”

He looked round the room, and then at her. “Of a phone call. Of finding out something happened while I wasn’t there. Of being too late. But I don’t want to spend every night treating you like someone I’ve already lost.”

“Then don’t.”

He touched her cheek. “Tell me what you need.”

She thought about it. “Stay close. And leave the lights on.”

“I can do both.”

She kissed him, a small kiss and then another, and put her arms round his neck. He stopped long enough to ask if she was sure, and she said yes. She wanted him close tonight: not to forget the letter, not to prove she wasn’t afraid, but because she was afraid and he was there and she wanted to be held by someone she loved. They took their time. He undressed her slowly, a button and then another, and kissed each place he uncovered: her shoulder, the inside of her wrist, the soft skin under her ribs. He asked as he went, without turning it into an interrogation. She told him what she wanted, and when, and he did it. When his mouth moved lower she put her hand in his hair and held on, and the fear in her chest went somewhere else for a while, and she came with her head pressed back into the pillow and his name caught in her throat.

Afterwards she pulled him up to her and wanted him inside her, and said so. He moved carefully, like she might break, until she held his face in both hands and told him she wanted to feel him, not be handled, and then he stopped being careful. She held on to him. He held on to her. Every light in the flat stayed on, and she watched him over her, and when it took him he said her name like a promise and didn’t look away.

Afterwards she lay with her head on his chest and traced a line along his wrist. “Do you regret moving in?”

“No.”

“Even with my hair ties?”

He looked down at her. “I’ve made my peace with the hair ties.”

She laughed, and then grew serious. “Thank you for coming here.”

He kissed her temple. “Thank you for letting me.”

“Stay tomorrow too.”

“I live here now.”

She smiled with her eyes shut. “Right.”

✦ ✦ ✦

In the small hours Arthur woke. The bedroom light was still on. He looked at her face, and at the earrings on the bedside table, and remembered the safe flat, and the folder, and the argument. He’d wanted to move her somewhere he could control every door. Instead he’d moved himself into her home. It wasn’t perfect, and it wasn’t a guarantee. But they’d decided it together.

He reached for the notebook and turned past the October page to a new one.

13 December 2025.
Si-Jie’s twenty-second birthday. All three sisters together. Three cakes. Si-Yuan home from Paris. Her mother reorganised the kitchen. Si-Wei was loud. Si-Jie wore the earrings.
There was a police car outside.
She was frightened. So was I.
I asked whether I could stay. She said yes.
The flat is smaller than mine. There are too many hair ties. The kitchen cupboards follow no system I recognise.

He looked at her, and wrote one more line.

I am home.

He closed the notebook and left the light on. When she stirred he moved closer without waking her. For now they were together, and she was home. And somewhere in the city the investigation into Kot Siu-ming was starting again.

chapters.title: Her Sisters’ Plan
chapters.desc: Her sisters call a family meeting, Si-Yuan on a laptop from Paris. Sung Jae offers six men, once, and she says no. Arthur thanks him anyway, and the two of them agree on four words.
chapters.content:
The message came on the last Sunday of December, a little after eight in the morning, in YEN GIRLS AND A SECOND HOSTAGE. Si-Wei had made the chat the day Arthur moved in, added him without asking, and named it before anyone could object.

Si-Wei (Business Hours): Family meeting. Today.

Si-Yuan (Eldest, Allegedly): Is something wrong?

Si-Wei (Business Hours): Nothing’s wrong. We’re discussing something.

Si-Jie: That sounds worse.

Si-Yuan (Eldest, Allegedly): What time? It’s one in the morning here.

Si-Wei (Business Hours): Two o’clock ours. You can do it on video.

Si-Jie: Where?

Si-Wei (Business Hours): Yours. You can’t go anywhere else.

Si-Jie: Why are you being mysterious?

Si-Wei (Business Hours): Because if I tell you, you’ll complain before we arrive.

Si-Jie: I’m already complaining.

Si-Yuan (Eldest, Allegedly): I’ll send dessert to the flat.

Si-Jie: You’re bribing me.

Si-Yuan (Eldest, Allegedly): Obviously.

Si-Wei (Business Hours): Arthur, you’re attending.

Arthur was sitting up beside her with a book. He read the last message on her screen.

“Should I be concerned?”

“You’re in the group. You’re the hostage,” said Si-Jie.

“I’d noticed.”

She leaned against his shoulder. “Do you think they’re planning something?”

“Yes.”

“What?”

“I don’t know.”

She narrowed her eyes. “You’re a profiler.”

“That doesn’t make me psychic. I’m about to attend a meeting organised by your youngest sister. I’m managing my expectations.”

She laughed until she nearly dropped the phone.

✦ ✦ ✦

By two her sitting room had become a planning room. Their mother had stayed on after the birthday, sleeping at Si-Wei’s, and had come over early to make tea and inspect the kitchen she’d reorganised a fortnight before, which Si-Jie had since disorganised. Si-Wei sat on the sofa with a notebook. Si-Yuan was propped up on the coffee table on Si-Jie’s laptop, in a cream cardigan, with her hair tied back and a mug of something hot, at seven in the morning in Paris. A box of pastries had arrived from a bakery round the corner with a card that said Bribe.

Si-Jie sat down beside Si-Wei, facing the screen. “All right. What is this?”

Si-Wei opened the notebook. “We’ve been discussing your situation. The letter. The old case. The car outside. The fact that you’re still going to work.”

“We don’t want you to feel you’re handling it all alone,” said Si-Yuan from the laptop.

Si-Jie looked from one sister to the other. “I’m not.”

Si-Wei glanced at Arthur. “We know. Arthur lives here. But he can’t be the only person you rely on. And we don’t want you to stop living your life. We also don’t want you to be careless.”

“I haven’t been careless.”

“We know that too.”

Si-Yuan leaned closer to her camera. “We’re not here to tell you to stay at home. We want you to have people you can ring, people who know where you are, and people who can help if something happens.”

Si-Jie looked down at her hands. “Thank you.”

Si-Wei turned a page. “I’ve made a list.”

Si-Jie groaned. “Of course you have.”

“Emergency contacts, transport, check-in times, and the people who can go with you if you want someone.”

Arthur looked at the notebook. It was divided into sections. Naturally.

Si-Wei saw him looking. “What?”

“Nothing.”

“You’re judging my formatting.”

“I’m not.”

“Your face is.”

Si-Jie laughed. “Now you know how it feels.”

On the laptop, Si-Yuan gave a small nod.

Si-Wei put the notebook down. “I’ve also asked someone who might be able to help. Sung Jae.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The doorbell went at twenty to three.

Si-Wei stood up. “That’s him.”

Si-Jie looked at her. “You invited him? Without telling me? You’re getting very difficult.”

Si-Wei smiled. “I learned from you.”

Geum Sung Jae came in with the calm of a man used to being noticed without needing to announce himself. He wore a dark coat over a black shirt. His face was composed, and his eyes went straight to Si-Wei.

She went to meet him. “You’re late.”

“Three minutes.”

“Still late.”

He gave her a small smile, and then looked at the others. He bowed slightly to their mother, and nodded at the laptop. “Si-Yuan.”

“Hello, Sung Jae. It’s very early here. Be quick.”

He turned to Si-Jie. “Happy belated birthday.”

“Thank you.”

Then he looked at Arthur. “Chen.”

“Geum.”

That was the whole greeting. Neither man seemed interested in extending it. Si-Wei took his coat and told him to sit down, and he sat.

Si-Jie watched them. She’d known about the two of them for a long time now. She knew what Sung Jae did, and that he ran the Iron Dogs, and that the world he lived in wasn’t a harmless one. She also knew her sister. Si-Wei didn’t wander into danger without understanding the person beside her. But she was still her sister, and Si-Jie was never going to be entirely comfortable with it.

Sung Jae listened while Si-Wei explained. He didn’t interrupt. He asked a few questions: when the letter had come, whether the police had established a connection to the old case, what precautions were in place. Arthur answered only what he could properly share. When they’d finished, Sung Jae looked at Si-Jie.

“I can arrange six men.”

The room went quiet.

Si-Jie blinked. “Sorry?”

“Six men. They’d go with you when you leave work, stay nearby when you have appointments, make sure you’re not alone when you travel. They won’t interfere with the police. They won’t approach anyone unless there’s an immediate danger. Their job would be to watch your surroundings and get you home.”

“They’re people I trust,” said Si-Wei.

Si-Jie looked at Sung Jae. “For how long?”

“As long as necessary.”

She shook her head. “No.”

Si-Wei frowned. “Si-Jie, listen first.”

“I did.”

“They’re not going to bother you.”

“I know that’s what you’re trying to do. But I don’t want six men following me about.”

Sung Jae said nothing.

She turned to him. “I appreciate it. I know you’re doing it because you care about Si-Wei, and because she’s worried about me. But I don’t want private security from the Iron Dogs. It’d feel like being watched every time I left the flat.”

He considered her answer, and nodded. “Understood.”

Si-Wei looked dissatisfied. “At least think about it.”

“I have thought about it.”

“You’re stubborn.”

“So are you.”

“That’s not the point.”

“It is a little.”

On the laptop, Si-Yuan hid a smile behind her mug.

Arthur, who’d said nothing all this time, spoke at last. “She’s already agreed to the precautions the assigned team recommended. We shouldn’t add another arrangement without thinking about what it would do to her.”

Si-Wei turned to him. “You’re agreeing with her? You’re the one living with her.”

“That’s why.”

Si-Jie glanced at him. He wasn’t trying to win the argument for her. He was saying that her decision mattered. Under the edge of the table she touched his hand.

✦ ✦ ✦

After tea Si-Wei carried the cups into the kitchen and Si-Jie went to help her mother with the dishes. Si-Yuan had gone to find more coffee in Paris. That left Arthur and Sung Jae in the sitting room.

For a moment neither of them spoke. Sung Jae poured himself more tea.

“You’re not going to take the offer.”

“No.”

“Even if you think she might need it?”

Arthur looked at him. “She said no.”

Sung Jae nodded, as a man nods at a complete answer. “I wasn’t offering to put her under my control. I was offering because Si-Wei asked me to think of something useful.”

“I understand that.”

Sung Jae put his cup down. “She matters to Si-Wei.”

“She matters to me.”

There was a pause. Sung Jae studied him. “You look tired.”

“I am.”

“But you’re staying with her.”

“Yes.”

“Good.”

Arthur glanced towards the kitchen. “Thank you for offering.”

Sung Jae gave a small nod. “She has to say yes.”

“I know she does.”

They sat in silence for a while. Then Sung Jae said he wouldn’t send anyone, and Arthur thanked him again.

A few seconds passed. Sung Jae looked at him once more. “Four words.”

Arthur raised an eyebrow. “Which four?”

“She decides. We listen.”

Arthur held his gaze, and nodded. “That’s right.”

It wasn’t friendship, not exactly. They came from different worlds and had different ideas about what it meant to protect someone. But they both understood that sentence, and for now it was enough.

✦ ✦ ✦

Si-Wei came back with a plate of cut fruit and looked from one man to the other. “Are you behaving?”

Sung Jae picked up his tea. “Yes.”

Arthur said nothing.

Si-Wei narrowed her eyes. “Why do I feel you’ve been discussing something without me?”

“Because we were. Your sister. She refused, and we’ve agreed to respect it,” said Sung Jae.

Si-Wei looked at Arthur, and he nodded. She breathed out. “Fine.”

Sung Jae reached for a piece of fruit.

She slapped his hand lightly. “Wash your hands first.”

“I just did.”

“Then why are you touching everything?”

He put his hand down.

Si-Jie came back from the kitchen in time to see it, and looked at Si-Wei, and at Sung Jae, and at Arthur. “He’s very obedient.”

Sung Jae gave her a look.

Si-Wei smiled. “Only when he wants to be.”

Arthur sipped his tea. “That sounds familiar.”

Si-Jie turned to him. “Excuse me?”

He met her eyes and calmly ate a strawberry.

“You’re all exhausting,” said Si-Yuan, who’d come back to the laptop with her coffee and caught the end of it.

✦ ✦ ✦

The six men had been refused, but the meeting wasn’t over. Si-Wei’s list was practical, and she read it out.

The charity to be told the current risk assessment and agree workplace safety measures.
Si-Jie to tell the assigned officers about any new letter or unusual contact.
Si-Jie to share her travel plans with her sisters and Arthur when she wants to.
A simple check-in for late evenings.
If she feels unsafe, she goes somewhere public or secure and calls the police. She doesn’t confront anyone.
Arthur stays her emergency contact. He is not expected to manage the investigation.

Si-Jie read it over her shoulder. “You’ve thought about this a lot.”

“Obviously,” said Si-Wei.

“We’re your sisters. What did you expect?” said Si-Yuan.

“I don’t know. A normal birthday present?”

“That was a fortnight ago. This is the late one,” said Si-Wei.

Si-Jie laughed, and looked at both of them, the one beside her and the one on the screen. “Thank you.”

Si-Wei shrugged. “Don’t make it emotional.”

“You’re already emotional.”

“I’m not.”

“She is,” said Si-Yuan.

The three of them began to talk over one another. Arthur watched from the armchair, and Sung Jae sat beside him looking faintly resigned. Their mother came in from the kitchen, listened for a moment, and went back out again.

After a while Arthur said they did this often.

Sung Jae glanced at him. “Yes. They don’t notice they’re doing it.”

They watched the sisters argue about whether the check-in should be at a fixed time or a flexible one.

Sung Jae drank some tea. “Your girlfriend’s difficult.”

Arthur looked at him. “Your girlfriend is my girlfriend’s sister.”

“That wasn’t a denial.”

“No.”

Sung Jae laughed under his breath.

✦ ✦ ✦

Si-Yuan rang off with a yawn and a kiss blown at each sister. They left just after six: Si-Wei, Sung Jae, and their mother, who was going back to Si-Wei’s for the night and had packed Si-Jie three boxes of leftovers. Si-Jie and Arthur went down with them as far as the door of the building. The police car was where it always was. Sung Jae opened the passenger door for Si-Wei, and she didn’t get in straight away.

“You’re not angry? That she refused?”

“No.”

“You offered because I asked.”

“I offered because I thought it might help. Now she doesn’t want it.”

Si-Wei studied his face. “You don’t mind?”

He reached up and tucked a loose strand of hair behind her ear. “No.”

She smiled. “Good.”

He kissed her hair. “Message me when you’re home.”

“I will. And don’t send anyone.”

“I won’t.”

“Promise.”

“I promise.”

She got in beside her mother and shut the door. When Sung Jae turned round, his eyes met Arthur’s across the pavement. He gave a slight nod, and Arthur returned it. Nothing more needed saying.

✦ ✦ ✦

Upstairs, Si-Jie put the leftovers in the fridge and Arthur washed the last of the cups. After a few minutes she asked whether she’d been rude.

“No.”

“To Sung Jae? I refused six men.”

“He offered. You declined.”

She looked at him. “You’re very concise.”

“Would you prefer a longer answer?”

“Maybe.”

He dried his hands. “You thanked him. You explained why you didn’t want it. You didn’t insult him or dismiss his concern. He accepted your answer.”

She smiled. “That’s a good answer. I liked that you thanked him too.”

“He was trying to help.”

“Even though you didn’t want six men following me?”

“Refusing his offer doesn’t mean his concern wasn’t welcome.”

She was quiet, and then she came and put her arms round his waist from behind. “You’re getting better at this. Letting people help without making it a competition.”

“I wasn’t aware it was a competition.”

She laughed into his back. “Of course you weren’t.”

He turned round in her arms. “If you ever change your mind about more security, we can talk about it again. The decision will be yours.”

“I’ll remember,” said Si-Jie, and took his hand, and turned it over and kissed his knuckles.

✦ ✦ ✦

At nine the chat woke up again.

Si-Wei (Business Hours): Home.

Si-Jie: Good.

Si-Wei (Business Hours): Arthur. Did you eat?

Arthur (Thirty-Nine): Yes.

Si-Wei (Business Hours): Properly?

Arthur (Thirty-Nine): Yes.

Si-Jie: She asks you more than she asks me.

Si-Wei (Business Hours): Because you forget when you’re working.

Si-Yuan (Eldest, Allegedly): Both of you stop. Some of us are trying to have lunch.

Si-Wei (Business Hours): And no more emergency meetings until next year.

Si-Jie: Promise?

Si-Wei (Business Hours): No promises.

Arthur (Thirty-Nine): That seems consistent.

Si-Wei (Business Hours): Don’t encourage her.

Si-Jie laughed and put the phone down. Arthur picked his book up again. She moved closer and put her head on his shoulder and slipped her hand into his.

“Do you think they’ll keep worrying?”

“Yes.”

“Even when the case is over?”

“Probably.”

She sighed. “That’s annoying.”

“They love you.”

She looked up at him. “Do you?”

He lowered the book. “Do I what?”

“Love me.”

He looked at her. Then he closed the book and put it aside. “Yes.”

She smiled. “Good.”

He kissed her, and she kissed him back, and then settled with her head on his chest, listening to the steady sound under his shirt. Her sisters had a plan. The police had an investigation. The Iron Dogs had offered six men and accepted a refusal. Arthur had moved into her home. For the first time in weeks she felt that the people round her weren’t trying to decide her life for her. They were making sure she didn’t have to face it alone. That, she thought, was what protection should have looked like all along.

chapters.title: The Second Letter
chapters.desc: The second letter is about Arthur: the black notebook, its pages, a line from March. There’s no sign of forced entry at her flat, but her hairbrush is gone.
chapters.epigraph: “He thinks the book belongs to him because he wrote it.”
chapters.content:
The second letter came to the charity at 10.41 on a Monday morning in January. This time the receptionist didn’t leave it on Si-Jie’s desk. She rang Si-Jie’s supervisor first.

The envelope was white and unmarked and addressed in the same unfamiliar hand. But something about it was different. Her name wasn’t in the middle. It was written small, near the bottom right-hand corner, and the rest of the envelope had been left empty.

Si-Jie stood beside her supervisor’s desk. “Is it from the same person?”

Her supervisor put on gloves before she touched it. “We don’t know yet. Don’t handle it. We’ll document it and follow the same procedure as last time.”

Si-Jie nodded. Then she saw the ink. Green. Her stomach tightened. “Can I read it?”

“Not until it’s been documented.”

She nodded again. She knew the procedure. She’d helped other women through procedures like this one. It was different with her own name on the envelope.

An officer arrived soon afterwards. The envelope was photographed, the circumstances of its delivery recorded, and the contents handled as the investigation team had instructed. Three pages, again. But this time the first sentence wasn’t about her. It was about Arthur.

The man who keeps the black book is careful with his pages.

For a moment Si-Jie forgot to breathe. She read the sentence again, and the next.

He writes in black ink. He used to keep it in a drawer. He doesn’t any more.

Her fingers curled.

He thinks the book belongs to him because he wrote it. Perhaps he forgets that the pages are about you.

She looked up. Her supervisor was watching her.

“Si-Jie?”

She swallowed. “It’s about Arthur.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The letter described the notebook, and not vaguely. It described the black cover and the shape of the spine and the pages filled with Arthur’s precise handwriting. It mentioned entries from the first time he’d met her. It mentioned the comments she’d written in the margins. And it quoted one line from the night she’d come back to him in March.

She came back at 7.46.

Si-Jie went cold. That entry had been written in Arthur’s flat. She’d never posted it anywhere. Nobody at the charity could have known it. The third page was worse.

You have made him change the way he writes. He leaves space for your corrections now. I wonder if he knows that someone else has read those pages.

She put the letter down. “How?”

Her supervisor looked at her. “Do you recognise anything in it?”

Si-Jie shook her head. “No.”

“Does it mention anything that suggests the writer has been in your home?”

She looked at the page. “Yes.”

Her supervisor didn’t ask her to explain straight away. She waited until Si-Jie was ready.

“The notebook’s at my flat. Arthur and I are the only ones with keys. The building has a controlled entry system. And there’s been a police car outside since November.”

“Has anyone else been in recently?”

Si-Jie tried to think. Her mother. Her sisters. A delivery once. Someone from building maintenance about a radiator. Nothing stood out. Then she remembered the hairbrush.

She’d used it that morning, before she left. A wooden brush with a dark handle, worn smooth along one edge. She’d put it on the chest of drawers beside the mirror. She could see it clearly.

She looked at her supervisor. “I need to go home.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Arthur was in a meeting when she rang. He answered on the second ring. “Si-Jie?”

“Are you at work?”

“Yes. What’s wrong?”

She hesitated. “Someone’s sent another letter. To the charity.”

Silence. Then his voice changed. “Are you safe?”

“Yes. I’m with my supervisor. The officer’s here.”

“What does it say?”

“It’s about you. The notebook. It describes the cover and the entries and my margins. It quotes the night I came back.”

His breathing changed. “Has it been preserved?”

“Yes.”

“Good. Don’t take it home. Don’t handle it again.”

She closed her eyes. “Arthur. I think someone’s been inside our flat.”

There was a silence. “Why?”

She looked down at her hands. “My hairbrush. I used it this morning. I remember putting it down. I want to go and look.”

“Don’t.”

“Arthur—”

“Don’t touch anything. Don’t move anything. Don’t go in on your own. Tell the officer, and let them go in first.”

His voice was controlled. Too controlled.

“I will,” said Si-Jie.

“I’m coming.”

“You’re at work.”

“I’m leaving.”

“Don’t do anything stupid.”

He was quiet. “I won’t.”

She knew he meant it. She also knew how much it would cost him.

✦ ✦ ✦

The police reached the flat before Arthur did. Si-Jie waited outside on the landing with an officer and didn’t go in. The building manager was called. The access records were preserved and the security footage requested through the proper channels. The two officers from the car across the street came up and said they’d seen nobody they didn’t recognise go in or out since the morning change.

The officer beside her asked when she’d last seen the brush.

“About eight this morning, before I left. On the chest of drawers in the bedroom, by the mirror.”

“Anything else missing?”

“I don’t know. I haven’t looked.”

“Good. We’ll document it.”

Arthur came up the stairs twenty minutes later. He walked towards her quickly, and then stopped a few steps short. He looked at her face first, then her hands, then her eyes.

“Are you hurt?”

“No.”

“Did anyone come near you?”

“No.”

He nodded. For a moment he seemed unable to decide whether to touch her. She reached for him, and he held her: not hard enough to hurt, but hard enough that she could feel how frightened he was. She pressed her face against his chest.

“I’m all right.”

He shut his eyes and said nothing.

She heard him breathe in, and out. When at last he let her go he looked towards the open door of the flat. “Have they gone in?”

“Yes. They’re documenting it.”

He nodded. He didn’t go inside. He didn’t try to take over. He waited for the officer to come and speak to him. That was the first thing Si-Jie noticed. The second was that his hands were shaking.

✦ ✦ ✦

There was no sign of forced entry. The front door and the lock were undamaged. Nothing had been knocked over or broken. There was no sign of a struggle and nothing obviously disturbed. But the hairbrush was gone.

The officers photographed the chest of drawers and the mirror and the room round them, and examined every way into the flat. No forced entry didn’t establish how someone had got in, or when, or who. But the letter’s knowledge of the notebook made it a serious possibility that somebody had been there.

An officer spoke to Arthur in the hallway. “Does anyone else know where the notebook is kept?”

“Si-Jie.”

“Anyone else?”

“Not that I’m aware of.”

“Have you ever shown it to anyone? Photographed any of it?”

Arthur paused. “We’ve talked about some entries between ourselves. The notebook itself has never been shared.”

“Has it ever been left anywhere it could be seen?”

He looked towards the bedroom. “It’s been in the flat. On the bedside table.”

The officer nodded. “Don’t move it until we’ve recorded where it is. We may need to examine it.”

Arthur agreed.

Si-Jie stood beside him. “Do you think the person read it?”

He looked at her. “I don’t know.”

“But the letter knows what’s inside.”

“Yes.”

“Then someone saw it.”

“Possibly. Or they got the information some other way.”

She looked towards the bedroom. The notebook was still there on the bedside table: the black cover, the two handwritings, her comments in the margins. The record of something that had begun with a lecture and survived a terrible mistake. Someone had known it existed. Someone had known where it was. And someone had written to her about it.

✦ ✦ ✦

The officer recommended that they spend the night somewhere else while the flat was examined, and asked Si-Jie what she wanted. She looked at the bedroom door for a long moment and said yes, tonight, somewhere else. Arthur didn’t say a word until she’d decided.

The assigned team arranged a temporary flat across the city. Si-Jie rode in the back of the police car and watched the streets go past. Arthur followed in his own car. She hadn’t cried. The fear had settled somewhere too deep to reach.

When they arrived he came to her at once. “Do you want water?”

She shook her head.

“Do you want to sit down? Do you want me to—”

She held out her hand. “Arthur. Stay with me.”

He took it, and for several minutes they stood together without speaking. Then she asked whether he was angry.

“Yes. At whoever did this.”

“At me?”

“No.”

She looked down. “I should have noticed sooner. The brush. I should have seen it was gone before I left.”

His expression changed. “Si-Jie. You used it this morning. It was there. You noticed when you had a reason to look.”

“But—”

“Someone may have been in your home without your knowledge. That isn’t your failure. You’re not responsible for noticing an intrusion before you’ve any reason to suspect one.”

She nodded. Then she said she hadn’t told him about the first letter for a whole day.

“I remember.”

“I thought I was protecting you.”

He looked at her. “You don’t have to protect me from being frightened.”

She swallowed. “I know that now.”

He lifted her hand and kissed it. “Good.”

She leaned against him, and after a moment she looked up. “You’re frightened too. And you’re trying not to show it. Don’t.”

He held her gaze, and then his face gave way at last. “I’m frightened, Si-Jie.”

She put her arms round him and held on.

✦ ✦ ✦

Late in the evening the assigned officer came back with an update. The letter had been secured. The team would compare it with the first and with the material from 2022. The possible entry into the flat would be investigated separately, including the building’s access records and any footage. Nobody had been identified. Nobody had been arrested. There was still no confirmed evidence that Kot Siu-ming had sent either letter, and the officer made that clear. Arthur listened carefully.

Si-Jie asked one question. “Does the letter mean he knows where we are now?”

The officer answered her honestly. “We can’t tell that from what we have. We’ll review it and talk to you both about precautions.”

When the officer had gone, Arthur sat down beside her.

She looked at him. “Do you think he knows about us?”

“Yes.”

“How much? Does he know you live with me?”

He thought about the letter. “He may.”

She closed her eyes. The letter had described the notebook. The notebook had been in their home. The writer knew its colour and its pages and the changes she’d made to them. And the hairbrush was gone.

“Did he take it because it’s mine? Or because it smells like me?” said Si-Jie.

Arthur went still. He didn’t offer a comforting answer. He couldn’t. He took her hand instead. “We’ll let the investigators find out what they can. We won’t guess at a motive without evidence.”

She nodded, and leaned her head against his shoulder.

✦ ✦ ✦

That night she couldn’t sleep. Arthur sat beside her on the strange bed with his hand over hers.

“Can I ask you something? Do you wish you’d never written the notebook?”

He was quiet. “The first one?”

“Both.”

He looked down. “I regret keeping the first one without your knowledge. I regret making you feel studied instead of loved. But I don’t regret knowing you.”

Her eyes softened. “Even now?”

“Now more than ever.”

She leaned forward and kissed him, briefly, and rested her forehead against his. “I don’t want him to have it.”

“He doesn’t.”

“You don’t know that.”

“No. But the notebook isn’t what makes us what we are. It’s only pages.”

She smiled faintly. “You’re learning.”

“I’m trying.”

She touched his cheek. “Tomorrow I want to go through it with the investigators, if they need it. And I want to know whether someone really was inside our flat.”

“Then we’ll help them find out.”

She nodded and lay down. Arthur stayed beside her. He didn’t turn off the light.

✦ ✦ ✦

Some time after one he picked up his phone, and put it down again. He hadn’t opened a database. He hadn’t contacted anyone outside the investigation. He hadn’t searched for Kot Siu-ming. He’d done exactly what he’d promised her. But he couldn’t stop thinking about the hairbrush: a wooden brush with a dark handle and one worn edge. Something ordinary that belonged to her, taken out of their home.

He looked at her. She was asleep, one hand curled near her face. He wanted to move her somewhere else. He wanted to put every lock in the world between her and everyone outside it. He wanted to know who had been in their flat, and how, and why. He wanted to find him. But wanting wasn’t permission.

The officers had photographed the notebook and given it back before they left, and he opened it now at a blank page.

12 January 2026.
The second letter arrived today. It describes the black notebook and contains details that were not publicly available.
The writer may have been inside our flat. Si-Jie’s hairbrush is missing.

He stopped, and then wrote one more line.

I am frightened.

He looked at it. It wasn’t a behavioural observation, or a hypothesis. It was simply true. He closed the notebook.

Beside him Si-Jie stirred. “Arthur?”

“I’m here.”

She reached for his hand, and held it when he gave it to her. “Don’t leave me alone tonight.”

“I won’t.”

She closed her eyes again. Arthur stayed awake. For three years he’d carried an unfinished case. Now it had come into his home, and taken something that belonged to the woman asleep beside him: something small, something ordinary, something nobody should ever have touched. The hairbrush was gone. And someone knew exactly where they lived.

chapters.title: Inside the Mind
chapters.desc: A wall of photographs in his study: two women, four letters, one name he never proved. He stops sleeping. She brings a pillow and a blanket and sleeps on the study floor so he isn’t alone in there.
chapters.epigraph: “I don’t want you to be alone in this room.”
chapters.content:
After the second letter they didn’t go back to her flat. The assigned team agreed they could stay at his: a different building on a different street, an address that had never appeared in any of the letters. The police car moved with them. By the end of the week it was parked across from his entrance, and the officers who changed at eight and eight had learned to wave at Si-Jie when she came down for the post.

His study had never been a welcoming room. It was small, at the end of the flat, with a desk, two bookshelves, a filing cabinet and a window that looked at the building next door. Before January it had held books and work documents. Now it held photographs: a wall of them.

Two women. The first had been twenty-two when she disappeared in March 2022. Her photograph came from a university profile: long dark hair, a slight smile, an ordinary student picture. The second had been twenty-four. Her photograph came from an event programme. Her hair was longer, over one shoulder, and she was looking straight at the camera.

Beside them were timelines, copies of the letters, maps and documented locations. There was no red string. Arthur disliked theatre. Everything on the wall had a source, a date and a reason for being there. He’d put the two old letters side by side, the blue ink and the black, with different handwriting and similar language. He’d added the green letter Si-Jie had received in November, and then the second, the one about his notebook.

The case had changed. Not because he’d decided the four letters were connected, but because there was now enough material to justify examining the possibility formally. In the middle of the wall he’d written a name.

KOT SIU-MING
POSSIBLE CONNECTION — NOT ESTABLISHED

He stood and looked at the words. Three years ago the name had been one possibility among several. Now it had come back, and it had come back with Si-Jie attached to it.

✦ ✦ ✦

The assigned team had asked for his original behavioural assessment, and he’d given it to them through the proper channels. He’d also given them his notes on the language of the two new letters, and made it clear that the similarities didn’t establish a common author. He wasn’t the lead investigator. He had no business running searches of his own. He knew where the lines were.

He also knew how to think about the case. That was the problem. His mind had started working before he reached the study each morning. He woke up with questions. He ate breakfast thinking about timelines. He stood in the shower remembering phrases. At work he dealt with his assigned cases, and went back to the old material only when he was authorised to. At home he stood in front of the wall.

The first woman. The second woman. The new letters. He didn’t put Si-Jie’s photograph beside theirs. He refused to make her the third photograph. But her name was on the whiteboard under the wall, in his own hand.

YEN SI-JIE — RECIPIENT OF TWO COMMUNICATIONS

He looked at it, and wiped it off, and wrote something else.

CURRENT RECIPIENT — LIVING

He stepped back. It was more accurate. It was also worse.

✦ ✦ ✦

By the end of the first week he was sleeping about four hours a night. By the second it was less.

Si-Jie found out because she woke at some hour after three and his side of the bed was empty. The light was on in the study. He was at the desk with his sleeves rolled up and a cold half-cup of coffee by the keyboard, looking at the photograph of the second woman.

“Arthur?”

He turned round. “Why are you awake?”

“Because you’re not in bed.”

“I’ll come soon.”

She looked at the clock on his desk. “It’s three in the morning. Have you slept?”

“Earlier.”

“How much?”

He didn’t answer. She came into the room. There were documents on the desk and the wall and the floor: not scattered, but sorted into groups, each with its own small territory. She looked at the photographs, and then at him.

“How long have you been in here tonight?”

“Since eleven.”

“That’s four hours.”

“Approximately.”

She stared at him, and then crossed to the desk and put her hand flat over the laptop screen. “Come to bed.”

“Si-Jie, I need to finish going through—”

“No.”

He stopped. She hadn’t raised her voice.

“You’re not going to finish a three-year investigation tonight.”

“I’m aware of that.”

“Then come to bed.”

He looked at the wall again, and she followed his eyes, and for a moment she understood something. He wasn’t only trying to solve the case. He was trying to make sure the two women hadn’t disappeared for nothing. And now he was afraid the same thing could happen to her.

She took his hand. “Come with me.”

After a moment he closed the laptop.

✦ ✦ ✦

He slept for two hours, and woke before it was light, and slid out of bed without waking her and went back to the study. He didn’t turn on the overhead light. He sat at the desk and opened the file, and he was reading the first woman’s mother’s statement when he heard footsteps.

Si-Jie was in the doorway in his shirt, with a pillow under one arm and a blanket over the other.

“What are you doing?” said Arthur.

“Sleeping.”

She came in and put the pillow on the floor beside his chair, and shook out the blanket.

He watched her. “On the floor?”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“Because you keep coming in here.”

“You could sleep in bed.”

“I did. You weren’t in it.”

He said nothing. She lay down on the blanket and arranged the pillow under her head.

“This is uncomfortable,” said Arthur.

“Probably.”

“The floor is cold.”

“I brought a blanket.”

“You’ll wake up with a sore back.”

She pulled the blanket up to her chin. “Then I’ll complain about it all day. I don’t want you to be alone in this room.”

Something in his face changed. He looked at the wall again. The photographs were still there. The women were still missing. The case was still unresolved. But Si-Jie had brought a pillow and a blanket into the room. She wasn’t asking him to stop caring about the case. She was refusing to let it be the only thing in there.

He stood up and took the spare blanket from the cupboard and laid it over her, and crouched beside her. “Thank you.”

She opened one eye. “Go to sleep.”

“I’ll sit here.”

She reached for his hand. “Then I’ll sleep here.”

He stayed beside her until her breathing slowed. In the morning she complained about her back, exactly as promised. She complained while he made coffee, and while she ate the toast he’d cut into triangles without being asked, and while she put her coat on for a seminar with an officer waiting at the bottom of the stairs.

“You could have slept in the bed,” said Arthur.

She held out her hand for her keys, and he gave them to her, and she didn’t let go of them straight away. “So could you. Did you sleep at all?”

“Some.”

“In the chair?”

“Yes.”

She looked at him the way she’d looked at him in the second row of a lecture hall, a long time ago: as if he were a question she fully intended to have answered. “Tonight I’m bringing two pillows.”

“That isn’t a solution.”

“It’s a better one than yours.”

She kissed his cheek and went down the stairs, and the officer fell in a few steps behind her, and Arthur stood in the doorway and watched until the street door closed. Then he went back to the study and looked at the floor where she’d slept, and at the two folded blankets, and for once he didn’t sit down at the desk. He went to work.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the fourth night she asked about them. She was on the floor with her head on the pillow, and he was at the desk.

“Can you tell me their names?”

He looked at her, and then he told her. Both names were in the case file. He said them carefully, and didn’t reduce either woman to a description. The first had been studying literature and had a younger brother. The second had been finishing a degree in the evenings and working in a shop, and it was a close friend who had reported her missing. They’d had families and friends and plans. Their lives hadn’t stopped mattering because the investigation had become difficult.

Si-Jie listened. “Do you think they knew someone was watching them?”

“We don’t know.”

“Did their families know about the letters?”

“Yes.”

She looked up at the photographs. “They were real people. Not just two cases.”

“No.”

She was quiet for a while. Then she asked whether he thought he could have found them.

He looked at the desk. “I don’t know.”

“Do you think you missed something?”

“Possibly.”

She watched him. “I know what you’re doing. You’re trying to go back three years and find the one thing that would have changed everything. But you can’t know whether that thing even exists.”

He looked at her. “I should have found the connection.”

“You may have been wrong about the connection.”

“Or I may have been right.”

She reached out from under the blanket and put her hand round his ankle. “Both are possible. You don’t have to punish yourself for not knowing something you didn’t have enough evidence to know.”

He looked at her hand, and then at the photographs. “I keep thinking about the letters. About what happened after they received them.”

“So do I.”

He looked down at her. “You’re frightened. Why are you still sleeping here?”

She smiled faintly. “Because you’re frightened too.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At the end of January the team held a formal review, and Arthur attended as the profiler who’d worked on the original case. They went through the four letters, the known timelines and what evidence there was about the possible entry into Si-Jie’s flat. The similarities in the language were noted. The letters’ knowledge of private details was considered significant. The missing hairbrush was treated as possible evidence, though its absence couldn’t establish who had taken it or why. The building’s access records were still being examined. Kot Siu-ming remained a person of interest from the original investigation, not a proven offender, and nobody in the room said otherwise.

At the end a senior investigator turned to him. “Do you believe this is the same person?”

Arthur looked at the documents in front of him. “I believe the letters warrant a linked investigation. I believe the similarities are too substantial to dismiss. I don’t believe we’ve established a common author.”

“And Kot?”

“A possible connection. Not a conclusion.”

The investigator nodded. “Good. Keep that distinction clear.”

Arthur understood. He’d spent years telling investigators not to mistake a behavioural hypothesis for evidence. He wasn’t going to abandon that now. Not even for Si-Jie. Least of all for her.

Eugene Chak caught him up in the corridor afterwards and walked beside him as far as the lifts without saying anything. At the lifts he held out a paper bag. Inside was a sandwich, still in its wrapper.

“You missed lunch. And breakfast, by the look of you,” said Eugene.

Arthur took the bag. Eugene pressed the button for his own floor and didn’t wait to be thanked.

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening he came home earlier than usual, and Si-Jie was already in the study. She’d moved her blanket into the corner and was reading.

He stopped in the doorway. “You’ve made yourself a permanent arrangement.”

“I’ve thought about renting the space.”

“For how much?”

“One kiss a night.”

“Expensive.”

“You’re welcome to negotiate.”
