He came over and crouched beside her. “How was your day?”

“Fine. A seminar, then lunch with my supervisor, with an officer at the next table pretending to read the menu. I bought groceries.”

“Did you eat?”

“Yes.”

“What?”

She smiled. “You’re asking instead of working it out.”

“Yes.”

She put her book down. “Progress. How was the review?”

He told her. She listened, and asked whether they’d agreed the letters might be connected.

“They agreed the similarities need further investigation.”

“Did they say Kot wrote them?”

“No.”

“Good.”

He sat down beside her with his back against the wall, and she moved closer, and for a while they read in silence. Then she closed her book.

“Do you want to come to bed tonight?”

He looked at the photographs. “Yes.”

She studied him. “Properly? Not for two hours?”

“Properly.”

She smiled. “Then let’s go.”

He stood and held out his hand, and she took it. In the doorway she looked back at the wall. “Can we leave them there? I don’t want you to forget them.”

“I won’t.”

“And I don’t want you to forget me.”

He looked at her. “I won’t do that either.”

She touched his face, and turned out the light.

✦ ✦ ✦

Some time after two, Arthur woke again and lay still. Si-Jie was asleep beside him. He could hear her breathing. For a moment he thought about getting up. The study was waiting, and the photographs, and the questions. Then she moved closer in her sleep and put a hand flat on his chest.

He looked down at her. He thought about the two women, and the first letter and the second, and the green ink, and the missing brush, and how little anyone knew. He also remembered what she’d said on the floor of the study, about not punishing himself for what he hadn’t had the evidence to know.

He closed his eyes. He didn’t sleep straight away, but he stayed in bed.

A little later she stirred. “Arthur?”

“I’m here.”

“Don’t go.”

“All right.”

She settled again, and he put his arm round her. In the study the photographs were still on the wall: two women, two unfinished stories, four letters, a possible connection, a name that had come back after three years. In the bedroom there was only Si-Jie, warm under the blanket, her hand against him, her hair across the pillow. He’d go back to the case in the morning. Tonight he let the woman beside him sleep, and eventually he slept too.

chapters.title: Bait
chapters.desc: The task force wants her to answer the letters under supervision. Arthur says no. She says it’s her life, asks every question, and signs. In the car park he kisses her as if it’s the last time.
chapters.content:
The meeting began at a quarter past nine on the first Monday in February, and Arthur knew something was wrong when he saw the extra chair at the end of the table. There were five people in the room, counting him. The extra chair belonged to a senior investigator from the task force’s major investigations division, and there was a folder open in front of him. Arthur recognised the photographs: the letters, the timeline, and a photograph of Yen Si-Jie.

He didn’t sit down. “What is this?”

The senior investigator looked up. “We have a possible development. We’ve been through the letters again. The writer has shown a sustained interest in Miss Yen. The second letter shows knowledge of her private life, including your notebook.”

Arthur pulled out his chair. “That isn’t new.”

The investigator turned a page. “No. The pattern is. The writer wants a response.”

“Do we have evidence of that?”

“Not explicitly. But the letters are getting more personal. He appears to want some kind of relationship with her.”

“Appears.”

“Yes. We believe a controlled communication might encourage him to reveal himself. Miss Yen would receive a message through an agreed channel. She’d reply under supervision. We’d monitor the exchange and try to establish who’s on the other end.”

Arthur looked at him. “No.”

The investigator paused. “I haven’t finished.”

“You don’t need to.”

“Arthur.”

“No.”

The senior investigator closed the folder. “We’re not proposing to send her anywhere alone. This would be a controlled operation.”

“You’re proposing to use a woman who’s had two letters and whose flat may have been entered as bait for a man nobody has identified.”

“We’d take precautions.”

“Precautions don’t remove the risk.”

“We have reason to believe he’s focused on her.”

“That’s exactly why she shouldn’t be used to draw him closer.”

The room went quiet. The investigator folded his hands. “We have to consider that this person will carry on until we understand what he wants.”

Arthur looked at the photograph on the table: Si-Jie, a university picture, a face that had never belonged on that table. “Then find him. Don’t make her responsible for helping you.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He told her that evening. He didn’t ring her from the corridor. He waited until they were home, until she’d eaten, until they were sitting at the dining table. He’d learned the hard way that holding something back wasn’t the same as protecting someone.

Si-Jie was cutting strawberries. He put his phone down on the table.

“The task force has proposed an operation. They want you to respond to the person who sent the letters. Through a controlled channel. They think it might encourage him to keep writing, and help identify him.”

Her knife stopped. She thought about it. “Like bait.”

“Yes.”

She put the knife down. “And?”

“I refused.”

“Arthur.”

“No.”

“You haven’t heard what I think.”

“I can guess what you think.”

She looked at him. “Can you?”

He didn’t answer.

She pushed the strawberries aside. “It’s my life.”

His jaw tightened. “This isn’t an ordinary risk. We don’t know who he is, whether he can get into your home, whether he’s been following you, or what he means to do.”

“I know all of that.”

“Then you understand why I said no.”

“I understand why you’re frightened.”

“I’m not discussing fear.”

She lowered her voice. “You’re doing exactly that. You’re frightened, and you want to decide what happens next because deciding makes you feel you can control it.”

His face went still. “I’m trying to keep you alive.”

“And I’m trying to live.”

He looked away.

She reached across the table. “Listen to me. I don’t want to be reckless. I don’t want to meet someone alone in a dark car park, or take a strange phone call without knowing who’s listening. I’m not asking to do something stupid.”

“Then don’t agree.”

“That’s not the same thing. It’s my life, Arthur. I know the risk is real. I know someone’s written to me, and that he’s probably been in my flat, and that we don’t know who he is. But I can’t spend the rest of my life having every decision made round the chance that somebody might hurt me.”

“I won’t let them use you.”

“Then make sure they don’t.”

He was silent.

“If they want me to take part, I want to hear the actual plan. I want to know what I’m agreeing to. I want to know what happens if something goes wrong. And I want to be able to stop,” said Si-Jie.

He looked at her. “You’re asking me to help you do this.”

“I’m asking you to listen to me.”

He lowered his eyes. That was harder. It was also what he’d promised.

✦ ✦ ✦

The second meeting was two days later. Si-Jie came with her own support worker, arranged through a victim support service. Arthur was there as her partner, and he wasn’t the person responsible for getting her consent. The distinction mattered.

The task force went through the proposal in detail. No private meeting. No unsupervised contact. No invitation to her home. Nothing that would tell anyone where she was living now. No false promises of intimacy. No attempt to provoke the writer with threats or manipulation. Every message would pass through a channel the investigators controlled. She wouldn’t be expected to improvise; every reply would be drafted and reviewed, and she could refuse any of them. The operation would be suspended if the writer tried to arrange a meeting, threatened immediate harm, or showed he knew where she was. One named officer would be responsible for her safety throughout. She could withdraw at any point without explaining herself.

Si-Jie listened carefully, and asked questions. What would be shared? Who would see her replies? Would her address be kept out of everything? What would happen if he tried to reach her outside the channel? If she stopped, could the investigators carry on using what she’d already sent? The investigator answered each one.

Arthur said little. He sat beside her with his hands folded and his eyes on the papers. When the investigator had finished, Si-Jie turned to him.

“Do you have anything to add?”

He looked at the folder. “Yes. If she withdraws, you stop. Not after one more message. Not after one last attempt. At once.”

The senior investigator nodded. “Agreed.”

“Her safety can’t depend on the assumption that he’ll behave predictably.”

“Agreed.”

“If there’s any sign that he knows where she’s staying, the operation ends and the threat is reassessed.”

“Yes.”

Arthur looked at Si-Jie. “That’s all.”

She studied him. He hadn’t said yes. He hadn’t said no. He’d made sure the conditions were real. For now, that was something.

✦ ✦ ✦

They put the consent form in front of her. Si-Jie read it from beginning to end, and then read it again, while the investigator waited and Arthur watched her hand.

She picked up the pen, and he wanted, badly, to take it away from her. The feeling was so immediate that his fingers moved before he could stop them. He caught himself. His hand stayed on his own side of the table.

Si-Jie saw it, and looked at him. “Arthur.”

He met her eyes. “Are you sure?”

“No. I’m not sure about any of this. That’s why I asked so many questions.”

“Then you don’t have to sign.”

She turned back to the paper. “I want to.”

He didn’t answer. She signed her name, and the pen lifted. A small, ordinary movement. Arthur had watched people sign statements and reports and authorisations and consent forms all his working life, and he’d never hated the sound of a pen on paper as much as he did then.

The investigator collected the form. “Thank you. We’ll be in touch once the schedule’s finalised.”

Si-Jie nodded. Arthur stood and held out his hand, and she took it, and neither of them spoke until they were outside.

✦ ✦ ✦

They reached the car. He unlocked it, and neither of them got in. Si-Jie stood by the passenger door.

“You’re angry.”

“No.”

“You’re very quiet.”

“I’m thinking.”

“About the operation?”

“Yes.”

She stepped closer. “About me?”

He looked at her. “Yes.”

She reached for his hand, and his fingers closed round hers. “You can tell me you’re frightened.”

He looked down at their hands. “I am. I don’t like that someone has made you the centre of something you never asked to be part of. I don’t like that the task force thinks you can help them. I don’t like that I understand why. And I don’t like that you agreed.”

She squeezed his hand. “I know.”

“I wanted to refuse for you. I wanted to take you home and keep you there.”

“But you didn’t.”

“No.”

“Thank you.”

He let out a short breath with no laugh in it. “You shouldn’t thank me for doing what I promised.”

“I can thank you for trying.”

He looked at her face. For a moment he seemed unable to decide what to do with his hands. Then he lifted one and touched her cheek, and his thumb moved once under her eye, and he drew her in and kissed her.

It wasn’t like their usual kisses. There was no teasing pause, no dry observation, none of the small attempts to make her laugh halfway through. He kissed her with both hands holding her face, as if he were trying to memorise something he already knew. Si-Jie held on to the front of his coat. He kissed her again, longer, and when at last he drew back he kept his forehead against hers, and she could feel him breathing.

“Arthur? You’re kissing me like it’s the last time.”

He opened his eyes. For a moment he said nothing. “I know I am.”

Her fingers tightened on his coat. “Don’t. Don’t turn this into a goodbye before anything’s happened. I’m going to come home.”

He closed his eyes briefly. “You don’t know that.”

“No. But I’m going to do everything I can to. And you’re going to be there. Not in front of me. Not behind me. Beside me.”

He bent his head and pressed a kiss into her hair, and her cheek, and her mouth once more, gently this time. “Come home to me.”

“I will,” said Si-Jie.

✦ ✦ ✦

The operation wouldn’t start straight away. There were procedures to complete, messages to prepare and a final risk assessment to review, and two weeks of rehearsals before any of it. The investigators wouldn’t move until everything was confirmed.

That evening Arthur cooked. He made rice and steamed fish and greens, and he weighed nothing. Si-Jie noticed.

“You’re not using the scale.”

“No.”

“Are you feeling all right?”

“No.”

She smiled, a little sadly. He put the food on the table, and they ate together. Afterwards she followed him into the study. The wall was still there: the two women, the letters, the timelines, the name that was still a possibility rather than an answer. She stood in front of it.

“Do you think he’ll reply?”

“I don’t know.”

“Do you think he wants me to?”

“We don’t know what he wants.”

She nodded.

He came to stand beside her. “You’re allowed to change your mind. Even after signing. You don’t owe the task force anything.”

She took his hand. “I know. I also know you’d rather I never went near this case again.”

“Yes.”

“But I need you to understand something. I’m not doing this to prove I’m brave. I’m doing it because I want whoever sent those letters to be found. I want to stop wondering whether someone’s standing outside a door. I want the women on that wall to matter. And I want my life back.”

Arthur looked at the photographs, and then at her. “I understand.”

She leaned her head on his shoulder, and he put his arm round her, and they stayed there a long time.

✦ ✦ ✦

That night she fell asleep first. Arthur lay beside her looking at the ceiling. He’d spent years studying the moment before violence: the decisions, the escalation, the changes in behaviour that could signal rising risk. He knew the limits of that knowledge. He could identify possibilities. He could describe patterns. He couldn’t guarantee what another person would do, and he couldn’t guarantee that Si-Jie would be safe. That was the part he couldn’t bear.

He turned his head. She was asleep on her side with one hand under her cheek, and he reached out and moved a strand of hair off her face. Her eyes opened a little.

“Sorry,” said Arthur.

“Why are you awake?”

“Couldn’t sleep.”

She reached for him without opening her eyes properly. “Come closer.”

He moved towards her.

She tucked herself against his chest. “You’re thinking again.”

“Yes.”

“Can you stop?”

“No.”

She made a small, sleepy sound. “Then think here.”

He looked down at her. She was already drifting off. He put his arm round her, and for once he didn’t get up to look at the study, or the wall, or a file. He stayed where she’d asked him to stay, and when he finally slept he was still holding her hand.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the morning Si-Jie woke to the smell of coffee. Arthur was in the kitchen with two cups: one black, one iced oat latte, less ice, no syrup. She came up behind him and put her arms round his waist, and he put his hand over hers.

“Morning.”

“Morning. Did you sleep?”

“Some.”

“How much?”

“Enough.”

She leaned against his back. “That’s not a number.”

“No.”

She smiled into his shirt. He turned round, and for a moment they just looked at each other. Then he bent and kissed her: not desperately this time, and not like a goodbye, only a kiss between two people who still had breakfast to eat and work to do and a life to get back to.

Si-Jie touched his lower lip. “Better.”

“Was the previous one unsatisfactory?”

“It was too sad.”

“I’ll improve.”

She laughed, and he rested his forehead against hers. The operation hadn’t started. The writer hadn’t been identified. The two women were still missing, and Arthur was still afraid. But Si-Jie had signed her name because she wanted to make a choice about her own life. He wouldn’t pretend he liked it, and he wouldn’t pretend he could make the danger go away. He would respect it. And when the time came he’d be there: not as the man who decided what she was allowed to risk, but as the man she’d chosen to stand beside her.

He handed her the coffee. “Drink it before it gets warm.”

She looked at him over the cup. “You’re still bossy.”

“Consistently.”

“Unfortunately, I like you.”

“I’d noticed.”

“Don’t profile me.”

He paused, and then, deliberately, he asked whether she’d like him to kiss her instead.

Si-Jie put her cup down. “Yes.”

So he did.

chapters.title: The Plan
chapters.desc: Two weeks of rehearsing her ordinary days: the route, the café, the coffee. He walks behind her in every crowd. At night he won’t let her out of his arms. On Sunday her sisters vote three to nothing.
chapters.content:
The first thing Si-Jie learned was that an ordinary day could be rehearsed. Not performed, exactly. A performance had an audience whose attention she could feel. This was meant to make her life look unchanged to someone who might be watching without her knowing. The task force wanted consistency: her usual coffee, her usual walk, the places she always went, the small habits that made her recognisably herself.

They spent the first morning of the third week of February in a conference room going through the plan. There was a route map on the table, photographs of public places and a schedule the investigators had drawn up. Anything sensitive was kept to the officers who needed it. Si-Jie was given only what she needed for her part, and she read it twice.

“So I carry on with my ordinary routine.”

“Within the agreed arrangements. You don’t improvise. You don’t look into anyone yourself. If something feels wrong, you contact the designated officer. You don’t approach or follow anyone,” said the investigator.

“Understood.”

Arthur sat beside her. He’d barely spoken since they arrived. The investigator turned to him.

“Mr Chen, your role isn’t to direct her movements. You’re welcome to go with her when that’s part of the approved plan, but the operation has its own security staff and its own procedures. We don’t want you to become another variable.”

“I understand.”

Si-Jie glanced at him. He looked perfectly composed. She knew better. Under the table she found his hand, and his fingers closed round hers. The investigator worked through the arrangements, and Si-Jie listened, and Arthur held her hand, and neither of them let go.

✦ ✦ ✦

The café was one she’d been going to for almost a year: wooden tables, a narrow counter, a window that caught the afternoon light. The barista knew her order. On the first rehearsal Si-Jie stood at the counter and asked for it anyway.

The barista smiled. “The usual? Less ice?”

“Exactly. Thank you.”

Arthur stood a few steps behind her. He watched the barista make the drink, and watched Si-Jie take it, and watched her turn round and look for him. She found him at once.

“You look suspicious.”

“I’m standing here.”

“Very suspiciously.”

“I’ll try to improve my posture.”

She laughed and held out the cup. “Do you want to try it?”

“No. I know what it tastes like.”

“How?”

“I’ve tried it before.”

“That was three months ago.”

“Has the composition changed?”

She stared at him. “You’re unbelievable.”

“Reliably.”

She took a sip, smiling. His eyes went briefly to the street beyond the window, and she saw it.

“Are you working?”

“No.”

“Arthur.”

“I’m aware of where we are.”

“That isn’t what I asked.”

He looked at her, and then reached for her free hand. “I’m trying to be here with you.”

Her face softened. “Then be here.”

He nodded. For the next few minutes they talked about her thesis, and a lecturer who seemed to have a personal grudge against concise writing, and whether a cat could reasonably be called emotionally manipulative. Arthur argued that the cat’s behaviour couldn’t be assigned an intention without further evidence. Si-Jie informed him that he wasn’t invited to defend himself in the matter. He almost smiled. Almost.

✦ ✦ ✦

By the fourth day she’d noticed how often he walked behind her. Not beside her: behind. It was part of the agreed arrangement for the public parts of the plan. The task force had its own people for security and observation, and Arthur’s position was limited and agreed with them. He didn’t crowd her. He didn’t touch her every few seconds to reassure himself she was there. He followed at the agreed distance.

She could pick him out of almost any crowd: his height, his shoulders, the way he walked, like a man who’d already decided where his next step would land. Sometimes she caught his reflection in a shop window. Sometimes she turned a corner and saw him come round it after her. Once, at a pedestrian crossing, she looked back and found him looking at her. She raised her eyebrows. He raised his. She mouthed a question at him, and he shook his head, and she turned round smiling.

Later, when they were somewhere private and the day’s arrangements were finished, she asked whether he hated walking behind her.

“No.”

“Not even a little?”

“I dislike not being able to see your face.”

She considered that. “That’s a very specific complaint.”

“I have several.”

“Such as?”

“You walk too close to the edge of the pavement.”

“I do not.”

“You do.”

“Arthur, I’m not going to fall into the road.”

“I didn’t say you would.”

“You thought it.”

“I noticed it.”

She narrowed her eyes. “You’re not allowed to notice everything.”

“So I’ve been told.”

She laughed and slipped her hand into his. He looked down at their fingers, and held on.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first week went slowly. There were briefings, reviews and rehearsals, and days when part of the arrangement changed because something new had to be assessed. Nothing dramatic happened. No stranger came up to her. No letter arrived. Nobody tried to make contact. The absence of an incident wasn’t the absence of danger, and the team reminded them of that often.

Si-Jie began to understand how tiring it was to live inside a possibility. Every ordinary action took a little more thought. Every unexpected noise made her look up. Every time someone stood too close behind her she had to remind herself that she was in a public place, among people, and not alone.

Arthur noticed the changes, and didn’t ask her to explain every expression. Instead he started doing small things. He brought her coffee. He remembered to put food in front of her in long meetings. He walked with her when the schedule allowed it. And at the end of each day he asked one question: how was today. Not what had happened, not what she’d seen, not whether she’d noticed anything unusual. Only how she was. Sometimes she gave him a full account. Sometimes she said it had been tiring. Sometimes she leaned against him and said nothing at all. He accepted all three.

On the eighth day she came home and found him in the kitchen with dinner ready. She dropped her bag on a chair and walked straight into his arms, and he caught her.

“Hello.”

“Hi.”

“Long day?”

“Very.”

He kissed her hair. “The food’s ready.”

“Can I have you first?”

His hand settled on her back. “You have me.”

She held on a little tighter. “Good.”

✦ ✦ ✦

By the second week the rehearsals had become familiar: the same ordinary actions, the same public places, the same coffee. Si-Jie was good at looking natural because she wasn’t pretending to be anyone else. She still complained about her assignments, sent her sisters photographs of ridiculous things, and laughed too loudly when Arthur said something unexpectedly funny. The difference was that she knew now that someone might be watching.

On the eleventh day, waiting in a meeting room while an investigator finished a call, Arthur’s phone went.

Si-Jie (Question Forty): I’m bored.

Arthur: I can tell.

Si-Jie (Question Forty): How?

Arthur: You’ve sent me six messages in four minutes.

Si-Jie (Question Forty): Maybe I miss you.

Arthur: I’m three metres away.

Si-Jie (Question Forty): Emotionally that’s very far.

He looked up. She was sitting across the room. He put his phone away, walked over and sat down beside her. The investigator glanced at them, and Arthur ignored him.

Si-Jie smiled. “Better.”

“You were bored.”

“I’m still bored.”

“Would you like me to entertain you?”

She leaned closer. “Can you?”

He looked at her. “Not here.”

Her cheeks went warm. “Arthur! You can’t say things like that with a straight face.”

“I didn’t say anything inappropriate.”

“You know exactly what you did.”

He looked back at the investigator. Si-Jie covered her face with both hands, and the corner of his mouth moved. It was the first time that day she’d seen him smile.

✦ ✦ ✦

At night he held her differently. Not because he thought holding her could stop anything from happening; he knew better. He held her because she wanted him to. Because she’d spent the day being careful, and he’d spent it watching her move through a world that had become less ordinary. Because neither of them could promise the other that tomorrow would be easy.

On the twelfth night she came out of the bathroom in his shirt. He was sitting against the headboard reading the latest operational update, and he looked up, and his eyes stayed on her. She climbed onto the bed.

“Move.”

He put the document aside. “Where?”

“Here.”

She settled astride his lap and put her hands on his shoulders. His hands came to rest at her waist.

“You’re tired,” said Arthur.

“Yes.”

“Do you want to sleep?”

She studied his face. “Not yet. You’ve been very quiet.”

“I’ve been thinking. Partly about the operation. Mostly about you.”

She touched his cheek. “Tell me.”

He looked at her hand. “I don’t like watching you walk away from me.”

Her face softened. “Even when you know I’m coming back?”

“Even then.”

She bent and kissed him, and then again, and he returned the second kiss more slowly, his hand moving up her back. She could feel the restraint in him, the care he’d carried all day. She drew back far enough to see him.

“You can hold me.”

“I am holding you.”

“More.”

He understood, and his arms tightened round her.

She pressed her cheek to his. “Like that.”

He kissed her temple, her cheek, the corner of her mouth, and said her name: not as a question, not as an observation, only her name, against her skin. She smiled and asked him to say it again, and he did, and she kissed him and asked again, and his mouth brushed her cheek, and he said it once more.

She took his face in her hands. “Arthur. I love you.”

His expression changed. “I love you too.”

She rested her forehead against his. “Then stop thinking for a little while.”

He turned off the bedside lamp, and for the rest of the night he let the world outside the room go distant. He kissed her slowly, giving her time to meet him. His hands went under the hem of his own shirt, up her back, round to her front, and she pulled it off over her head and dropped it on the floor. He looked at her in the light from the street and said her name again.

She pushed at his clothes until there was nothing between them. He rolled her under him, and then stopped, because she was laughing, and asked what was funny. She said nothing was funny; she was happy; he could carry on. He carried on. His mouth found her breast, and his hand moved between her legs, slow and sure, and she stopped laughing and started saying his name instead, until she broke against his hand with her face pressed into his shoulder.

When he moved into her she wrapped her legs round him and kept him there. He didn’t hurry. Every time she said his name he answered with hers, and every time he said hers she kissed him, and they stayed like that, deep and slow, until neither of them could keep the pace and neither of them wanted to. He finished with his forehead on hers, holding her so tightly she couldn’t tell whose heart she could feel. When at last they settled under the sheets he drew her against his chest and kept her there.

“You’re holding me very tightly,” said Si-Jie.

He loosened his arms at once. “Sorry.”

She caught his wrist. “I didn’t say stop. Just don’t disappear into your head tonight.”

His fingers moved through her hair. “I’ll stay. I promise.”

He kissed her temple and told her to sleep. She was nearly asleep when he said her name again, and again a little later, as if saying it aloud reminded him she was there.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the thirteenth morning she woke before him. He was asleep on his back with one arm still round her waist and his hair fallen across his forehead. He rarely slept that deeply while the operation was under way, and she lay and looked at him. When she moved, his arm tightened without his waking.

“Where?”

She smiled. “Bathroom.”

He opened his eyes. “Oh.”

She leaned down and kissed him and told him to go back to sleep. He caught her hand before she could move. “Come back.”

“I’ll be two minutes.”

He looked at her, and let go. When she came back he was sitting up.

“You’re supposed to be sleeping.”

“I’m awake.”

“That’s not the same thing.”

She climbed back into bed, and he pulled the blanket over her and drew her against him.

She looked at the clock. “We have a briefing. And breakfast. And you have to stop looking at me like that.”

“Like what?”

“Like you want to cancel the entire day.”

He considered it. “I would prefer to.”

She laughed and kissed his chin. “Unfortunately, the world doesn’t revolve around you.”

“No.”

He looked down at her.

“Only my attention does.”

She went quiet, and then hid her face against his chest. “That’s unfair. You say things like that when I’m trying to be annoyed with you.”

His hand moved slowly over her back. “Are you still annoyed?”

“Very.”

He kissed her hair. “All right.”

She stayed there another minute, and then another. Eventually she lifted her head and announced breakfast, now, and he agreed, and neither of them moved.

✦ ✦ ✦

The last rehearsal ended on a Friday afternoon. The investigators went back over the fortnight, confirmed the security arrangements and talked through the next stage. The channel was ready. There were procedures for reviewing any reply and for suspending everything if the risk changed. There was still no confirmed identity, no proof that Kot Siu-ming had written the letters, and no proof that whoever was behind the old disappearances was the person who’d been in her flat. There were only connections worth investigating, and a woman who’d agreed to help.

The senior investigator looked at her. “How are you feeling?”

Si-Jie thought about it. “Ready.”

“You understand you can still withdraw? Even now?”

“Yes.”

He nodded. Arthur stood beside her. He hadn’t tried to talk her out of it again. But when they left the building he reached for her hand before she could reach for his.

She looked up. “What’s wrong?”

“Nothing.”

“Arthur.”

He stopped walking, and for a moment he seemed to be looking for the right words. “I don’t know how to make this easier for you.”

She stepped closer. “You don’t have to make it easy.”

“I want to.”

She lifted their hands and kissed his knuckles. “Then don’t make me do it alone.”

His fingers tightened round hers. “You won’t.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On Sunday her sisters took her to lunch at Si-Yuan’s. Arthur drove her there and waited downstairs in the car, as agreed, with a book he didn’t read. She came down three hours later looking extremely pleased with herself and got into the passenger seat.

“Three to nothing,” she said.

“For what?”

“Pengcheng. We voted. Don’t tell him.”

Arthur started the engine. “I wasn’t aware he was standing.”

“He didn’t know he was. That’s how it works.”

That night he checked the front door once, and then the windows, and then the locks. Not over and over, and not because he thought a ritual could keep them safe, but because the ordinary checks were part of what they’d agreed. When he came back to the bedroom she was already under the covers, and she lifted one corner of the blanket for him. He got in, and she moved into his arms at once, and he pulled her close.

“Too warm?” said Arthur.

“No.”

“Can you breathe?”

She lifted her head. “Are you conducting a survey?”

He paused. “No.”

She put one hand on his chest. “Good. Tomorrow. Whatever happens, we talk to each other. No deciding things for me. No disappearing because you’re frightened.”

His eyes held hers. “I’ll tell you when I’m frightened. I’ll respect your decision. I’ll follow the plan. I won’t interfere with the operation because I don’t like the risk.”

She waited.

His voice dropped. “But I’m going to be frightened every time you walk out of that room.”

Her eyes softened. “Then I’ll come back and tell you about my day.”

“Even if it’s boring?”

“Boring most of all.”

He kissed her, and she settled against him. A few minutes passed. Then she heard him say her name, and nothing after it, and she smiled against his shirt and kissed his chest through the cotton.

“I’m here.”

His arm tightened round her. Outside, the city carried on as usual. People went home, shops closed, the traffic thinned. Somewhere, someone was writing a letter, or deciding whether to send one. The task force had a plan, and the investigation had a direction, and tomorrow Si-Jie would go on living her ordinary life in a way that was no longer entirely ordinary. But tonight she was only a woman in her boyfriend’s arms. And Arthur, who’d spent years learning to recognise the moment before something terrible happened, held her until morning without pretending he could predict what came next.

chapters.title: The Café
chapters.desc: A man comes into the café, orders her drink word for word and sits two tables away while she laughs on the phone with Si-Wei. Then he waits for her at the back.
chapters.epigraph: “Iced oat latte. Less ice. No syrup.”
chapters.content:
The operation had been running for eight days. The first message had gone out through the investigators’ channel on the Wednesday. Three people had drafted it in a conference room while Si-Jie sat at the end of the table and read every version. The first said she’d received his letters and would like to understand what he wanted from her. She asked them to take out would like. She didn’t like anything, she said; she wanted to understand. They took it out. The final version was two sentences long and ended with her initial, and two more people approved it before it went. Arthur read it at the end and said nothing at all, which she’d learned meant he had a great deal to say and had decided it wasn’t his to say.

Nothing came back. Si-Jie went to her seminars and her placement and the library. She went to the café in the afternoons, because she always had.

On the second Tuesday in March, Arthur made coffee while she was in the shower, and when she came into the kitchen he was standing by the front door with his hand on the lock. He’d already checked it. She’d heard him.

“Same as yesterday,” said Si-Jie.

He took his hand off the lock. “As agreed.”

“Seminar, placement, café, home.”

“Yes.”

She took the cup he held out and drank half of it standing up. “And you’ll be across the street. Behind the newspaper stand. Where you look extremely suspicious.”

“I look like a man buying a newspaper.”

“You’ve bought eight newspapers in eight days and you haven’t read one of them.”

He didn’t argue. He watched her put her coat on, and when she reached for her bag he said her name, and she stopped.

“If anything feels wrong, you don’t wait until you’re sure. You tell them.”

“I know the rules. I helped write some of them.”

He came and did up the top button of her coat, which she’d left undone on purpose because it scratched her chin, and she let him. “I know you did. Tell them anyway.”

She kissed him at the door. The officer was waiting at the bottom of the stairs, as he was every morning, and he nodded to Arthur over her shoulder, and Arthur nodded back and shut the door and stood behind it for a while before he picked up his keys.

In the afternoon she went to the café at the usual time and ordered the usual thing.

The barista recognised her and smiled. “The usual today?”

“Yes, thank you.”

She took her receipt and went to the window. The café was moderately busy: a couple near the door, two students sharing a laptop at the long table, a woman in a grey cardigan reading by the counter. Si-Jie chose a seat by the glass, and her phone lit up before she’d got her coat off. Si-Wei (Business Hours). She answered at once.

“Where are you?”

“The café.”

“Alone?”

Si-Jie glanced round. “Technically. Arthur’s across the street and the team’s where they’re supposed to be. I’m perfectly fine.”

“You’re always perfectly fine until you’re not.”

“That’s a terrible thing to say to your older sister.”

“Older by minutes.”

“Minutes count.”

“Is Arthur behaving?”

“He’s behind a newspaper stand, pretending to read the sports pages.”

“So, no.”

Si-Jie laughed, and tucked the phone against her ear and drank some of her coffee, and she didn’t notice the man come in. Not at first. He was unremarkable in the way most people are unremarkable in public: a dark coat, ordinary shoes, no particular hurry. He looked up at the menu over the counter, waited behind another customer, and gave his order in a low voice.

“Iced oat latte. Less ice. No syrup.”

The barista looked at him for a second longer than she needed to, and then rang it up. He turned round, and his eyes settled on Si-Jie. He didn’t stare. He didn’t need to. He looked at her once and went to a table two along from the window, and sat down two tables away from her.

Si-Jie was still talking. “Did you eat?”

“Yes.”

“What?”

“Food.”

“Si-Wei.”

“Why are you asking me like I’m one of your clients?”

“Because you answer questions like a criminal.”

“That’s because I’m dating one.”

Si-Jie laughed out loud. Two tables away, the man put his phone face up on the table and waited.

✦ ✦ ✦

He collected his drink when it was called. He didn’t look at Si-Jie again. He didn’t go near her. He sat with the cup between both hands and watched the street through the glass.

The officer outside had noticed him. He’d been briefed on the possibility of contact, but a man buying a coffee wasn’t grounds for anything on its own. He watched, and noted the time, and reported an unidentified man matching no confirmed description to the control team. Across the street, behind the newspaper stand, Arthur heard it come through his earpiece and went still. He’d seen the man go in. He’d seen nothing about him worth seeing: a coat, a walk, a back. Through the glass he could see Si-Jie laughing into her phone with her coffee in her other hand, two tables from a man he couldn’t see the face of, and he didn’t move, because moving was the one thing he’d agreed not to do.

Inside, Si-Jie was complaining to her sister. “Pengcheng sent Si-Yuan a photograph of a restaurant menu.”

“Why?”

“He wants her to choose somewhere for dinner on Friday.”

“That’s romantic.”

“It’s a menu, Si-Wei. He sent it with the message: please assess the seafood selection.”

Si-Wei burst out laughing. “That’s exactly how a lawyer dates.”

“Don’t defend him.”

“I’m not. I’m saying Si-Yuan should marry a man who sends her menus.”

Si-Jie made a face at the window. “Absolutely not.”

“Does Arthur send you menus?”

“Arthur sends me nutritional information.”

There was a pause, and then Si-Wei laughed so loudly that Si-Jie had to hold the phone away from her ear. “You’re both hopeless.”

“Thank you.”

“That’s not a compliment.”

“I’m accepting it anyway.”

Two tables away the man finished his drink. He stood up, left money on the table and walked out, and Si-Jie never saw him go.

✦ ✦ ✦

A few minutes later her phone buzzed against her cheek. She took it away from her ear to read it.

Arthur (Thirty-Nine): Stay inside for now.

She looked at the window. She couldn’t see him.

Si-Jie: Why?

The answer came almost at once.

Arthur (Thirty-Nine): A man came in and sat two tables from you. He ordered your drink. Iced oat latte, less ice, no syrup.

Her smile went. She looked at the table two along from hers. The chair was empty, and there was a coin on the saucer beside the empty glass. Her fingers tightened round the phone.

Si-Wei’s voice was small and far away. “Jie? What’s wrong?”

Si-Jie put the phone back to her ear and swallowed. “There’s a man. He came in, and he ordered—” She stopped.

“Si-Jie?”

“He ordered my drink.”

Silence. Then her sister’s voice changed. “Listen to me. Don’t move.”

Si-Jie looked at the empty chair again. “Arthur says to stay inside.”

“Good. Stay there.”

“I didn’t see his face properly.”

“That’s fine. You don’t have to do anything.”

She looked at the door. A couple came in. Someone laughed near the counter. The coffee machine hissed. Everything was ordinary, and that was the worst part.

“Si-Wei. He ordered oat milk. Less ice. No syrup. That’s mine.”

“I heard you.”

Her breathing had gone shallow.

Si-Wei slowed down. “Look at me, Jie.”

Si-Jie almost laughed. “You’re on the phone.”

“Then listen to me. You’re not alone. Arthur’s there. The officers are there. You stay where you are.”

Si-Jie nodded, though her sister couldn’t see her. “All right.”

The phone buzzed again.

Arthur (Thirty-Nine): Don’t use the front door. The team’s arranging how to bring you out.

She read it twice, and typed.

Si-Jie: Is it him?

There was a pause.

Arthur (Thirty-Nine): We don’t know yet.

That was Arthur. Even now he wouldn’t give her a certainty he didn’t have. She was grateful for it. She hated it.

“Jie? Keep talking to me.”

So she did. She told Si-Wei about the woman reading by the counter, and the students sharing the laptop, and the ridiculous little ceramic vase on her table with one paper flower in it. She described everything except the empty chair two tables away.

Underneath the talking she was thinking about the wall in his study. She’d stood in front of it more nights than he knew, when he was asleep and she wasn’t. Two women had received letters like hers. Both of them had told someone. Both of them had been believed too late. She’d read their names on his whiteboard in his small square capitals, and under them, in the place where he’d first written hers, the line he’d rubbed out and rewritten: CURRENT RECIPIENT — LIVING. She’d never told him she’d seen it. She thought now that she would tell him tonight.

She wasn’t alone. That was the difference, and she held on to it. There were officers outside whose whole job that afternoon was her. There was a car at the end of a lane she hadn’t seen yet. There was her sister in her ear, pretending to be calm, and there was a man behind a newspaper stand who had bought eight newspapers and read none of them. The women on the wall had had none of that. She had all of it. It should have made her feel safe, and mostly it did. But a stranger had stood at the counter she stood at every day and said her order out loud, word for word, and she hadn’t even turned her head.

✦ ✦ ✦

Out in the street, the control officer reported that the man had gone. A second officer followed at a distance. The man crossed the road without hurrying, turned at the next junction and stopped beside a row of parked cars. He looked back. The officer kept walking. The man carried on round the block, and the officer lost him for a moment at the corner.

Inside, Si-Jie was told she could leave through the back with an escort. She stood up, and her legs felt oddly weak.

“Si-Wei, I have to go.”

“Stay on the phone.”

“I will.”

She picked up her bag and put her coat on, and an officer in plain clothes came over to her. “Miss Yen? We’ll take you out the back. Stay with me, please.”

She followed him down a narrow corridor past the kitchen. It smelled of steamed milk and burnt sugar. A boy washing cups at the sink stopped and stared at her with his hands still in the water, and the barista who’d made her coffee every afternoon for a year stood in the kitchen doorway with a cloth in her hand and a face that said she’d only just understood what she’d heard at the counter. Si-Jie wanted to tell her it wasn’t her fault. There wasn’t time. The back door opened onto a service lane, and for a moment she saw nothing unusual: a delivery scooter, a stack of empty crates, the bins. The officer checked both ways, and signalled.

“Let’s go.”

Si-Jie stepped outside with the phone still at her ear. “I’m outside now.”

“Good,” said Si-Wei.

The officer was guiding her towards the end of the lane, where a car was waiting, when someone came round the corner. A man in a dark coat, moving fast: too fast for Si-Jie to understand what was happening. The officer shouted and turned. The man hit him once, hard, and the officer went sideways into the wall and down onto one knee. Then a hand closed round Si-Jie’s arm and pulled.

Her phone fell. She heard Si-Wei’s voice shouting her name from the ground, and then the noise swallowed it.

He dragged her sideways, out of the lane and into a gap between two buildings, so narrow she could have touched both walls. Her shoulder struck the brick. Her bag slid off her arm. She tried to pull free, but his grip was locked round her upper arm, and he was stronger than she’d expected, and he moved with a horrible economy, wasting nothing.

“Let go of me.”

He didn’t answer. She twisted, trying to get her arm back, and then she saw the knife. It came up in his other hand, small and short, and he brought it in under her jaw. The metal touched her skin, and Si-Jie stopped moving.

“Don’t.” His voice was low. That was worse than shouting.

She could hear traffic at the end of the passage. Someone was talking out in the street. A delivery scooter went past the opening. The world was carrying on.

He leaned closer. “You don’t listen very well.”

Her throat tightened. She tried not to move. The blade pressed a fraction harder.

“Look at me.”

She didn’t.

“Look at me.”

Her eyes went to his face.

He was older than she’d expected. His face was calm, almost curious, and he seemed faintly disappointed in her. “You’re very difficult to reach. I’ve written to you.”

Her breath was shallow. “I know.”

“You didn’t answer.”

She said nothing.

His fingers tightened on her arm. “Do you know how long I’ve been waiting?”

She thought of the letters: the green ink, the pages about her hair, the brush that had gone from her flat, and the man who’d sat two tables away and ordered her drink. She understood then that the café hadn’t been an attempt to meet her. It had been a demonstration. He’d wanted her to know he could sit beside her without her noticing. He’d wanted her to understand how close he’d been. And now he wanted her to look at him.

She made herself breathe. “You’re Kot Siu-ming.”

His expression changed. For the first time she saw something in it like pleasure.

“Yes,” he said.

At the end of the passage somebody said her name. Not shouted it: said it, clearly, the way he said it when he wanted her to look up from a book. Si-Jie knew the voice before she could see him. Arthur.

chapters.title: The Alley
chapters.desc: Thirty seconds late. A knife under her jaw, and Arthur at the end of the passage. He breaks Kot’s wrist and doesn’t let go when he’s told to. She’s cut, not badly.
chapters.epigraph: “That I called your name. And you heard me.”
chapters.content:
The task force was thirty seconds late. Arthur would remember the number long after he’d forgotten what time it was. Not an hour, not ten minutes: thirty seconds. It was the distance between the second officer losing the man at a corner and the man getting his hand round Si-Jie’s arm. It was the time it took to turn a routine exit into an assault. And it was the time Arthur spent running.

The first call came through his earpiece while he was still behind the newspaper stand.

“Lost visual at the junction. Subject may be doubling back.”

He was already moving.

“Rear lane, rear lane. Male, dark coat, coming in from the east end.”

Then another voice, higher. “Officer down. He’s got her.”

Arthur ran. He didn’t remember putting his phone away or crossing the road or going through the gap between the café and the building next to it. He remembered the lane: a scooter, crates, an officer on one knee against the wall with his hand pressed to his face, a phone on the ground with a voice still coming out of it. And then the narrow passage off the lane, and at the end of it two people, close together.

The knife was at her throat. His mind took it in all at once, the way it took in a photograph of a scene: Kot’s right hand, Si-Jie’s position, the wall behind her, the width of the passage, the angle of the blade, and the thin red line that had already appeared along her neck. Everything else went.

“Si-Jie,” he said.

She looked at him. Her eyes found his and held on.

“Let her go.”

Kot turned his head, and smiled. “Arthur Chen.”

Arthur’s expression didn’t change. He stopped a few metres away. “Put the knife down.”

“You came quickly.”

“Let her go.”

Kot pressed the blade closer.

Arthur looked at Si-Jie only for a moment, and then back at Kot. “You don’t need to do this.”

“You think you can tell me what I need?”

“I think you know exactly what happens if you cut her.”

“Do I?”

Arthur took one measured step.

Kot’s grip tightened. “Stop.”

Arthur stopped. The earpiece crackled. “Chen, we’re thirty seconds out. Hold your position.”

Thirty seconds. Arthur looked at the knife, and at the angle of Kot’s wrist. He knew he couldn’t wait for the team. He also knew that moving too soon could make the blade move.

“Si-Jie. Don’t move.”

She didn’t. Kot’s eyes flicked from one of them to the other. “She’s frightened of me. She should be frightened of you too.”

“Put the knife down.”

“You’re very calm.”

“I’m not.”

It was the first thing Arthur had said that wasn’t an instruction, and Kot stared at him, and in that fraction of a second Arthur moved.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was fast. He closed the distance before Kot could turn properly towards him and caught the hand with the knife in it. The blade shifted, and Si-Jie felt it drag across her skin. Then Arthur drove the heel of his other hand against Kot’s wrist and forced the joint the wrong way. There was a short, ugly crack. Kot screamed, and the knife fell.

Arthur didn’t let go. He twisted the broken wrist again and forced Kot down against the wall. He heard Si-Jie say his name. He heard officers shouting at the mouth of the passage. He heard Kot struggling. His hand stayed locked round the wrist. The bone had gone; he could feel it moving under his fingers where it shouldn’t. Kot dropped to one knee, and Arthur kept twisting.

“Chen! Release him!”

He didn’t.

Kot tried to pull away, and Arthur pushed him back against the brick. “Don’t touch her.”

“Arthur!”

This time it was Si-Jie, and he turned his head. She was against the opposite wall with one hand pressed to her neck, and there was blood between her fingers. Not much. Enough. He looked at it, and his grip tightened.

Then the officers were there. One took Kot’s shoulder. Another took his good arm.

“Chen, let go!”

Arthur’s eyes were still on the blood. “He had a knife.”

“The knife’s on the ground. We’ve got him.”

“His hand—”

“We’ve got him!”

Arthur let go of the wrist. Two officers put Kot on his front on the ground and cuffed his hands behind his back. He was still screaming. Arthur barely heard him. He was already going to her.

✦ ✦ ✦

His hands came up, and stopped. “Si-Jie. Can I see?”

She took her fingers away from her neck. The cut was thin: a narrow line under her jaw, with a little blood running down towards her collar. He looked at it, and for several seconds he didn’t say anything at all.

“Arthur?”

His eyes stayed on the cut. “Does it hurt?”

“A little.”

“Are you dizzy?”

“No.”

“Can you breathe normally?”

“Yes.”

He looked at her pupils, her face, her breathing, and then he seemed to realise what he was doing. His hands were shaking.

Si-Jie reached for him. “Hey. I’m all right.”

He didn’t answer. She touched his cheek and said his name, and his eyes dropped to her neck again. The blood was still there. A small amount, a thin line, nothing like the pictures his mind had already made. He breathed in, and out.

“Don’t touch it. Keep your hand there.”

“I wasn’t going to touch it.”

He took off his coat and put it round her shoulders. Behind them the officers were calling for an ambulance. Someone was reading Kot his rights. Someone else was reporting the knife recovered at the scene. Arthur heard none of it clearly. He couldn’t stop looking at her neck.

Kot had stopped screaming. He was speaking now, low and almost pleasant, to the officer kneeling on his back.

“She drinks it with oat milk.”

Arthur’s whole body went still. The officer looked down. “What did you say?”

Kot smiled into the ground and didn’t answer. Arthur turned his head. Kot lifted his eyes, and for one moment they looked straight at each other. Then the officer hauled Kot up and turned him away.

✦ ✦ ✦

The paramedics came. One of them asked Arthur to step back, and he didn’t, and she asked again.

He looked at her. “She has a cut along the left side of her neck. The blade made contact. There was bleeding. She says she isn’t dizzy and can breathe normally. Her shoulder hit the wall.”

The paramedic nodded. “Thank you. I’ll take over.”

He stepped aside and watched. The cut was shallow, but where it was meant it had to be looked at carefully. They cleaned it, checked round it and said she’d need to be seen at the hospital. Si-Jie answered their questions: her name, her date of birth, whether she’d lost consciousness, whether anything else hurt.

A second paramedic came to Arthur. “Your hand.”

He looked down. His knuckles were scraped raw, and there was blood on his fingers. He couldn’t tell whether it was his or Kot’s.

“It’s fine.”

“You’re injured.”

He looked at his hand, and then at Si-Jie. “Check her first.”

“We are.”

He let the paramedic look.

The officer who’d reached the passage first came over. “We’ve got him. The knife’s recovered. He’s going for medical assessment and then processing.”

Then he glanced at Arthur’s hand.

“You broke his wrist.”

“Yes.”

“You’ll need to give a statement.”

“I know.”

The officer hesitated. “Are you all right?”

Arthur looked at Si-Jie. “No.”

He rode with her in the ambulance. She lay with his coat still over her and the dressing taped to her neck, and watched the ceiling sway, and after a while she turned her head as far as the paramedic would let her.

“Was it him?”

“They’re identifying him.”

“He told me. In the passage. I said his name and he said yes.”

Arthur took her hand. “Then they’ll confirm it. I won’t tell you it’s him until they have.”

“I know you won’t,” said Si-Jie, and for the first time since the café she nearly smiled.

✦ ✦ ✦

At the hospital they closed the cut with strips and confirmed it was superficial, with no sign of anything deeper. Her shoulder was bruised. Arthur’s knuckles were cleaned and dressed, and someone looked at his shoulder, which he’d hit on the wall when Kot went down, and told him it was bruised too. He didn’t complain once.

Si-Wei arrived first. She came through the doors so fast that the receptionist hadn’t finished her sentence, and found her sister sitting on a bed with a blanket round her shoulders, and stopped dead. Then she crossed the room.

“Jie.”

Si-Jie looked up. “Hi.”

Si-Wei’s face crumpled. She put both arms round her, careful of the shoulder. “Oh, you idiot.”

Si-Jie laughed weakly. “That’s not a very comforting greeting.”

Si-Wei held on tighter, and then pulled back to look at her. “I don’t care. Your neck.”

“It’s not deep.”

“Your shoulder?”

“Bruised.”

Si-Wei looked across the room at Arthur, who was standing by the door while a nurse finished with his hand. For a moment she looked as if she wanted to hit him. Then she saw his face, and understood, and turned back to her sister.

“Don’t ever do that to me again.”

Si-Jie blinked. “Get attacked?”

Si-Wei’s voice broke. “Make me listen to you disappear. Your phone was on the ground. I could hear the street. I could hear someone shouting your name, and then I couldn’t hear you.”

Si-Jie reached for her hand. “I’m sorry.”

“Don’t apologise.”

Arthur came over before he left to give his statement. Si-Wei turned to look at him.

“Thank you for staying on the line,” said Arthur.

Si-Wei looked at the bed. “Don’t thank me. Just make sure she gets home.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He gave his statement in a small room down the corridor. He described what he’d seen: where Kot stood, where the knife was, how he’d approached, the contact, the disarming, the force he’d used. He didn’t soften any of it. He didn’t leave out that he’d kept hold of the broken wrist after the knife fell. The investigator asked him why.

“I saw blood on her neck. I was focused on removing the threat.”

“Was the threat still active after the knife was dropped?”

Arthur paused. “No.”

“Then why did you keep applying force?”

He looked at the statement in front of him. “Because I was angry. That isn’t a justification. It’s the answer.”

The investigator wrote it down, and Arthur signed.

When he came back, Si-Yuan was there too. She’d come straight from a press call with her make-up still on and her sunglasses pushed into her hair, and she was sitting on the end of the bed holding Si-Jie’s foot through the blanket and not letting go of it. She looked at Arthur’s hand, and at his face, and said nothing at all, and moved up so that he could have the chair. He’d remember that later, too.

The sisters went at nine, when the nurse made them. Si-Wei kissed Si-Jie’s forehead and told Arthur to eat something. Si-Yuan kissed her cheek and told Arthur nothing, and touched his arm on the way past.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was nearly midnight before the room was finally quiet. Arthur had moved the chair close enough that their hands stayed joined on the side of the bed.

Si-Jie looked at his bandaged hand. “Did they ask about your hand?”

“Yes.”

“And his wrist?”

“Yes. I told them what happened.”

She was quiet. Then she asked whether he’d stopped when they told him to.

He looked at her. “Not straight away.”

She didn’t say anything.

He didn’t offer an excuse. “I should have.”

She reached for his hand. “I know why you were angry.”

“That doesn’t make it acceptable.”

“No. But I don’t want you to pretend you weren’t frightened. I saw your face.”

He lowered his eyes. “I thought he’d cut you badly. I thought—”

His voice stopped.

She pulled his hand closer. “You don’t have to finish.”

She kissed his knuckles, avoiding the dressing, and rested her forehead against his hand.

After a while she opened her eyes. “You’re still looking at my neck.”

He didn’t deny it.

“Stop.”

He tried.

His eyes came back to hers, and she smiled faintly. “That’s better.”

He stood and bent over her and kissed her hair, and her temple, careful not to touch the dressing.

“Does it hurt?”

“A little.”

“Do you need anything? Water?”

“No.”

“Are you sure?”

She laughed. “Yes.”

He sat down again.

She looked at him. “Arthur. You reached me.”

His face changed. “Not before he hurt you.”

“But you reached me. Don’t make the thirty seconds the only thing you remember.”

He looked at her. “What should I remember?”

Her fingers closed round his. “That I called your name. And you heard me.”

He bent and kissed her hand. “Yes.”

She was quiet for a while. Then she said she had something to tell him, something she’d meant to say tonight anyway, before any of this.

“I’ve stood in front of your wall at night. When you were asleep. More often than you know.”

He looked up.

She turned her hand over in his. “I saw what you wrote under their names, where you’d written mine first. You rubbed it out and wrote living. I thought about it in the café. When he’d gone, and I was waiting. I thought: he wrote living. So I’d better be.”

Arthur didn’t say anything. He couldn’t. He held her hand against his mouth, and she let him, and after a while she closed her eyes.

A few minutes later she was asleep. Arthur stayed awake. He looked at the dressing on her neck, and then at his own hands: the hands that had held the knife wrist, and broken it, and not let go when they should have. He turned them over slowly. For the first time that night he looked at them without thinking about Kot. He thought about Si-Jie instead: the way she’d reached for him while she was still frightened, and the blood under her jaw, and the way she’d asked him to look at her and not at the cut.

He’d answer for what he’d done in the passage. He’d accept whatever came of it. But tonight, while she slept, he stayed. When she stirred, he was there.

“Arthur?”

“I’m here.”

Her fingers tightened round his, and she went back to sleep. He looked once more at the thin line under her jaw. Then he bent his head and said her name, once, low, and nothing after it, and held her hand until morning.

chapters.title: Interview
chapters.desc: Four hours across a table from Kot, against every rule, with no notes: the two women, the brush, both notebooks. He comes out grey, and she’s waiting in the corridor.
chapters.content:
Arthur wasn’t assigned to the interview. He knew that before anyone told him. Kot Siu-ming was in custody with his wrist in a splint, and the investigation team had the case: the knife, the café footage, the letters and whatever could be taken from Si-Jie’s flat were being processed separately. Arthur was a profiler, not the lead investigator, and he was certainly not supposed to question a suspect whose wrist he’d broken less than a day before.

The senior investigator made that clear. “You’re not going into that room.”

Arthur stood by the conference table. “Why?”

“You’re asking me why? Because you’re personally involved. Because you witnessed the assault. Because you used force on him. Because he’s already identified you as someone connected to the victim. You’re not objective.”

“I’m aware of that.”

The investigator closed his folder. “Then behave accordingly. The interview team will question him. You can give us your observations afterwards.”

Arthur looked at the photographs on the table: Kot leaving the café, Kot sitting two tables from Si-Jie, the knife. “He’s going to talk. He wants to be heard.”

“That’s an assumption.”

“Yes. He’s tried again and again to make contact with her. He’s written to her, been inside her flat and approached her in public. Yesterday he used a weapon. That isn’t a man whose main aim is to avoid being caught.”

“It doesn’t mean he’ll confess. Let the team do their job.”

Arthur picked up his file. “Understood.”

He left the room. The investigator watched him go, and didn’t believe him.

✦ ✦ ✦

Si-Jie came in mid-morning to give her own statement. They’d let her out of hospital first thing. The cut on her neck had been closed and covered with a small plaster, and she was wearing a high-necked cream jumper over it, with her hair tied loosely back. She looked tired. Arthur saw her from the end of the corridor and stopped. She smiled.

“Hi.”

He walked towards her. “You’re supposed to be resting.”

“I rested.”

“For how long?”

“Long enough. That’s all the answer you’re getting.”

He looked at the plaster. “Does it hurt?”

“Only when I turn my head too fast.”

“Have you taken the tablets? Eaten breakfast? What did you have?”

She narrowed her eyes. “Are you my boyfriend or a discharge form?”

The corner of his mouth moved. “Both, apparently.”

She reached for his hand and asked about his shoulder, and his knuckles, and he said they were fine, and she looked at him carefully. He looked like he hadn’t slept, and there was something else in him she couldn’t name.

“Are you going to see him today?”

He didn’t answer at once. “There’s an interview scheduled.”

“Are you part of it?”

He held her gaze. “No. Not officially.”

Her fingers tightened round his. “Arthur.”

“I won’t do anything that compromises the investigation.”

It wasn’t quite an answer. She knew it, and he knew she knew it. She lifted their hands and kissed his knuckles. “Come back to me when you’re finished.”

“I will.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The interview began just after half past ten. Arthur walked into the room without authorisation, and the assigned investigator was on his feet at once.

“Chen. What are you doing?”

“Taking over.”

“You can’t.”

“I know.”

“Then leave.”

Arthur looked through the glass. Kot was at the table with his wrist in the splint, pale, his eyes alert. He saw Arthur and smiled. Arthur turned back to the investigator.

“Stay if you want. Record the time.”

The investigator knew exactly what he was doing, and knew it was a serious procedural problem. “You’re making a mistake.”

“Possibly.”

Arthur went in and sat down opposite Kot. The door closed. The recording stayed on. He put nothing on the table: no notebook, no file, no photographs, no pen.

Kot looked at the empty table. “You’re not taking notes?”

“No.”

“You’re very confident.”

Arthur looked at him. “You’re very pleased with yourself.”

For the first time, Kot’s smile slipped.

Arthur folded his hands. “Let’s begin.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t start with the letters. He started with the café.

“What did you order?”

“Iced oat latte. Less ice. No syrup.”

“Why?”

“That’s how she has it.”

“How do you know?”

“I watched.”

“Where?”

“Her university. Her charity. The café. Her flat.”

“Since when?”

Kot smiled. “Since February last year. The week you bought her tulips.”

Arthur’s face didn’t move. His hands didn’t move. “Did you go into her flat?”

“Yes.”

“How?”

Kot said nothing. Arthur didn’t repeat the question. He waited, and eventually Kot answered. “People come and go in buildings like that. You’d be surprised how little attention anyone pays.”

“Did someone let you in?”

“You’re asking the wrong question. You want to know how I got in. What matters is that I was there. I saw her things. Her clothes. Her brush. The things she leaves where she thinks they’re safe.”

“Where’s the brush?”

“Not with me. Somewhere she’d never think to look.”

Arthur filed it away: not as a location, but as a claim that would need to be corroborated.

An hour in, he asked why Kot had written to her. Kot looked almost offended.

His voice softened. “Because she didn’t know me. She should have. I knew her. I knew when she was tired. I knew when she was happy. I knew when she was waiting for someone. Most of all when she was waiting for you.”

“Did you follow her because of me?”

“I followed her because she was interesting. You made it worse. You kept appearing. You walked behind her. You carried her bag. You touched her hair. You looked at her as though she belonged to you.”

“She isn’t an object.”

Kot laughed. “That’s what you tell yourself.”

“And the other women?”

Kot stopped smiling.

✦ ✦ ✦

By noon he was talking about them. He remembered the first woman’s name, and the colour of her bag, and that she bought a particular drink on Fridays, and the route she walked from campus. He remembered the second woman’s shoes on a stairwell, and the last place he’d seen her. Arthur didn’t interrupt. He asked for dates, places, times, specific actions. Some answers came at once. Some needed prompting. Some details changed when Arthur came back to the same question from a different side, and he noticed every one, and didn’t correct a single one. He let Kot talk.

“Did you kill them?”

“Yes.”

“Both?”

“Yes.”

Arthur asked how. He didn’t ask for anything graphic. He asked for things that could be checked: the name of a street, a building entrance, a date, something thrown away, a place that had never appeared in any report. When Kot had finished, Arthur asked where they were.

Kot smiled. “Now you’re asking the right question.”

When he got to the second woman’s last day, Arthur stopped him. “Her family searched for her. Her mother gave interviews. She kept her daughter’s room as it was. She’s still waiting for her to come home.”

Kot looked at him. “That’s not my problem.”

For several seconds the room was silent.

“Why Si-Jie?”

“Because she reminded me of the first one. Her age. Her hair. The way she talks to people, always looking right at them.”

“Did you think she was replacing the first woman?”

Kot leaned forward. “She wasn’t replacing anyone. She was there. And you loved her. I remembered you from last time, across a table like this one. I wanted to see what you’d look like.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Early in the afternoon, outside, the senior investigator had already been told. The interview should have been stopped. Arthur was too close to the victim and to the arrest to be anything but compromised, the recording would need careful legal review, and anything he obtained would have to be verified independently. But nobody stopped it.

Arthur asked about the brush. Kot described its handle and its worn edge and where Si-Jie usually left it. He said he’d kept it because it smelled of her. Arthur’s face went still.

“Where is it?”

“You want it back?”

“Yes. It’s hers.”

Kot smiled. “You’re very possessive. You think you’re different from me.”

“I am.”

“Because she chose you?”

Arthur looked straight at him. “Because she can leave. She can refuse you. She can refuse me. She can decide she doesn’t want either of us. You don’t understand the difference.”

Kot looked away first. Then Arthur asked about the second letter, and Kot told him about the notebook. He’d seen it. He’d seen both.

For the first time, Arthur’s expression changed. “How?”

Kot smiled. “Your flat. Twice. The week of the tulips, the black one in your drawer. And the fortnight she was gone, the new one on your desk. You wrote about her. You were very unhappy. I liked reading it, because you were doing what I was doing.”

“No.”

“You watched her. You wrote her down. You kept things.”

Arthur’s voice was low. “I was wrong. She found it. She challenged me. I stopped.”

“Did you? How would you know?”

Arthur leaned forward. “Because she told me what she needed, and I listened. You never listened to her once.”

For the first time, Kot had no answer ready. Later, more slowly, he told Arthur the rest: that in January he’d been in her flat as well, and the notebook had been on her bedside table, and that was where he’d read her handwriting in the margins, and the line about seven forty-six.

The last forty minutes were the hardest. Kot gave details about the two women that had never been made public. He described a place connected to the first, and another connected to the second. He gave a name, a vehicle and a sequence of events. Arthur made him repeat the dates, and then separate what he’d done himself from what he’d heard or guessed. Kot grew irritated and asked why it mattered.

“Because I want to know what’s true.”

Eventually Kot gave more precise answers. Some could be checked against existing records, some against evidence that had never been disclosed, and some would have to be treated with caution until they were corroborated. Arthur’s last question was why he’d attacked her.

Kot looked at him. “She was leaving.”

“She was leaving the café.”

“She was leaving me.”

“She never belonged to you.”

Kot tilted his head. “She belonged with someone who understood her. Then why did she look at you, when I had the knife?”

Arthur stood up. “Because she wanted to live.”

He opened the door. The interview had lasted four hours, and he hadn’t written down a single word.

✦ ✦ ✦

The corridor was quiet. The senior investigator was on his feet at once, and said his name, and asked what Kot had said, and Arthur kept walking, and then stopped. For a moment he seemed to have forgotten where he was. His face had gone grey: not pale, grey. His eyes were fixed on something past the end of the corridor, and his mouth was slightly open. The investigator came closer and said his name again, and Arthur looked at him and then away, and couldn’t speak.

Si-Jie was sitting in a chair against the far wall. She’d waited. The plaster on her neck showed above the collar of her jumper. She stood up when she saw him.

“Arthur?”

He looked at her, and everything he’d held down in that room seemed to reach the surface at once. She crossed the corridor. He didn’t move. She stopped in front of him and took his hand, and his fingers were shaking.

“It’s all right,” said Si-Jie, and opened her arms.

He bent his head, and she put her arms round him, and he held her: not carefully, not with the measured restraint he’d used round her bruised shoulder all morning, but like a man who’d reached the end of something and had nowhere else to go. He didn’t cry. He didn’t speak. He stood with his face against her shoulder and his hands pressed flat to her back. The investigator looked away.

✦ ✦ ✦

They sat in a small waiting room. She put a bottle of water in front of him, and he looked at it until she told him to drink, and his hand shook a little when he did. She waited until he’d had a few mouthfuls. Then she touched his cheek.

“What happened in there?”

“He talked. About the women. He gave us places. Details nobody’s ever made public.”

“Did he say where they are?”

“Two places. They’ll have to be checked.”

“Did he admit what he did? To both of them?”

He closed his eyes. “Yes. He remembered everything. Their routines, their clothes, what they used to buy. What their mothers said in interviews. How long their families waited. He remembered everything except that they were people.”

She held his hand more tightly. “What else?”

He looked at the floor. “He’s read my notebook. Both of them. He was in my flat, twice. Once before you found the first one, and again while you were gone. And he was in yours in January.”

Si-Jie went still. She thought of his flat: the kitchen where she’d stood that morning, the study with the wall in it, the bed. “He’s been where we’re living.”

“Yes. He read what I wrote about you.”

She was quiet. Then she moved closer. “Are you all right?”

“No.”

She nodded, and didn’t tell him to calm down, and didn’t tell him everything would be fine. She stayed beside him.

✦ ✦ ✦

The senior investigator came for him at half past four, and asked to speak to him alone. Si-Jie told him to go, she’d wait, and he kissed her cheek and went. The investigator was direct. Arthur had had no authority to conduct the interview. It was a serious breach. His relationship with the victim and his struggle with the suspect raised obvious questions about impartiality. The recording would be kept and reviewed. Every claim would be checked independently. Arthur would give a full account of what had happened, including his own actions.

“Why did you do it?”

“Because I wanted answers.”

“That’s not sufficient.”

He looked at his hands. “No. I wanted to know what he’d done to them. Whether he’d been in her flat. Where the brush was. And I wanted to hear him say it.”

The investigator’s face hardened. “That last part is exactly why you shouldn’t have been in the room. You’re removed from the suspect interview process, effective immediately. You won’t contact him again. You’ll submit a written account tonight, and you’ll cooperate with the review. Go home.”

“She’s waiting.”

“I know.”

When he came back, Si-Jie stood up and asked whether he was in trouble. He said yes, and told her everything, and she listened without interrupting.

“You shouldn’t have gone in.”

“No.”

“You’re not going to tell me you had no choice?”

“No.”

She nodded. “Good. Come home.”

✦ ✦ ✦

In the car she asked whether he’d eaten, and he said he’d forgotten, and she made him stop for noodles before she’d let him drive another street. At a red light she asked whether Kot had said anything about her.

His hands tightened on the wheel. “He said you were leaving him.”

She stared at him. “I’ve never met him. He doesn’t know me. Did he think he loved me?”

“I don’t know what he thought.”

She looked out of the window. “Good. I don’t want you to explain him to me like he understands something about me nobody else does.”

“I won’t.”

At home she put the food out, and he sat at the table and didn’t eat it, and then did, when she looked at him. After a while he said that Kot had remembered the colour of the first woman’s bag, and her mother’s interviews, and the room she’d left behind. “Things her family probably wishes they could forget. I don’t know what to do with that.”

She moved her chair next to his. “You don’t have to do anything with it tonight. You listened for four hours to things nobody should have to hear. You don’t have to carry every word into this room.”

He looked at her, and stood up, and she stood too, and he pulled her into his arms and put his face in her hair and breathed in, twice. Then he said he should have kept the flat safer.

“Stop. You made a mistake with the notebook. You admitted it. You changed. You didn’t know someone had been in our home. His actions belong to him.”

He looked at her a long time, and nodded.

Close to midnight he sat at the dining table with a pad of paper and wrote his account: when he’d gone in, how long he’d stayed, the recording, what he’d been told and what he’d done. He didn’t turn it into a notebook. He didn’t write down what she’d said in the corridor. He wrote what the investigation needed him to disclose, and put it in an envelope.

Si-Jie was in the doorway. “Finished?”

“For tonight.”

She held out her hand. “Come to bed. Tomorrow you can tell me more, if you want. Not tonight. Tonight you’re just my boyfriend.”

He bent and kissed her, and let her lead him down the hall. He saw the plaster on her neck, of course he saw it, but this time he made himself look at her eyes instead. When she reached for him under the covers, he went to her, and she tucked her face against his chest.

“Goodnight, Arthur.”

“Goodnight.”

For the first time in four hours he had nothing to ask, and for the first time since the passage he let himself rest.

chapters.title: The Two Women
chapters.desc: A field and a hillside. Arthur tells both families himself, with the liaison officer beside him and Si-Jie holding his hand at both doors.
chapters.epigraph: “At least now someone’s told me where to look.”
chapters.content:
The call came a little after six on Saturday morning, and Arthur was already awake. He’d slept badly since the interview, waking before dawn with pieces of Kot’s answers coming back to him: dates, names, places, details that had sounded almost casual across a table.

His phone buzzed on the bedside table, and he answered it. “Chen.”

The senior investigator’s voice was unusually quiet. “The search teams went out on Thursday to the places Kot gave you. They’ve found something.”

Arthur looked at the other side of the bed. Si-Jie was asleep with one hand on his pillow. He got up carefully and went to the window. “Where?”

“The first is an open field outside the city. The second is on a hillside to the north. The dogs marked two separate areas, and the teams have secured both. We’ve recovered human remains.”

Arthur’s hand tightened round the phone. “Both sites?”

“Both. Formal identification is pending, but the locations match what Kot told you.”

“Have the families been told?”

“Not yet. The liaison officers are ready. I wanted to speak to you first, because you were in that room, and because they’ve been waiting nearly four years.”

Arthur was silent. Then he said he’d tell them.

“Arthur, the family liaison officers—”

“Can come with me. They should. But I’d like to be the one who says it.”

There was a long pause at the other end. “With the liaison officer in the room. And you stop if she tells you to.”

“Yes.”

He ended the call and stood by the bed. Then Si-Jie stirred and opened her eyes. “What’s happened?”

He sat down beside her. “They’ve found them.”

She blinked. “Who?”

“The two women.”
