She pushed herself up, and for a moment she didn’t speak. Then she reached for his hand. “Both?”

He nodded. “Nothing’s formally identified yet. But the search teams found remains in both places he gave us.”

She looked down. “After all this time.”

He looked at their hands. “Yes. Someone has to tell their families.”

She understood at once. “And you’re going. Then I’m coming with you.”

“Si-Jie. You don’t have to.”

She touched his cheek. “I know I don’t. You went into that room because you wanted answers. Now there are people who have to hear them.”

He looked at her, and nodded.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first place was a field beyond the outer housing estates. There was nothing remarkable about it: rough grass, uneven ground, a narrow road along one side, a few trees by the boundary. The morning was cold and the grass was wet. Police vehicles were parked by the gate, and the search area was taped off.

Si-Jie stayed in the car while Arthur spoke to the officer in charge. She could see people moving in the distance in white suits, and a forensic team working by the first marked spot. She didn’t ask to see. She didn’t need to.

When Arthur came back his face had changed. She looked past him at the field.

“Was she here all this time?”

He followed her eyes. “According to what he said, yes.”

There was no great discovery to see, no revelation: only a field, a search team, and the remains of a woman whose family had been looking for her since 2022. He’d been given a name, a photograph and an address, and he’d been told the family had never stopped hoping.

“Are you ready?” said Si-Jie.

“No.”

“Neither am I.”

He opened the passenger door for her, and they left the field together.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first family lived in an older block. There were shoes outside the door, a small potted plant beside it and a delivery box against the wall. Ordinary things. The liaison officer was waiting on the landing, a quiet woman who’d sat in that flat more times in four years than she could count, and who nodded to Arthur and looked at Si-Jie and asked nothing. Arthur stood in front of the door with the folder in his hand.

“Do you want me to wait outside?” said Si-Jie.

He shook his head. She held out her hand, and he took it, and the liaison officer knocked.

A woman in her late fifties opened the door, in a pale cardigan and house slippers, with her hair tied back. She saw the liaison officer first, and then Arthur, and then Si-Jie.

“Mrs Fung? My name is Arthur Chen. I worked on the investigation into your daughter’s disappearance.”

Her face changed. She opened the door wider. “Have you found something?”

He didn’t answer too quickly. “May we come in?”

She stepped aside. The living room was small and tidy, and there was a photograph on the shelf: a young woman smiling at the camera, twenty-two years old, the face that had been on posters and in newspapers and on the wall in his study.

Mrs Fung followed his eyes. “That’s my daughter.”

“I know.”

She sat down, and Arthur sat opposite her, and Si-Jie beside him, and the liaison officer took the chair by the door. He put the folder on his knees.

“Mrs Fung, a search team has found human remains at a place outside the city. The place matches information given by a man who’s now in custody. We have reason to believe the remains may be your daughter’s. Formal identification hasn’t been completed yet.”

She stared at him, as though she’d heard every word and couldn’t put them in order. “May be? You’re saying you’ve found her?”

“We’ve found remains at that place. We can’t confirm who it is until the forensic work is finished.”

She looked at the photograph, and back at him. “Is she dead?”

His fingers tightened on the folder. He didn’t look away. “We believe she was killed.”

The room went silent. Mrs Fung put a hand over her mouth, and a sound came out of her: not a scream, not quite a sob, something smaller, something that seemed to have been held in for years.

“No. She was supposed to come home.”

Si-Jie reached for her hand.

Mrs Fung looked at her. “She was supposed to come home.”

Si-Jie held her fingers. “I know.”

The woman began to cry. Arthur sat opposite her and didn’t try to fill the silence. He didn’t offer an explanation to make it easier. He didn’t tell her it would be all right. After a long time she looked up.

“Did he tell you?”

“Yes.”

“What he did?”

“Yes.”

“Did he say her name?”

“He did.”

She bowed her head, and for a long time she cried without speaking. Si-Jie stayed beside her. Arthur stayed in his chair. When at last Mrs Fung looked up again, she asked whether her daughter had suffered.

Arthur paused. He knew what Kot had said. He also knew what he could responsibly say before the forensic findings were in. “We’re still establishing what happened. I don’t want to tell you anything I can’t verify.”

She nodded slowly. It wasn’t the answer she wanted, but it was honest. “Thank you for coming.”

Arthur stood. “I’m sorry we couldn’t bring you this sooner.”

“At least now someone’s told me where to look.”

He bowed his head. Si-Jie held her hand a little longer before she let go. At the door Mrs Fung stopped them and asked whether they’d tell her when they knew for certain.

“Yes. Your liaison officer will contact you directly, and I’ll make sure you hear,” said Arthur.

She nodded, and closed the door. Arthur stood on the landing still holding Si-Jie’s hand.

✦ ✦ ✦

They sat in the car without starting the engine. Si-Jie looked up at the building.

“She kept the photograph there. She must have looked at it every day, and she didn’t know where her daughter was. She had to keep living without knowing whether to grieve.”

Arthur rested both hands on the steering wheel. “Yes.”

She turned to him. “How do you do this? Tell someone the person they’ve been waiting for isn’t coming home?”

He was quiet. “I don’t know.”

She put her hand over his. “You’re doing it anyway.”

He looked at their hands. “Someone has to.”

She leaned over and kissed his cheek, and he closed his eyes, and then started the engine.

✦ ✦ ✦

The second place was on a hillside north of the city. The road narrowed as they climbed. There were trees along the slope and the ground was uneven, and from a distance it looked peaceful. The search team had the area secured. This time the information was more specific: Kot had described a spot beyond a line of trees, near a patch of bare earth, and the dogs had marked it. The remains had been recovered, and the forensic team was documenting the site.

Arthur asked where the evidence stood, and whether the place matched Kot’s statement.

“Broadly. There are details we’ll need to check,” said the officer in charge.

“Keep the two recoveries separate in the documentation until identification’s complete.”

“Already done.”

“Good.”

Si-Jie stood a little way off and watched the trees move in the wind. She thought about the second woman: twenty-four, finishing a degree in the evenings and working in a shop, someone who’d probably complained about her assignments and bought groceries and sent messages without ever imagining they’d become part of an investigation. Someone whose family had spent years asking where she was.

Arthur came back to her. “Ready?”

“Yes.”

He held out his hand, and she took it, and they left the hillside.

✦ ✦ ✦

The second family’s flat was quieter. A man in his early sixties opened the door. He looked tired. A television was playing in the room behind him. The liaison officer said his name, and Arthur said his own, and the man’s face changed at once.

“Is it about my daughter?”

“May we speak to you?”

He stepped back. There was a photograph on the television cabinet: a young woman with shoulder-length hair, smiling at someone outside the frame. The father didn’t sit down. He stood with his hand on the back of a chair.

“Tell me.”

“We’ve found human remains at a place on a hillside. It matches information given by a man in custody in connection with your daughter’s disappearance,” said Arthur.

The man stared at him. “Is it her?”

“Formal identification is still pending.”

“But you think it is.”

“Yes.”

His grip tightened on the chair. “How long has she been there?”

Arthur didn’t understand at first, and then he did, and answered carefully. “From what we’ve been told, it may be since 2022. The forensic team is establishing the timeline.”

The man sat down then, and looked at the photograph. “She was twenty-four. She was going to finish her degree. She worked in a shop in the evenings. She used to complain about the customers.”

His voice broke on the last word, and he waited until it would hold again.

“She complained about everything. She used to ring me when she missed the last bus, and I’d tell her to get a taxi, and she’d say it was too expensive. She should have rung me.”

He laughed once, a small, broken sound, and pressed his palms against his eyes. Arthur sat and didn’t speak.

The man lowered his hands. “Did she ring anyone?”

Arthur didn’t pretend to know. “We’re still putting together her last movements.”

The man nodded. Then he asked whether the man in custody had killed her.

Arthur met his eyes. “Yes. He’s admitted killing both women. What he’s said is being investigated and checked.”

For a long time the father didn’t move. Then he reached for the frame and held it in both hands, and looked at it. “She was a good girl. Stubborn. She never took an umbrella when I told her to. She hated being told what to do. She was supposed to come home.”

Arthur lowered his eyes. “I’m sorry.”

The man nodded once. He didn’t cry straight away. He sat holding the photograph. After a while he asked whether they’d find out everything.

“The investigation will go on. We’ll establish what can be established, and make sure the evidence is properly examined,” said Arthur.

The man looked at him. “Don’t let him lie.”

“Nothing he says will be treated as fact until it’s been checked.”

“Good.”

When they stood to go, he walked them to the door.

“Thank you for coming yourself.”

Arthur bowed his head. “I thought you should hear it directly.”

The father looked at Si-Jie. “Thank you for coming with him.”

She nodded. “I’m sorry.”

He closed the door gently.

✦ ✦ ✦

At the car Arthur stood by the driver’s door without opening it. Si-Jie came round in front of him. His face was controlled, but his eyes were far away.

“Look at me. You told them. Both families. You didn’t make them hear it on the phone, or from a stranger.”

He looked down. “They deserved to hear it properly.”

She took his hand. His fingers were cold. “Did you know what to say?”

“No.”

“Did you say it anyway?”

“Yes.”

“Then you did what you could.”

He looked at the road. “I told a mother her daughter wasn’t coming home. I told a father his daughter had been killed. I watched them look at photographs they’ve kept for four years, waiting.”

She held his hand tighter. He seemed to be looking for a sentence that could hold it, and there wasn’t one. She lifted his hand and pressed it against her cheek.

“You don’t have to make this smaller. You don’t have to make it bearable for me. You can just be sad.”

His jaw tightened. Then he bent his head until his forehead rested on hers, and for a while they stood beside the car holding each other and saying nothing.

✦ ✦ ✦

They drove back towards the city with the radio off. Messages came in from the team. The remains were being processed. The families would be updated through their liaison officers. Both sites would stay secured. There was still identification to do, and forensic examination, and every one of Kot’s statements to check, and the women’s last days to reconstruct. The investigation wasn’t over. But two families knew now where their daughters had been found.

Si-Jie looked out of the window. “Do you remember their names?”

He glanced at her. “Yes.”

She waited, and he said them: not as case numbers, not as entries on a board, but as their names. Si-Jie said them after him.

“Say them again.”

He did.

She nodded. “I don’t want them to become the two women from the case.”

“They won’t. I’ll remember.”

She put her hand over his on the gear stick. “Good.”

✦ ✦ ✦

That night Arthur took the notebook down from the shelf, the one that had once held his observations of her, the one she’d read and corrected and filled with her own handwriting. He sat at the dining table and opened it at a blank page, and for a long time he didn’t write anything. Si-Jie watched him from the sofa. Then he wrote two names at the top of the page, and under them a few lines.

Their families have been informed. The remains were found at two separate sites on 14 March 2026. Formal identification and forensic examination are pending.

He stopped there. He didn’t write how the mother had held the photograph, or how the father had remembered the last bus. He didn’t turn their grief into something to keep. He closed the notebook, and Si-Jie came and asked if he’d finished.

“For tonight.”

He let her read it. She touched the two names. “They should have been able to come home.”

“Yes.”

She took his hand and led him to the sofa, and leaned against him, careful of his shoulder. For a while they watched the lights across the street. Then he told her the first mother had asked whether her daughter suffered, and what he’d said.

“That was right.”

“I wish I could have told her something else.”

“I know you do.”

He looked at the window. “The father remembered her ringing him about the bus.”

Si-Jie rested her cheek on his chest. “He loved her. They both did.”

He put his arm round her. The room was quiet: no recording, no questions, nobody asking for another statement. Only the two of them, sitting together in the aftermath of something that couldn’t be undone.

Near midnight, when she was almost asleep, he said her name and thanked her for coming with him.

She opened her eyes. “You held my hand at the first door. And at the second. So I’ll keep doing it.”

His face softened, and he pressed a kiss into her hair.

She tucked herself closer. “Tomorrow we’re having breakfast. You’ll eat properly. And no working before coffee.”

He considered that. “All right.”

She closed her eyes again. He stayed awake a long time, thinking about the field and the hillside and the two photographs, the mother who’d kept waiting and the father who remembered a missed bus, and the names on the page. He’d spent four hours listening to Kot describe the women, and two hours telling their families what had happened to them, and neither had felt like enough. But the women had names, and their families had been told, and tomorrow the investigation would go on.

He bent his head and kissed Si-Jie’s hair. Then he said the two names once more, under his breath: not to remember what Kot had done, but to remember who had been lost.

chapters.title: After
chapters.desc: He stops talking for three days. She reads him both notebooks aloud, from the first page. He tells her what he wants: her, in daylight.
chapters.epigraph: “I’m here because I want to be.”
chapters.content:
The liaison officer rang on the last Thursday in March. Both identifications had been confirmed. Arthur listened, thanked her, put the phone down on the kitchen counter, and after that he didn’t talk. Not properly. He answered when he had to. He said yes when Si-Jie asked if he wanted tea, and no when she asked if his shoulder hurt, and thank you when she put food in front of him. But he didn’t start a conversation. He didn’t ask about her day. He didn’t make dry remarks about the television or the neighbours, or tell her she’d left her phone on the counter again.

On Friday it was the same. On Friday evening she found him at the dining table with the notebook closed in front of him, and she knew what he was thinking about: the two names, the field, the hillside, the families. She pulled out the chair beside him.

“Can I sit?”

He nodded. She rested her head on his shoulder, and for a while neither of them spoke. Then she said she was going to read something to him tomorrow.

He looked down at her. “What?”

“Our notebook. From the first page.”

His eyes went to the black cover. “Si-Jie.”

“From the first page.”

He didn’t object, and she took that as an answer.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Saturday morning she found him in the kitchen, just after eight, looking at the kettle. It had already boiled.

“You’re staring at the kettle.”

“I’m waiting for it.”

“It’s boiled.”

He looked at it, and switched it off.

She leaned against the counter. “Did you sleep?”

“Some. Four hours.”

“That’s not enough.”

“It’s sufficient.”

“For what? Remaining technically alive?”

The corner of his mouth moved: the nearest thing to a smile she’d seen in two days.

She came closer and straightened the collar of his shirt. “You’re allowed to be unhappy.”

“I’m not unhappy.”

“Then what are you?”

He didn’t answer. She waited, and he looked away.

She nodded slowly. “All right.”

She didn’t push. She made breakfast, and told him about a video Si-Wei had put in the chat. He listened, and didn’t say much.

In the afternoon she brought both notebooks to the sofa. He was at the other end with a report he’d been asked to look over: he’d been taken off Kot’s interviews, but the team still had to assess what he’d got out of him, and every place and statement was being checked. He put the report down when she sat.

“Ready?”

He looked at the first page. “No.”

She smiled. “Good. Neither am I.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The first page had her name at the top in capitals, and a date.

YEN SI-JIE
16 October 2024

“You wrote my name like a file,” said Si-Jie.

“It was a file. On the first day.”

She read on, aloud. “Second row, beside the girl with the notebook. Forty questions. I answered thirty-nine. Maintained eye contact throughout. Appeared amused by my answers.”

She looked up at him, and back at the page.

“I was amused. You were very serious.”

“I was answering questions.”

“Followed me to the staff car park at dusk. Her sisters held her bag. Question forty: whether she could kiss me. Asked before she touched me.”

Her voice softened. Then she read the next line and burst out laughing.

“Subject appeared surprised when I kissed her back. Subject, Arthur.”

“It was accurate. You were surprised.”

She touched the line with one finger. “I was delighted. That was your first page. Before I knew you liked me. Before you knew what to do with me.”

He glanced at her. “I still don’t always know.”

“That’s all right,” said Si-Jie, and turned the page.

She read slowly. Not every line was romantic. Some were dates and times and things she’d left behind, her coffee order, how she moved her hands when she explained something. Some she’d answered in the margins in April.

She sings in the shower. Not well.
Beautifully. Strike this.
Disputed.

“You can’t dispute your own girlfriend,” said Si-Jie.

“You wrote that at the time.”

“And I was right at the time,” said Si-Jie, and turned another page.

Arthur waited.

“Twenty-third of November. Accepted the apology after approximately eleven minutes. It was ten.”

“I timed it.”

“From when? You can’t have started timing until you’d finished apologising, and you apologised for ages.”

He opened his mouth, and shut it again, and she laughed, and kept reading.

17 January. Home at 3.08. She was asleep on the sofa. Had waited although I told her not to.
Did not ask about the case. Held me without speaking.
She does not need me to explain everything.
I should still tell her when I will be late.

Her voice went quieter. She looked at him. He was staring at the page.

“Do you remember that night?”

“Yes. The woman on the stairs.”

“You didn’t tell me what had happened.”

“You didn’t ask.”

“I didn’t want you to have to explain.”

He nodded.

She put her hand on his. “Keep listening.”

She came to Valentine’s Day and the tie, and he looked so pleased with himself that she had to stop reading. Then the entries got harder. The last page of the old notebook was from the ninth of March, and in the margin beside it, in her own writing from April, was the question she’d asked him out loud the night she found it.

Am I a case?

Under it, in his handwriting, smaller:

No. I did not know where the distinction began. I do now.

She read both aloud. His face tightened. She didn’t look away from the page.

“The night I left, you said you didn’t know. Partner or experiment. That was the worst thing you ever said to me.”

“I know it was.”

“I hated that answer.”

“So did I.”

She looked at him. “But I came back. Not because you’d earned it. Because I wanted to.”

He looked at her, and lowered his eyes. “I’m glad you did.”

She opened the second notebook. “So am I.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The second notebook was the one he’d bought the night she left. He’d shown her the entries when she came back, and she knew what was in them. But she’d never read them aloud, from beginning to end.

13 March.
She left at 1.56. Took the original notebook.
Refused my offer to drive her home.
Reached her building safely. I followed her taxi.
Stopped outside. Did not go to her door.
I wanted her to ask me to come upstairs.

She stopped, and looked at him. “You wanted me to ask you up.”

“Yes.”

“Why didn’t you ring the bell?”

“Because you’d asked for space. Ringing would have been asking you to comfort me.”

She nodded, and read on. The toothbrush in the bathroom and the mug by the sink, which he hadn’t moved. The hair tie under the sofa, which he’d put in her drawer. The sixteenth, when he woke early and reached for the empty side of the bed, and wrote no further comment, and then, underneath, wrote that he missed her. The nineteenth, when Si-Wei asked if he’d eaten and called his answer stupid. The twenty-second, when he looked at a photograph of a strawberry for no reason he could defend.

“You looked at a picture of a strawberry,” said Si-Jie, and her eyes had gone wet.

“It was the last photograph you sent me.”

“That’s very stupid.”

“Yes.”

She leaned over and kissed his cheek, and kept reading. The entries were short. None of them asked her to come back. None of them blamed her for going. They recorded the absence of ordinary things. At the last page she read the line that a stranger had quoted back to her in green ink, and she read it in her own voice, so that it was hers again.

27 March. She came back at 7.46. Kissed me before I could speak. Said she missed me. We talked. She set boundaries. I agreed to them. She stayed for dinner. She is asleep in my bed.

She closed the notebook and rested her head on his chest. “You were lonely.”

His hand moved slowly over her hair. “Yes.”

“You could have told me.”

“I didn’t know how.”

She lifted her head. “Do you now?”

“I’m learning.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On Sunday morning, three days since he’d last said more than he had to, the notebooks were on the coffee table and he was sitting beside her with his hand on her knee. He’d listened to every page.

“Do you want to tell me what happened?”

He looked at their hands. “The families. The mother kept the photograph on a shelf. The father remembered his daughter ringing about the last bus. I keep thinking about them waiting four years. Waking up every morning not knowing whether she was alive.”

His voice was steady, but quieter than usual. She didn’t interrupt.

“And then I think about what Kot said. The things he remembered. How he talked about them. I listened to him for four hours. I asked questions. I wanted the information. I thought if I understood the sequence and the places and the details, I could make something useful out of it.”

He looked at her.

“Then I went to those flats, and I understood that information wasn’t what those families had been waiting for.”

She held his hand. “They were waiting for their daughters.”

His jaw tightened. “I couldn’t give them that. I could only tell them where they were.”

“That’s still something.”

“It doesn’t feel like enough.”

“It isn’t enough. Nothing could be. But you didn’t pretend it was. You told them the truth. And you remembered their names.”

He looked down. “Yes.”

She brushed her thumb over his knuckles. “You’re allowed to be sad about people you never knew.”

“Even if I only worked on the case?”

“Most of all then. You heard what happened to them. You saw their families.”

He bowed his head. She moved closer and put her arms round him, and this time he didn’t only let himself be held. He held her back.

They stayed like that a long time. Eventually she leaned away far enough to see his face. “Can I ask you something? What do you want? Not what’s reasonable. What do you want, Arthur?”

He looked at her hand on his chest. Then he said, “You.”

She blinked.

“I want you here. In the kitchen when I’m making coffee. Your things on the counter. I want you to interrupt me when I’m reading. I want you to tell me when you’re upset instead of deciding to make it easy for me. I want you to ask me questions even when I don’t know how to answer them. I want to come home and find you here, and when you’re not, I want to be able to tell you I miss you. I don’t want to spend three days making you guess whether I’m still with you.”

She looked at him. “Then don’t.”

“I’ll try.”

“Don’t promise you’ll never be quiet. Sometimes you need quiet. Promise you’ll tell me when you need it. And tell me when you’re having a hard time, even if you can’t explain it.”

“I will.”

He took her hand, and held it a moment before he spoke.

“I want you, Si-Jie. Not because I need someone to make the flat less empty. Not because I need looking after. I want you because my life is better when I share it with you.”

She looked at him, and then leaned in and kissed him. He kissed her back without hesitating, and when she drew away he followed her a little.

She smiled. “Again?”

“Yes.”

She kissed him again, and this time he was the one who kept her close.

✦ ✦ ✦

The afternoon sun had moved across the floor. The curtains were open. The notebooks lay on the coffee table, the old one soft at the corners, both of them full of two kinds of handwriting. Si-Jie stood in front of him. He was looking at her: not at the healed line under her jaw where the plaster had finally come off, but at her.

She reached for the buttons of his shirt, and he caught her hand gently. “Are you sure? You’re not doing this because you think I need it? Or to make me feel better?”

She lifted his hand to her cheek. “No. I want you too.”

Something in his face loosened, and he kissed her: slowly, with no hurry in it and no attempt to outrun the last three days, like a man who’d finally let himself stay in a moment instead of measuring how long it might last. She took his hand and drew him down the hall, and he followed, and stopped once in the bedroom doorway to make sure she was comfortable.

The daylight stayed in the room. He kissed her temple, her cheek, the corner of her mouth, and looked at her.

“Tell me what you want.”

“You.”

“More specifically?”

She laughed. “You’re doing it again.”

“I’m asking.”

She touched his mouth. “I want you to stop thinking so much.”

“I’ll try.”

She kissed him, and he let himself be kissed. She finished the buttons he’d stopped her undoing, and he pulled her jumper over her head, and in the daylight there was nowhere for either of them to hide, and for once neither of them wanted to. He laid her back on the bed and took his time with her, attentive without turning anything into a problem to solve. He kissed down her body. He found the healed line under her jaw and kissed that too, once, and then moved on, and she loved him for moving on.

When his mouth reached between her thighs she stopped thinking about anything at all. He was patient. He listened to every sound she made and answered it, and when she came it was with both hands in his hair and her heels pressed into the bed, and he stayed with her until the last of it had gone through her.

Then she pulled him up and over her, and guided him in, and they both went still at the same moment, and she laughed at that, breathless, and he smiled down at her properly for the first time in days. When she said his name he answered with hers. She asked for it again, and he said it again, with something nearly unguarded in it, and she pulled him closer and told him she wanted to know what he wanted too.

He rested his forehead on hers. “I want to stay here with you.”

“Then stay.”

The afternoon went by without either of them looking at a clock: no investigation, no reports, nothing Kot had said. Only the warm room, and Arthur finally letting himself want something without working out the risks.

When they were quiet again he held her, and she lay with her cheek on his chest. “Are you happy?”

“Yes. Very.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Towards evening he got up for water, and came back with a glass for her and the old notebook from the living room, and sat on the edge of the mattress with a pen.

“Are you writing?”

“Yes.”

She shifted closer, and he turned the page so she could read it as he wrote.

Sunday, 29 March 2026.
I was quiet for three days. I did not know how to speak about the two women or their families, or what I heard in the interview, or what it meant to see their parents waiting for answers.
She read the notebook aloud from the first page. I listened.
She reminded me that there were days before the case, and that there will be days after it.
She asked what I wanted. I told her. I want her.

Si-Jie smiled. “That’s all?”

“Is it insufficient?”

She took the pen out of his hand and wrote underneath, in blue.

He said it without making me ask twice.
I want him too.

He read it. “That isn’t a correction.”

“No.”

“A clarification?”

She kissed his cheek. “An answer.”

He closed the notebook. There was nothing else he needed to write that night.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the evening Si-Wei rang on video, and Si-Jie answered on the sofa with Arthur beside her.

“You’re alive! You’ve been suspiciously quiet.”

“I’ve been busy.”

Si-Wei narrowed her eyes at the screen. “Doing what?”

Si-Jie looked at Arthur, and he raised an eyebrow, and she told her sister it was none of her business. Si-Wei said that was an extremely unconvincing answer. Then the screen split, and Si-Yuan was there too, with a towel round her hair.

“What’s happening?”

“Si-Jie’s being suspicious,” said Si-Wei.

Si-Yuan looked at her sister properly. “Are you all right?”

Si-Jie smiled. “I’m all right.”

Si-Yuan studied her face, and then her eyes moved to Arthur. “And him?”

Arthur leaned a little towards the phone. “I’m fine.”

Si-Wei snorted. “That’s what he says when he’s absolutely not fine.”

“Thank you for your assessment,” said Arthur.

“You’re welcome.”

Si-Jie laughed, and for the first time in three days Arthur laughed with her. It was a quiet sound, but it was real.

Si-Yuan smiled. “There he is.”

After the call he stayed beside her. The flat wasn’t silent any more. Si-Jie’s phone buzzed with another message from Si-Wei, and Arthur looked at the screen.

“Forty messages tomorrow?”

“At least.”

“I’ll answer them at nine.”

“In order?”

“Of course.”

She leaned against him. “You’re back.”

He kissed her hair. “I’m here.”

This time he didn’t leave the rest of the sentence unsaid.

“I’m here because I want to be.”

chapters.title: Suspended
chapters.desc: Suspended for three months. He puts the kitchen scale in a cupboard and learns her mother’s braised beef by text, with no quantities.
chapters.content:
The letter came on the first Tuesday in April. Arthur read it once, and then again, more slowly, though there was nothing complicated about the wording. After an internal review of the unauthorised interview on 11 March, his failure to withdraw when instructed and his personal involvement in the investigation, he was suspended from operational duties for three months, with immediate effect. He wasn’t to access task force systems, attend investigative briefings, contact witnesses or suspects in a professional capacity, or use departmental resources. A further review would decide whether anything more was needed.

He put it on the dining table. Si-Jie was hulling strawberries, and looked up. “What’s that?”

“My suspension notice. Three months. From today.”

The knife stopped. She wiped her hands and came over and asked if she could read it, and he gave it to her. She read it carefully, and her face grew more and more serious, and when she’d finished she looked at him.

“How do you feel?”

“I expected disciplinary action.”

“That isn’t what I asked.”

He looked at the letter. “I don’t particularly mind being away from the task force. I was taken off the interviews. My conduct was reviewed. The decision fits the breach.”

“You’re not angry?”

“No.”

“Disappointed?”

He thought about it. “Possibly. In myself.”

She folded the letter and put it back on the table. “Do you want to talk about it?”

“Not particularly.”

“All right.”

She went back to the strawberries. He watched her, and then asked whether she was disappointed in him.

Si-Jie looked up. “No. I’m not going to tell you what you did was acceptable. You know it wasn’t. You knew it when you walked into that room. And there are consequences, and you have to accept them.”

“I am.”

She put a strawberry in his mouth. “But I’m not disappointed that you’re my boyfriend. Those are two different things.”

He ate the strawberry. “Understood.”

A little later he said, to nobody in particular, that three months was ninety-one days.

“Arthur.”

“Exactly ninety-one.”

She laughed. He looked at the letter again. For the first time in his working life there were three months in his diary with nothing in them, and he had no intention of filling them with anything. Not yet.

✦ ✦ ✦

By Wednesday the flat had a new routine. Arthur woke at half past six. He showered. He made coffee. He looked at the time. Then he stood in the kitchen with nothing to do. Si-Jie found him there a little after seven, looking at the fridge.

“What are you doing?”

“Nothing.”

She came closer. “That’s unusual. How does it feel?”

“Unproductive.”

She laughed. “You’re suspended, not dead.”

“I understand the distinction.”

She opened the fridge. “Do you want to do something today? Go for a walk. Read. Watch a film.”

He was quiet. Then he said he’d like to cook something.

“You cook every day.”

He looked at the scale on the counter, where it had lived since the day he moved in. “I cook four things. Rice, eggs, fish and porridge. All of them by weight. I’d like to learn something I can’t weigh.”

She turned round slowly. “Such as?”

“Your mother’s braised beef.”

Si-Jie stared at him, and then she started to laugh, and couldn’t stop. “Arthur. Mama doesn’t measure anything. She’s never measured anything in her life.”

“Then I’ll ask her.”

“She’ll tell you to look at it.”

“Then I’ll look at it.”

She put her arms round his neck and kissed him. “This is the most romantic thing you’ve ever said to me.”

“It’s a recipe.”

“It’s my mother’s recipe,” said Si-Jie, and got out her phone.

✦ ✦ ✦

He started with rice, because rice he understood. He put a bowl on the scale, pressed the button and poured. One hundred grams. One hundred and twenty. One hundred and forty. One hundred and fifty-one. He stopped, picked out a single grain, and the scale said one hundred and fifty.

Si-Jie, on the counter with her phone, made a noise into her hand.

He looked at her. “What?”

“You’ve made rice two hundred times.”

“Two hundred and twelve.”

“And you still take the grain out.”

“It was over.”

She laughed so much she had to put the phone down. He rinsed the rice until the water ran clear, measured the water by weight, put the pot in the cooker and turned to the beef, which was the part he didn’t understand at all. Si-Jie picked up her phone again and read the messages aloud as they came.

Si-Jie: Mama. Arthur wants to make your braised beef.

Mama (Packs Fruit): Why?

Si-Jie: He’s suspended from work for three months.

Mama (Packs Fruit): Good. He works too much.

Mama (Packs Fruit): Beef shin. Not the expensive one. The butcher will know.

Si-Jie: How much?

Mama (Packs Fruit): Enough for two and some for tomorrow.

Si-Jie: He wants grams.

Mama (Packs Fruit): Tell him to look at it.

Arthur looked at the beef on the board, which he’d already weighed, and said nothing.

Mama (Packs Fruit): Soy sauce, some. Dark soy, a little, for the colour. Rock sugar, a little more than you think. Star anise, two or three. Ginger. Spring onion. Shaoxing wine. Cook it slowly until it smells right.

Si-Jie: He wants to know what right smells like.

Mama (Packs Fruit): Like my kitchen.

Mama (Packs Fruit): Is he eating properly? Send a picture.

Arthur stood in front of the hob for some time. Then he picked up the scale, opened the cupboard above the fridge, and put it inside, and shut the door.

Si-Jie watched him. “Are you all right?”

“No. Pass me the soy sauce.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The beef he’d weighed turned out to be the wrong cut, so they walked to the market for shin. The police car had gone from outside his building the week after Kot was charged, and the officers who changed at eight and eight had waved goodbye to Si-Jie from the window as they drove off. It was the first time in three months that Arthur had walked down a street with her and not been a few steps behind. He kept noticing it. He walked on the kerb side without thinking, and she let him, and at the crossing she took his hand and didn’t let go.

The butcher knew. Si-Jie said her mother had said he would, and the butcher, who had never met her mother, nodded as if that settled it and wrapped up a piece of shin without being told how much.

“How much is that?” said Arthur.

“Enough for two and some for tomorrow,” said the butcher.

Si-Jie had to go and stand outside.

✦ ✦ ✦

The beef took most of the afternoon. He browned it in batches, which he’d read about, and burnt the first batch slightly, which he hadn’t planned. He poured in some soy sauce, and then looked at it, and then poured in a little more. He broke the rock sugar with the back of a spoon and put in what he thought was a little more than he thought, which took him a while to work out. He counted the star anise out of the jar and put in three, and then took one out, and then put it back. Every ten minutes he lifted the lid and smelled it. Si-Jie sat on the counter and watched him do it, and didn’t say anything, because she was enjoying herself far too much.

“Does it smell right?” she said, at about four.

“I don’t know what right smells like.”

“Like her kitchen.”

“I’ve been in her kitchen once.”

“Then remember it.”

He was quiet. He remembered it: a house in Taipei with too much furniture, a fruit knife, her father asking him what his own tell was, her mother saying keep him when she thought he couldn’t hear. He lifted the lid again. “Closer.”

At six he put the rice and the beef on the table, two bowls, two pairs of chopsticks, and a plate of strawberries because he didn’t know what else to put beside it. Si-Jie sat down, and picked up her chopsticks, and then stopped.

“Wait.”

She took out her phone and held it up. He looked at the camera with the expression he used for official photographs.

“Smile.”

“I am.”

“You’re not.”

“This is my face.”

She took the picture anyway, and sent it to her mother. Then she tasted the beef, and looked at him, and he waited.

“Well?”

She took another mouthful. “It’s good.”

He blinked. “Good?”

“Very good. It’s a little too sweet, and the sauce is too thin, and you’ll want to cook it longer next time. But it tastes like home.”

He looked down at his bowl. For a moment he looked almost embarrassed. Then he ate. Her phone buzzed on the table.

Mama (Packs Fruit): He looks thin. Feed him.

Mama (Packs Fruit): The colour is good. Next time less sugar.

Si-Jie turned the screen towards him, and he read it twice, and something in his face eased that hadn’t eased in a month.

✦ ✦ ✦

He washed up. She tried to help, and he told her he’d started the job and would finish it, so she sat on the counter again and watched.

“You could use these three months to learn to cook properly. Breakfast, lunch and dinner.”

He rinsed a plate. “Three meals a day is a substantial commitment.”

“You’ll have to eat anyway.”

“You’re very persuasive.”

She slid off the counter and put her arms round him from behind. He dried his hands and turned round and held her.

“Thank you,” said Arthur.

She looked up. “What for?”

“For staying.”

She frowned a little. “I’m not going anywhere.”

“I know. I wanted to say it.”

Her face softened, and she kissed him. When she drew back she touched his cheek. “You’re allowed to have a life outside work, Arthur.”

“I’m aware of that.”

“Are you?”

He considered the question. “Not particularly.”

She smiled. “Then we’ll practise.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At half past four on Thursday, Eugene Chak rang. Arthur answered at the dining table.

“Chen.”

“How’s retirement?”

“I’m suspended.”

“Three months. That’s retirement with paperwork.”

Arthur waited.

“What are you doing?”

“Braising beef.”

There was a longer pause.

“Have you checked the case?” said Eugene.

“No. I’m not permitted to access the systems or take part in the investigation.”

Eugene was quiet. “Good. The review’s still going. Kot’s statements are being checked. Not all the forensic results are back. We’re handling it.”

“I’m not worried.”

“No. Are you all right?”

Arthur looked at the kitchen. Si-Jie was putting strawberries into a box and humming. “Yes.”

“Good. Stay that way,” said Eugene, and rang off.

Si-Jie looked over. “Eugene?”

“Yes. He wanted to know what I was doing.”

“What did you tell him?”

“Braising beef.”

She smiled. “What did he say?”

“Nothing, for some time.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On Sunday he cooked again, and this time she cooked with him. He weighed the rice: one hundred and fifty grams, no grains removed, because he poured more carefully. He didn’t weigh anything else. His knife work was precise and slow.

“You’re taking a long time.”

“I don’t want to cut myself.”

She came and stood beside him. “Reasonable. Can I help?”

He looked at her. “Yes.”

She reached for the board, and he moved the knife away from her hand first, and she smiled. “You’re very careful.”

“With knives, yes.”

They made rice and greens and the beef again, from the beginning. Si-Jie seasoned it. He asked how much salt she’d used, and she refused to tell him, and he asked why.

“Because cooking isn’t a laboratory.”

“That’s an imprecise explanation.”

“You’re hopeless.”

“Possibly.”

When they sat down, the beef was slightly overdone, the greens were good and the rice was perfect. Si-Jie tasted everything, and looked at him. “You’re learning. Do you like cooking?”

He considered it. “I like that you’re here.”

“That’s not the same thing.”

“No. But it’s a sufficient reason to carry on.”

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening he opened his diary. Ninety-one days, less five. He hadn’t deleted his task force commitments. They were still there, marked suspended, with nothing attached to them. Si-Jie sat down beside him.

“Planning?”

“No.”

She put her head on his shoulder. “Good. You don’t have to turn your suspension into a project.”

He closed the diary. She said they could go out tomorrow, somewhere with good food, as a celebration, because he’d cooked twice. He said that seemed unrelated. She said the day after that he could cook again, and he pointed out that she was making a schedule, and she laughed and said fine, no schedule.

He took her hand. “One thing. Tomorrow I’d like to make breakfast.”

“What are you making?”

“Rice.”

She stared at him. “Rice for breakfast?”

“Yes.”

“Arthur.”

“It’s the thing I’m best at.”

She laughed until she had to lean against him, and he watched her, almost amused, and kissed her hair.

✦ ✦ ✦

At nine, Si-Jie’s phone held forty-two messages from her sisters, Eliana and a friend from her course. Arthur was on the sofa with a book, and didn’t reach for it.

She looked over. “You’re not answering my messages.”

“It’s nine.”

“You’re not answering them?”

“You’re sitting beside me.”

She stared at him, and then smiled. “Are you replacing the nine o’clock rule?”

He closed the book. “No. I’m making an exception. I’d rather spend this hour with you.”

Her smile softened. “That’s a good reason.”

He kissed her, and she settled against him with her head on his chest. After a while she asked whether he missed work.

He thought about it. “Some of it. The team. The work itself. Having a reason to get up every morning.”

“Do you miss being a profiler?”

He looked at the ceiling. “I don’t know.”

She lifted her head. “That’s all right.”

He touched her cheek. “I don’t miss it enough to wish I were anywhere else.”

“Good,” said Si-Jie.

The suspension would last three months. There would be reviews and reports, and whatever consequences were still to come, and at the end of it he’d go back to a profession his own decisions had made complicated. He didn’t pretend otherwise. But for the first time in years he had mornings with nothing waiting for him. And he’d learned two things that week: that rice took exactly one hundred and fifty grams, and that her mother’s braised beef took as long as it took. He considered that a reasonable beginning.
